Now to prove that in the present place Moab is to be understood of the pride of the philosophers, of whom it is said: I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the understanding of the understanding I will reject, a few examples from the prophet must be unfolded: Amos says: Thus says the Lord: For three impieties of Moab and for four I will not turn away from him, because he burned the bones of the king of Edom to ashes — for truly, whatever there is in the world of perverse doctrines, whatever pertains to earthly knowledge and is thought to be robust, this is overthrown by the dialectical art and, like a fire, dissolved into ashes and embers, so that what was thought to be strongest is proved to be worth nothing —; Isaiah too rebukes the pride of Moab, saying: We have heard the insolence of Moab, he is exceedingly insolent; I have taken away his pride; Jeremiah also, prophesying against all the nations, speaks specifically to Moab: Because you trusted in your fortifications, and a little after: You had confidence in your glory, and again: How do you say: We are strong?, and then: Near is the day of Moab, that it should come, and its malice is exceedingly swift, and more plainly: Say: How has the glorious staff been broken, the rod of magnificence?, and again: The horn of Moab is broken; and these things are said so that, under the name of Moab, the foolish pride of the world that lifts itself up to heaven may be crushed.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Thus says the Lord God: Because Idumaea took vengeance, to avenge itself on the sons of Judah, and sinned in transgressing and sought vengeance on them, therefore thus says the Lord God: I will stretch out my hand over the Idumaeans, and I will take away from it man and beast, and I will make it desert from the south, and those who are in Dedan shall fall by the sword. And I will lay my vengeance on Idumaea by the hand of my people Israel, and they shall do in Edom according to my anger and my fury, and they shall know my indignation, says the Lord God. (LXX: "Thus says the Lord Adonai: Because Idumaea acted so that they avenged a vengeance on the house of Judah, and they kept the memory of evil and avenged themselves with vengeance, therefore thus says Adonai the Lord: I will stretch out my hand over Idumaea, and I will slay from it man and beast, and I will make it desert, and those fleeing from Theman shall fall by the sword. And I will lay my vengeance on Idumaea in the hand of my people Israel, and they shall do in Idumaea according to my anger and my fury, and they shall know my vengeance, says Adonai the Lord.") Above he had set out two: Because Moab and Seir said, and afterwards, keeping silent about Seir, he spoke against Moab only; now he returns to the πρόβλημα [problem, the question set] he had begun: what Seir, that is, Idumaea, did — that Esau and Seir and Edom and Idumaea and Duma are called one nation, no one who has knowledge of the Scriptures will doubt; and, to say nothing of the other prophets — Isaiah, Jeremiah, Amos, who prophesied against Idumaea and Duma and Edom — the prophet Obadiah directs his whole prophecy against this nation; we expounded him long ago as best we could —. So Seir is rebuked, who, because he was shaggy, received the name of hairy, and bloody Edom, who for the cooking of red lentils lost his birthright and took his name from the dish; Esau too they interpret as 'made'; and this must be known, that in the Hebrew Idumaea is never written, but always Edom, which the Greek translation expressed as Idumaea. So Idumaea did not speak, as Moab did, but took vengeance on the sons of Judah, and sinned, or kept the memory of the former pain, so as to take vengeance on those by whom he had been supplanted in the womb.
Commentary on Ezekiel

According to tropology, this seems to me the sense: Idumaea is called 'earthly' and 'fleshly', which rises up against the spirit so that we do not do the things that are of the spirit, and hastens to draw to itself the soul placed in the middle, and wishes to repay vengeance on the sons of Judah, to whom it had formerly been subject, and remembers the old pain, that it was not in its own power, and therefore seeks vengeance on those who, withdrawing from the flesh, followed the spirit; therefore this Lord, being the avenger of the sons of Judah, stretches out his hand over Idumaea and takes away from it man and beast — whatever it seems to have either of reason or of simple faith — so as to reduce it to solitude, and of 'Theman', which means 'failing', and 'Dedan', which itself signifies 'kinship', he slew all with the sword which he placed in the hand of his people Israel, so that Edom may be overthrown, and feel the anger and fury of the Lord, and understand that his vengeance has served to this end: that it should serve the house of Judah. This is what the Apostle too argues about, writing: Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated; and he loves Jacob because he supplants and overcomes what is fleshly and earthly, and deserves to receive its blessings; for first we live according to the flesh and afterwards according to the spirit. First the vices, then the virtues by which the vices are undermined, because the heart of man is set on malice from boyhood, and mature age condemns the errors of youth; hence David too: The offenses, he says, of my youth and my ignorances do not remember. And yet it must be known that Jacob receives the first blessing, Esau the second, and at the last it is said of him: You shall be the servant of your brother, so that, after the flesh has been made subject to the spirit and joined to it, it may cease to be flesh, and Idumaea may pass over into Judea.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Therefore not through angels nor through anyone else, but the Lord himself, stretching out his hand over Idumaea, took away from it man and beast, and reduced its cities to desert, that is, 'Theman', which we rendered 'south', from which, and from the other city, Dedan, the slain will fall by the sword; 'and when they have avenged themselves on Judah, I will lay vengeance on the Idumaeans by the hand, or in the hand, of my people Israel, so that they may be crushed by those on whom they exercised vengeance, who will do in Edom, or Idumaea, according to my anger and fury, so as to fulfil my indignation, and so that, through the hands of my people Israel, my anger may rage against the hostile nation, and they may understand that, against the unjust vengeance of Idumaea, my vengeance was just,' says Adonai the Lord.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Thus says the Lord God: Because the Philistines acted in vengeance, and avenged themselves with their whole soul, slaying, and fulfilling old enmities, therefore thus says the Lord God: Behold, I will stretch out my hand over the Philistines, and I will slay the slayers, and destroy the remnants of the maritime region; and I will execute great vengeances on them, rebuking in fury, and they shall know that I am the Lord, when I have laid my vengeance on them. (LXX: "Therefore thus says Adonai the Lord: Because the foreigners acted in vengeance, and stirred up retribution, mocking from the soul, so as to destroy for ever, therefore thus says Adonai the Lord: Behold, I will stretch out my hand over the foreigners, and I will destroy (or slay) the Cretans, and destroy the remnants of the shore; and I will execute great vengeances on them in the retribution of fury, and they shall know that I am Adonai the Lord, when I have laid my vengeance on them.") After the Ammonites, Moab and Seir — who are the Edomites, and who through Lot and Esau are joined by kinship to the people of Israel and the house of Judah — he comes to the Philisthiim — whom the Seventy translated 'allophylos', that is, 'foreigners', not by the general name of all the nations that are not of the race of the Jews, but by the special name of their own nation, which is now called Palaestina, the letter 'phe' having been changed into 'pi' according to the custom of the Greeks, just as among us, in place of the Hebrew 'phascha', the Greek and Latin 'pascha' is celebrated —. 'Philisthiim' they interpret as 'falling by the cup'; they too were made drunk from the golden cup of Babylon, and they rage, and mock with their whole soul, remembering their old enmities against Israel, by which they were divided from the people of God; and whereas the Lord says: Vengeance to me, I will repay, the Lord says: They themselves avenge themselves, slaying and fulfilling ancient hatreds; on account of which they will feel the hand of the Lord stretched out over them, who will slay the 'slayers' — for which the Seventy, intending I know not what, translated 'Cretans', whereas Aquila and Symmachus and Theodotion rendered either the Hebrew word itself, 'chorethim', or 'slayers' and 'slaying', not only in the present place but also in Zephaniah, where these things are said against the Philistines: Gaza shall be plundered, and Ashkelon given to destruction, and Ashdod and Ekron shall be uprooted. Woe to the inhabitants of the cord of the sea, neighbors of the Cretans! The word of the Lord is upon you, Canaan, land of the foreigners; and I will destroy you from habitation. And Crete shall be pasture for shepherds and a fold for sheep. For there too, whereas the Seventy rendered 'Crete', the other translators translated ὄλεθρον, that is, 'slaying' or 'destruction', about which we said what seemed right to us in the above-mentioned prophet, God granting it; hence too, of David's two legions, one of which was called 'Phelethi' and the other 'Cerethim', the latter, because they slew and cut throats, received the name 'Chorethim', that is, 'of the slayers' —; and the Lord destroys all the remnants of the maritime region, which is beaten by salt waves, and will execute vengeances, not small but great, in fury, so that his fury may have mercy as its end and, after he has executed vengeances, rebuking with fury, then the Philistines may know that he himself is the Lord.

n: Year of the prophet's captivity. (Haydock) --- He still dates from the transmigration of Joachin, chap. i., &c. (Worthington) --- Some think he speaks of the first, fourth, or fifth month. Tyre was not besieged till after the ninth day of the fourth month, when Jerusalem was taken; nor could she express her joy for that event before, unless God allude to her dispositions, &c., chap. xxv. 1. (Calmet)
Gates: places of resort and commerce. The Jews came to Jerusalem frequently from all parts, which increased her beauty and trade. New Tyre expects that more will come to her.

Up. Nabuchodonosor besieged the city for thirteen years. The profane historians read by St. Jerome took no notice of this; but Josephus quotes several. (Antiquities x. 11., and contra Apion i.) (Calmet)
Dust. She shall be demolished, and the rubbish thrown into the sea, to make a road by which New Tyre in the island might be attacked, ver. 12. (Haydock)

Sea. St. Jerome explains this of New Tyre; Marsham of the Old. To reconcile the different texts, we only need to suppose that both cities were connected by a road thrown up in the sea by Hiram, and repaired by Nabuchodonosor with great labour, (chap. xxix. 18.) after it had been destroyed by the inhabitants of New Tyre, when they saw the old city on the continent fall a prey. (St. Jerome) (Calmet)
Kings: Nabuchodonosor (4 Kings xxv. 28.) or Alexander [the Great], who took Tyre. (Menochius)

Daughters. Many towns were subject to Tyre: almost all Phœnicia acknowledged her dominion, as well as (Calmet) the seas to which her fleets went, ver. 15. (Selden, Mare i. 6.; Curtius iv.) --- These smaller cities shall fall, and the town shall be of no service except to dry nets. (Worthington)
Engines. Literally, "vines." (Haydock) --- A covert was thus made for the soldiers, (Veget. iv. 15.) when they approached the walls. (Menochius)
Destroyed. Old Tyre was taken by storm. It is doubtful whether it was pillaged, chap. xxix. 18. (Calmet)

Statues. The citizens chained the golden statue of Apollo to the altar of Hercules, for fear of its leaving them, when Alexander [the Great] attacked the town. (Curtius iv.) --- Hiram placed a pillar of gold in the temple of Hercules. (Josephus, contra Apion i.) --- Herodotus (ii. 44.) saw another also of emerald stone, (smaragdon) which illuminated the temple in the night. On such the Tyrians might depend; though some render, "the substance or guard of thy strength," denoting the soldiers (Calmet) and towers. (Haydock) --- The gods were treated like the people, and their precious ornaments plundered.

More, for seventy years, Isaias xxiii. 15. The people returned at the same time as the Jews. (The year of the world 3468.) Soon after, Zacharias (chap. ix.) speaks of Tyre as then subsisting. It was very strong in Alexander's time, (who took it with difficulty, as Antigonus did eighteen years later) and had a very extensive commerce when St. Jerome wrote. But all this must be understood of New Tyre. The old city never regained much splendour. (Calmet) --- It is still in ruins. A modern traveller was struck with the completion of this prophecy, beholding a few miserable fishermen drying their nets on the spot!

Sea: colonies, or tributary to Tyre, ver. 8. (Haydock) --- Leptis, Utica, Carthage,and Cadiz, were founded by Tyrians. (Pliny, [Natural History?] v. 19.) --- Some pretend that these cities were attacked by the conquerors, for manifesting their grief. See Josephus, Antiquities x.; Pineda, &c. --- But we shall not here follow conjectures. --- Astonishment. Hebrew, "troubles," or mourning. (Calmet)
Dwellest in. Hebrew, "of the seas." Protestants, "seafaring men," (Haydock) being near the sea, or thence deriving thy riches.
Because. Hebrew, "at thy departure." (Calmet) --- Septuagint, "into captivity." (St. Jerome)

Waters; great armies, (ver. 3.) or when thou art in the regions below, Job xxvi. 5. (Calmet) --- Tyre was humbled for her pride, but restored after seventy years, Isaias xxiii. Our Saviour retired into those parts, Matthew xv. 21. (Worthington)

Everlasting: in the grave, till the day of judgment, Psalm xlviii. 12., and Wisdom xii. 5. --- Living, assigned to Israel, (chap. xxxii. 24.; Calmet) where holy people adore the true God, and shall rise to life eternal. (Menochius)

For ever: for a long time, (Theodoret) not at all in thy ancient glory. (Haydock) --- The city subsisted after the days of Nabuchodonosor and of Alexander [the Great], (Calmet) ver. 14. --- But the ancient city was reduced to a mere nothing. (Haydock)

f: Commentary on Ezekiel

And it came to pass in the eleventh year, on the first (or one) of the month, that the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, because Tyre (or Sor) has said of Jerusalem: Aha, the gates of the peoples (or nations) are broken, she is turned to me, I shall be filled, she is laid waste (or she who was full is laid waste); therefore thus says the Lord God: Behold, I am against you, O Tyre, and I will make many nations come up to you, as the surging sea comes up; and they shall break down the walls of Tyre and destroy her towers, and I will scrape (or winnow) her dust from her, and I will make her a most clear (or most gleaming) rock. There shall be a drying of dragnets in the midst of the sea, for I have spoken, says the Lord God; and she shall be for plunder to the nations. Her daughters also who are in the field (or in the plain) shall be slain by the sword, and they shall know that I am the Lord. The order of the prophecy is woven together in sequence. He had spoken against the Ammonites and Moab and Seir, who are themselves the Edomites, and the Philistines who are on the coast; and he keeps the same boundary along the cord of the sea: for after the Palestinians comes the region of Phoenicia, whose metropolis is the city 'Tyre', which in the Hebrew and Syrian tongue is called 'Sor': 'And because, when Jerusalem was taken, she too rejoiced and insulted her and said: The gates of the peoples are broken; I have a most secure harbor, and now that she is overthrown, the whole multitude that was ruled by her will has turned to me; and because she is laid waste, therefore I shall be filled; or, she who was full before will be reduced to a wilderness: you have said these things, then, and have insulted the ruins of Jerusalem, which was overthrown by the judgment of God because of her sins; therefore, not through messengers nor through any others, but I myself will be against you, O Tyre, and like the waves of the sea I will make the Babylonians come up against you with very many nations, by whose assault your walls and towers will be destroyed, so far that they fall right down to the ground and its dust is scraped away or winnowed into various parts; and she will be so humbled that she is compared to a most gleaming rock, and so great will be the desolation in the city, once most thronged, that the dragnets of fishermen will be spread out and dried in its midst; for I the Lord have spoken, whose words cannot be void, and I will hand her over for plunder to the nations; her daughters also who are in the field, or in the plain, that is, on the coast of Phoenicia, cities and towns, villages and forts, will be slain by the sword — μεταφορικῶς [metaphorically]: because he called them daughters, he speaks of a slaying by the sword —, so that by the outcome of events they may know that I am the Lord, who commanded these things to happen'. According to tropology, since the Hebrew name 'Sor' is rendered 'distress', every soul that is seized by passions can be called 'Sor'; when it sees Jerusalem, in which were the temple and the vision of peace, overthrown by the judgment of God for her vices and sins, it exults and thinks that the dominion of the once famous city is to be transferred to itself. This is understood both of contrary doctrines and of the men of the world: for when they see that a holy man has slipped through negligence, they rejoice and exult, as if the ruin of others were their own resurrection. Therefore the Lord threatens that he himself will fight against men of this kind, and will make very many nations come up against them like the waves of the sea, which destroy in them whatever seems most fortified and firm, and that he will so overthrow all their arguments that they are reduced to dust; that he will also make the dragnets and nets with which they formerly fished for the deceived multitude cease, and have them spread out and dried on the ground of the deserted city, so that in their place other fishermen may come in, whom the Lord sent to fish; and also that her daughters, who were formerly kept as if in a chamber and, being mystic and more secret doctrines, were not readily entrusted to anyone, will come forth and be dragged out into public and cut down by the Church's blade, so that then they may understand that he is the Lord, who both abandoned Jerusalem for a little while on account of her sins and destroyed the fortifications of Tyre on account of her insulting and her rejoicing.
Commentary on Ezekiel

But it is doubtful to no one that, according to the ἀναγωγὴν [anagogy, the higher sense], Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, who comes from the north, is understood as the devil, who, though he is a most harsh wind and a left-hand one, is called by the name 'right-hand', claiming for himself the dignity of the name; and he is the king of kings and of all the kingdoms which he showed to the Lord, when he said to him: All these have been handed over to me, and I will give them to you if you fall down and worship me. He has horses and chariots, of which it is written: A horse is deceitful for safety, and: All who mount horses have fallen asleep, and in another place: Horse and rider he has thrown into the sea.
Commentary on Ezekiel

For thus says the Lord: Behold, I will bring to Tyre (or to you, Sor) Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon from the north, king of kings, with horses and chariots and horsemen and a company and a great people. Your daughters who are in the field he shall slay with the sword, and he shall surround you with siegeworks, and heap up a mound round about, and raise the shield against you, and he shall direct mantlets and rams (or lances) against your walls, and destroy your towers with his weaponry. By the flood of his horses their dust shall cover you; at the sound of horsemen and wheels and chariots your walls shall be shaken, when he has entered your gates as through the entry of a city laid waste (or as one entering a city from the plain). With the hoofs of his horses he shall trample all your streets, your people he shall cut down with the sword, and your noble statues shall fall to the ground (or he shall bring down the substance of your strength to the ground). They shall lay waste (or he shall lay waste) your riches, they shall plunder your merchandise (or he shall despoil your substance), and they shall destroy (or he shall destroy) your walls, and your splendid (or desirable) houses they shall overthrow (or he shall overthrow), and your stones and your timber or your dust they shall put in the midst of the waters (or he shall cast into the midst of the sea). And I will make the multitude of your singers cease (or he shall destroy the multitude of your musicians), and the sound of your lyres (or the voice of your instruments) shall be heard no more, and I will make you a most clear (or a most gleaming) rock; you shall be a drying of dragnets, nor shall you be built any more, for I have spoken, says the Lord God. As is my custom, I have joined both editions, and where they differ I have coupled them side by side, looking to the brevity of the volumes. So what he had said: I will make many nations come up to you as the surging sea comes up, and Tyre shall be for plunder to the nations, he now sets out more plainly: that the Lord will bring Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon from the north, the king of kings, with horses and chariots and with a boundless multitude of troops, who will first overthrow the cities and forts on the coast that are subject to Tyre, and afterwards cause Tyre to be besieged, and wall her in with his army and mound and siegeworks, and assail her walls with mantlets and rams, and destroy them; and so great will be the multitude of his horsemen that, by the dust of the cavalry and the noise of the howling army and the rattle of wheels and the neighing of horses, the foundations of the city will be shaken; and so he will enter the city, its walls torn down, like one entering securely from the plain; and so great will be the security of the conquering army that the hoofs of horses will trample the streets of Tyre, and all the people will fall in the midst of the city, and the once noble statues, or all her substance, will fall to the ground, and nothing of her former riches will be preserved in the captured city; but along with the walls the noble houses too will be destroyed, and so great will be the savagery of the victors that the timber and stones left over from the fire will be thrown into the midst of the sea; and either Nebuchadnezzar or the Lord himself will make cease all the gladness of the city with which it once resounded in songs and psalteries, and, overthrown right down to the ground, it will be a drying of dragnets.
Commentary on Ezekiel

He slays the daughters of Tyre, souls placed in distress and in a kind of prison of sins, in the field and the widest plain, and surrounds Tyre with his siegeworks, so as to hold her shut in, so that no one from her can escape the dominion of the Babylonian king; he destroys her walls and overthrows her towers, and whatever she may have had in the way of doctrines trembles violently at the flood of his horses and the sound of his horsemen and the clatter of wheels and chariots; and he will enter her gates with no one preventing him, and the hoofs of his horses will trample the streets of the city — for wide and spacious is the way that leads to death —, and he will cast down to the ground all her substance — or the noble statues, by which they had fashioned for themselves images of falsehood, of which it is written: Lord, in your city you will scatter their image —; and, the walls destroyed, the noble houses too will be overthrown which she had prepared for herself and in which she exulted; and she will come to such desolation that they throw into the deep her stones and timber, with which she had built her walls and constructed her masonry, and her songs and music, by which she trusted in herself in the wisdom of this world, and all the sound of lyres will be heard no more; and her fishing will cease, and she will be brought so low that she is a drying of dragnets and is not built any more, because, handed over to Nebuchadnezzar at the sentence of the Lord, she has been utterly overthrown, in accord with what the Apostle also says: Whom I have handed over to Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme. The passages are difficult, and the prudent and diligent reader ought to pardon my labor; or if he can find something better, I too shall pass over to his opinion, provided he knows that he will receive from others the pardon he grants to me.
Commentary on Ezekiel

But what follows: Nor shall you be built any more, seems to raise a question: how has she not been built, when today we see her as the most noble and most beautiful city of Phoenicia? — whence some will have it that Tyre is to suffer these things in the last time, and is not to be built afterwards —; but how will they be able to keep to the person of Nebuchadnezzar — especially since we read in what follows that Nebuchadnezzar besieged Tyre and did not receive the wages of his labor, and that Egypt was therefore handed over to him, because he had served the sentence of God in the siege of Tyre —? Those who contradict this history say that they have read the Greek histories and those of the Phoenicians, and especially of Nicolaus of Damascus, and others of the barbarians, and have found nothing about a siege of the city of Tyre by the Chaldeans; whereas we can prove that many things are said in the Scriptures to have been done which are not found in Greek volumes, and that we ought not to acquiesce in the authority of those whose faithlessness and lies we detest. So what is said: Nor shall you be built any more, can be taken thus: that she will by no means any longer be queen of the peoples, nor have her own dominion as she had under Hiram and the other kings, but will be in servitude either under the Chaldeans or the Macedonians or the Ptolemies and, last of all, the Roman kings.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Thus says the Lord God to Tyre: Shall not the isles be shaken at the sound of your fall and the groaning of your slain, when they have been killed in your midst? And all the princes of the sea shall come down from their seats, and shall take off their spoils, and cast away their varied garments; and they shall be clothed with astonishment, they shall sit on the ground, and, dumbfounded at your sudden fall, they shall marvel. And taking up a lamentation over you, they shall say to you: How you have perished, you who dwell in the sea, renowned city, who were strong in the sea with your inhabitants, whom all shall dread! Now the ships shall be astonished in the day of your terror, and the isles in the sea shall be troubled, because no one goes out from you. (LXX: "For thus says the Lord God to Sor: Shall not the isles be shaken at the voice of your fall, when your wounded groan, when the sword has been drawn in your midst? And all the princes of the sea shall come down from their seats, and shall take off their crowns, and shall be stripped of their varied garments; they shall go mad with frenzy, they shall sit on the ground, and they shall dread their own destruction, and shall groan over you. And they shall take up a lamentation over you, and shall say to you: How you have perished and been scattered in the sea, praised city, who were strong in the sea, she and her inhabitants, who gave her fear to all her inhabitants! And the isles shall dread in the day of your fall, and the isles in the sea shall be troubled at your going out.") First let us lay open the very words of the history, disclosing the sense of what is said by a very brief μεταφράσει [paraphrase]. 'Thus says Adonai the Lord to Tyre, which is called 'Sor': In the day of your fall, when you have collapsed under Nebuchadnezzar's assault, and at the groaning of the wounded or slain who have been killed in your midst, shall not the isles be shaken? And all the kings will come down from their seats or thrones, and the princes of the sea who rule over various isles, and they will take the diadems off their heads, laying aside all the glory of reigning, and will cast from them their most precious garments, gleaming with incredible variety; and by the greatness of their astonishment they will be turned to madness and, cast down in humility, will sit on the ground; and when they see that you have collapsed, they will dread like things for themselves, and will think that no good thing on earth is lasting; rather, on the contrary, they will take up a lamentation over you and recite a tearful song, saying: How you have perished, you who dwell in the sea, renowned city (or praised)' — for we read in Greek and Latin and barbarian histories that Tyre was an island and had no approach from the land, but that afterwards mounds were thrown up by Nebuchadnezzar king of the Chaldeans or, as some affirm, by Alexander king of the Macedonians, and the place was prepared by siege and with mantlets and rams, and from an island a peninsula was made —; 'you, then, O Sor, O Tyre, who were once the strongest among all the isles, or praised by the voice of all among the cities, together with your inhabitants whom all feared, how suddenly you have collapsed! Now the isles will be astonished or terrified over you, and — as it stands better in the Hebrew — the ships, in the day of your terror and fall, and the isles in the sea will be troubled — hence it is more consistent to read 'ships' above, so that 'isles' is not set down a second time —, because no one goes out from you — or, as the Seventy translated, in the day of your going in —, when you have been led away captive'. Let these meanwhile be laid as a kind of foundation of the history; now we shall strive to set the spiritual roof upon it. Imagine someone who, having long kept his chastity, flourished in many virtues, and afterwards collapsed into some grave and mortal sin: will not all the isles be moved at the sound of his fall and of his slain virtues, those, namely, who are beaten by the salt and bitter waves of this world? And all who seemed to be princes in the brine of this world will come down from the throne of their pride and, cast down in humility, will take off from their heads the diadems they seemed to possess through good works, and will cast away the garments varied with a diversity of virtues, and will be clothed with astonishment, or through the greatness of their fear will seem in some way insane, and will sit on the ground, and, stunned at his sudden fall, will marvel, so much so that all take up wailing and lamentation over him who has collapsed, and say: How you have perished, you who were formerly safe; how you have collapsed, you who had stood so long, who in the sea of this world were thought renowned among all, who were strong in the opinion of all; and your inhabitants, that is, your most strong thoughts that resisted all the fiery darts of the devil, which formerly were a terror to all adversaries, have been turned to astonishment! And the ships too, namely all the saints, who cross the waves of this world, are stunned when they see that you have fallen, in the day of your terror and fall; and the isles will be troubled, lest they too suffer like things — for the falls of others are examples for the righteous, since we all dwell in this world in a weak and feeble state and with wavering step, and our victory is never certain and secure, when those who had stood before go out from you, or at your going out, in your end and consummation —. For we are judged not by things past but by things present; and we must beware and always fear lest the storm of a single hour overthrow old glory and solid firmness.
Commentary on Ezekiel

For thus says the Lord God: When I make you a desolate city like the cities that are not inhabited, and bring up the deep upon you, and many waters cover you, and I drag you down with those who go down into the pit (or to those who go down into the ditch) to the everlasting people, and set you in the uttermost land (or in the depth of the lands) like the ancient wastes, with those who are led down into the pit (or go down into the ditch), so that you are not inhabited, and I give glory in the land of the living (or so that you do not rise again in the land of the living), I will reduce you to nothing (or I will give you to destruction), and you shall not be, and when sought you shall not be found any more forever, says the Lord God. Join what has been said with what preceded. 'When I make you, O Tyre, a city desolate forever, as are other cities that are not inhabited at all, and bring up the deep upon you, and many waters, or boundless multitudes of enemies, cover you — or certainly, because he is speaking to an island and to a city set on an island, he τροπικῶς [figuratively] compares the throng of adversaries to the waves of the deep —, and drag you down, with those who go down into the pit or into the ditch, to those who are in hell — of whom we also read in the Psalms: They shall go into the lower parts of the earth and shall be delivered into the hands of the sword, they shall be portions for foxes —, to the everlasting people, where there is weeping of eyes and gnashing of teeth, and set you in the uttermost land, in which the ancient dragon has been placed, and like the ancient wastes and deserts, where there is no remembrance of good things but punishments are everlasting, and do not cause you to be raised up in the land of the living — of which it is written: Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the land, and in another place: I will please the Lord in the region of the living —, then you will be reduced to nothing, or you will perish forever, and you shall be no more', according to what is written in another psalm: Spare me, that I may be refreshed before I depart and shall be no more: not that he who is in everlasting punishments ceases to be, but that he who does not live to God is said in the holy Scriptures not to subsist. Hence Esther too, speaking against idols: Do not hand over, she says, your scepter to those who are not: surely those to whom she begs that it not be handed over existed, but they were not, to God, since they had ceased to be to the virtues and to the living God.
Commentary on Ezekiel

This we have said briefly about Tyre μεταφραστικῶς [by way of paraphrase]; it can also be referred to those who, set in the distress of this world, are led down to the underworld and are covered by the deeps and waves of punishments, and are dragged to the lower parts of the earth, and are joined to those who are in the ancient wilderness, and are led down into the pit or the everlasting ditch, so that they are no longer inhabited by the Holy Spirit; of whom it is written: The ungodly, when he has fallen into the depth of evils, despises; and henceforth they will not be in the land of the living, but will perish, and be reduced to nothing, and cease to be to God. These testimonies are made use of by those who say that the punishments of the ungodly, and not of sinners, are perpetual: of the ungodly who, sought by God, were not found, and have ceased to be forever, because by their own fault they lost him who says: I am the life.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And this is to be noted: that Tyre is sought by him who came to seek and to save what had perished, and who, leaving the ninety-nine sheep on the mountains, seeks the one straying sheep — the woman too who had lost one drachma seeks and finds it, and calls together her neighbors to share her joy —; but if Tyre, when sought, is not found, the fault is not the seeker's but his who has fled the hand of the good shepherd. 'And no more', he says, 'shall you be forever' — or, as is written in the Hebrew 'lolam' and in the Greek αἰών [age], it signifies 'one age', according to that passage of Isaiah, who says that after seventy years Tyre is to be restored to her whole state; and they say that 'one age', that is, the span of a human lifetime, is reckoned at the number of seventy years, as the psalmist says: The days of our years in them are seventy years; but if in the strong, eighty years; whatever is beyond is toil and pain —.

n: Lamentation. Such canticles were usual, and very poetical.
Entry, whence merchants may proceed from an excellent harbour to any place.

Neighbours of Sidon, Josue xix. 29. (Calmet) --- Septuagint, "thy children." Protestants, "thy builders." (Haydock) --- The description of the Tyrian grandeur, shews their more woeful ruin. (Worthington)
Thee. Hebrew, "all thy ship-boards." (Septuagint) (Protestants) (Haydock) --- St. Jerome has divided (Calmet) leuthim, "decks of the sea," as yam denotes the sea. (Haydock)
Benches. Septuagint, "temples." --- Italy. Hebrew Cetim. Macedonia. (Bochart) (Calmet) --- All distant places were styled islands, (Haydock) when they went by water to them.

Linen. Cotton, (Exodus xxv. 4.) used for standards. Septuagint, "for bed coverlets," or for sails. --- Mast. Cleopatra and Caligula were still more sumptuous in their sails. --- Elisa, or Elis, famous for purple: yet Tyre was more so.
Aradians. Sidon and Arad were then subject to Tyre, and supplied rowers. --- Pilots. They studied no other science.
Gebal. Septuagint, "Biblos," which is the same, 3 Kings v. 18. --- Furnished. Hebrew, "were in thee to repair thy breaches." Septuagint, "strengthened thy designs."

Lybians. Hebrew, "Phut." They had been expelled by the Cyreneans. Tyre had in her pay the most warlike nations of Persia, &c. Cyrus soon after shook off the yoke of the Medes, and conquered the Lydians. --- Hung up, ver. 11. This was very usual, Canticle of Canticles iv. 4., and Isaias xxii. 8. (Calmet)

The Pygmeans. That is, strong and valiant men. In Hebrew Gammadim. (Challoner) --- He does not speak of those fabulous men hardly a cubit high. Gomed signifying a "cubit," has caused them to be styled so here. Septuagint, "guards;" or Symmachus, "Medes." Ezechiel (xxxviii. 6.) speaks of the Gomerim.
Carthaginians. Hebrew, "Tharsis," in Cilicia; (Genesis x. 4.; Calmet) or distant merchants, who came by sea. (Haydock)
Slaves. Those from Greece were much esteemed. (Calmet) --- Alas! thirty thousand Tyrians were themselves thus sold by Alexander [the Great]! (Haydock)
Horses. Those of Sarmatia (Calmet) were in high repute. (Pliny, [Natural History?] viii. 42.

Dedan. Septuagint, "Rhodians;" or rather Arabs are meant, ver. 20. They might receive ivory from Ethiopia. --- Teeth. Hebrew, "horns or tusks," which the elephant casts every year. The ivory is less brittle, 3 Kings x. 18. (Calmet) --- Ebony; a hard black wood, like horn. (Bochart)

Syrian: always much addicted to commerce. (St. Jerome) --- Septuagint read Adam for Aram, as if the traffic in men was meant: (Calmet) "ivory, and to those who brought, thou gavest thy rewards. (16) Men of thy traffic," &c. (Haydock) --- Linen. Hebrew buts, "silk" extracted from the pinna fish, 1 Paralipomenon xv. 27. Silk. Hebrew ramoth, may rather denote unicorns, Job xxviii. 18. (Calmet) --- Chodchod. It is the Hebrew name for some precious stone, but of what kind in particular, interpreters are not agreed. (Challoner) --- Some say the carbuncle, &c. St. Jerome renders it the jasper, Isaias liv. 12. (Worthington) --- Here he confesses he knows not the meaning. (Calmet)
Rosin. Our version generally renders this, balm. (Haydock) --- It was much used to heal, Jeremias viii. 22., and Genesis xxxvii. 25.
Rich. Hebrew Chelbon; perhaps the city Chelba, Judges i. 31. The kings of Persia used this wine, and planted vines at Damascus on purpose.
Dan: the citizens of Peneas, the tribe of Dan was in captivity. Grotius places these nations in Zeilan, (Calmet) or Ceylon. (Haydock)
Seats, such as the Turks still use, or to throw over horses instead of saddles.
Haran, or Charæ, famous for the residence of Abraham and the defeat of Crassus. --- Eden, the province where Paradise was situated.
Cords, in boxes, which had then no locks.
Sea. Hebrew Tharsis, in Cilicia; or large, and fit for long voyages. Thine were the best. (Calmet)

South. Hebrew kodim, (Haydock) "eastern," or rather "burning," here means Nabuchodonosor, who came from the north, (chap. xxvi. 7.; Calmet) or east. The fall of Tyre is described as a shipwreck. (Haydock)
Ashes. They followed the same customs as the Jews. (Calmet) --- The latter were ordered to avoid cutting the hair, like them; yet did so, Deuteronomy xiv., and Isaias xxii. 22. (Worthington)
Hissed, through pity and astonishment. (Calmet)

f: Commentary on Ezekiel

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: You therefore, son of man, take up a lamentation over Tyre, and you shall say to Tyre, which dwells at the entrance of the sea, the trade of the peoples to many islands (or from many islands): Thus says the Lord God. If I should wish to comprehend the whole prophecy against Tyre, or over the lamentation of Tyre, in a single discourse, I shall both make it long and obscure the reader's understanding, since he cannot hold everything in mind at once, especially the places in which the edition of the Seventy differs from the Hebrew in this passage, that is, what they have added or what they have taken away. Therefore we shall be content with our own translation, and wherever they disagree we shall attach theirs alongside, leaving the perfect knowledge of all things to God, and we shall briefly point out what seems right to us in each point. He who is lamented is still a concern to the one by whom he is lamented; hence Samuel too wept and lamented over Saul, and the Apostle Paul laments and mourns over those who have committed fornication and have not done penance, and Jeremiah writes lamentations over the overthrow of Jerusalem in four alphabets.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Tyre, then, or Sor, according to the letter, dwells at the entrance of the sea, either because it was formerly an island or because it receives ships coming from the deep into a most safe harbor, and it is the trade of the peoples to many islands, or from many islands, which indeed continues to this day, so that the commerce of almost all nations is carried on in it. But following the interpretation we have begun, let us refer whatever is said of Tyre to the συνοχὴν, that is, the 'straits', of this world, which is set in the evil one and is hemmed in and battered by various disturbances as if by waves — of traders of this sort it is told also in the Psalms in mystical language: Those who go down to the sea in ships, doing business in many waters, these have seen the works of the Lord, and his wonders in the deep —.
Commentary on Ezekiel

O Tyre, you have said: I am of perfect beauty (or you have said: I have surrounded myself with beauty), and set in the heart of the sea. The first charge against Tyre is that, if she seems to have anything good, she thinks it not God's but her own, and reckons all the beauty that came to her from various regions to be the work of her own diligence and strength; for she said: I am of perfect beauty, or: I have surrounded myself with beauty, although she is set in the heart, that is, in the middle, of the sea, and is tossed about like an island, and is shattered by the surge and the dashing of the waves. That the heart of the sea signifies its middle, that prophetic saying also shows: Therefore we will not fear when the earth is troubled, and the mountains are carried into the heart of the sea. Their waters roared and were troubled; and our Lord too is said to have descended into the heart of the earth, that is, into its middle, and to the underworld. But true and perfect beauty is in no human being except in the body of Christ, which is interpreted as the Church, and which is gathered together from the virtues of many saints; hence he himself also speaks to the bride: You are all beautiful, my nearest, and there is no blemish in you.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Your neighbors, who built you, have filled up your beauty; with firs from Sanir they constructed you, with all the planking of the sea; they took a cedar from Lebanon to make a mast for you. (In place of which, intending I know not what, the Seventy translated thus: Beelim your sons surrounded you with beauty; cedar from Sanir was built for you; they took thin boards of cypress from Lebanon to make masts of fir for you; for the word 'Beelim' is not found at all in this place among the Hebrews, but in place of 'Beelim' is written 'gebulaich', which means 'your borders'; in what they said, 'your sons', too, they were deceived by the ambiguity of the word and the similarity of the writing, since the same letters, with a different pronunciation, are read as 'of masons' and 'of sons', 'bonaich' and 'benaich'.) 'O Tyre, then, you who said in pride: I am of perfect beauty (or: I have surrounded myself with beauty), although you are set in the middle of the sea, hear how much has been bestowed on you by the bounty of God: your neighbors and those who border on you, who are not from distant but from nearby regions, they themselves have filled up your beauty; and you think yours what is another's!'
Commentary on Ezekiel

And he speaks as if to a ship, τροπικῶς [figuratively] signifying the beauty of the city and its abundance of all things, so that, after he has described all its equipment — mast, yards, oars, sails, prow, keel, ropes, coverings, hides, and the other things which the use of the best-fitted ships requires — he may then announce that a storm and the south wind, by which the greatest waves will be stirred up, will come upon it, and that it will be subjected to shipwreck — by which he signifies the overthrow of the Tyrian city by king Nebuchadnezzar, or, as many think, by Alexander king of the Macedonians, who is related to have besieged and taken that very city in six months, after he had defeated Darius in Lycia —. According to the mystical understandings, the planking of the Tyrian ship, with which it is fitted and joined together, is cut from firs or cedars from Sanir, and its mast is raised from a cedar or cypress from Lebanon: from firs because of their lightness and the joints of the boards, which hold and bite into one another more gently, or from cedars because it is a wood that does not rot; and they are said to be 'from Sanir', which means 'way of the lamp' or, as we judge more truly, 'tooth of the watches', because all the prosperity and illumination of the ship came from the true light; Sanir, moreover, according to the letter, is the very mountain that is also Hermon, which others call Sarion — read the history —; it means 'whiteness' or 'whitening', which itself also pertains to grace coming from elsewhere.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Oaks from Bashan they hewed into your oars, your benches they made for you of Indian ivory, and cabins from the islands of Italy. (LXX: "From Bashan they made your oars, your temples they made for you of ivory, forest houses from the islands of Chetthiim.") How great the beauty of the ship and of its equipment, that it should have oars of cedar — not from just anywhere but from Bashan —, and benches of ivory, and cabins — or storerooms in which the most precious merchandise is laid up — from the islands of 'Chetthiim' — which we have rendered as 'Italy' —, from that region which is nearer to Greece, understanding by it all the parts of the western islands! Let us say, then, according to the ἀναγωγὴν [anagogy, the higher sense], that the oars of the Tyrian ship are made from Bashan — of which it is also written in the Psalms: The Lord said: From Bashan I will turn back, I will turn back from the depth of the sea; Basan in our language means 'ignominy' —; those, then, who were in the depth of the sea and in the ignominy of sins, the Lord turns back, and turns them into oars, so that, sailing with the apostles, they may reach the land and the shores; and benches are made of ivory when they have mortified their bodies, or have devoted the use of their teeth to the praises of God; and cabins or storerooms from the islands of 'Chetthiim', which, according to the ἐτυμολογιὰν [etymology] of the Hebrew language, is rendered 'struck', so that it has been not so much killed as tested by the blows of the devil. We can speak of the 'of ivory, and forest houses' 'from the islands of Chetthiim' as those which the heretics try to construct not in the house of God but in the Tyrian ship, they themselves having their own ivory of speech, and building temples of the tongue contrary to the temple of God, and forest houses, the dwellings of beasts, whereas Scripture says that groves and woods and sacred groves are not to be planted in the house of God.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Embroidered byssus from Egypt was woven for you into a sail, to be set on the mast; hyacinth and purple from the islands of Elishah became your covering. (LXX: "Byssus with embroidery from Egypt was made for you into a spread to surround you with glory, and to cover you with hyacinth and purple from the islands of Elisee, and they became your coverings.") Because Tyre had said: I am of perfect beauty (or: I myself have surrounded myself with beauty), she is convicted as to what she has received from each region, according to that word of Scripture: What do you have that you have not received? But if you have received it, why do you glory as if you had not received it? So it is described what each province sends, according to that line of Vergil: India sends ivory, the soft Sabaeans their incense, But the hardy Chalybes iron, and Pontus the rank castoreum, and the rest. Byssus grows most of all in Egypt, and from it was woven the sail of the Tyrian ship, which is hung on the mast; and its covering, which in the heat of the sun and in calm weather affords shade to sailors and passengers, is made of hyacinth and purple, which come from the islands of Elishah, so he calls the islands of the Ionian Sea. Further, according to the Seventy, coverings of byssus are woven for the spread and for the repose of the Tyrian ship, so that, covered with these, it may be more glorious, and, surrounded with them, may have a more beautiful garment. Now we have often pointed out that byssus is referred to the earth because it springs from the earth, and hyacinth to the air, purple to the sea, from which it is made, with the twice-dyed scarlet added, of which the vestments of the high priest are woven, because it signifies the four elements: earth, fire, air and waters, of which all things consist; and these Tyre takes to herself, so as not to use God's creatures with thanks, but to say: I am of perfect beauty (or: I myself have surrounded myself with beauty).
Commentary on Ezekiel

So much meanwhile according to the letter; but according to the mystical understandings, since 'Sidonians' means 'hunters', and 'Aradians' 'those who put down', we say that Tyre, the glorious and most proud city, which is afterwards to be shattered when the wind blows, has citizens or princes who are hunters — of whom it is written: Our soul has been snatched like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters; for where we read 'of the hunters', in the Hebrew is written 'of the Sidonians' —; these hunt: they draw unwary souls, set on high, down to earthly things, and they become rowers to lead them to shipwreck; but the wise men of Tyre, who are taken in the bad sense, in which the sons of darkness are wiser than the sons of light, they themselves steer what has been made ready for Tyre for shipwreck; the elders of Byblus and its prudent men provided sailors to Tyre for the service, or strengthened its counsel — sacred history relates that very many elders were rejected by the Lord, and younger ones chosen, as a type of the Synagogue and the Church: the elder Cain is cast off, and the younger Abel is chosen; Ishmael, the son of Abraham, is estranged from his father, and Isaac the younger received the inheritance; of the sons of Isaac too, the elder Esau is a hunter and roams in the woodlands, the younger Jacob dwells simply at home, whence it is written also in Malachi: Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated; and certainly, according to the Apostle, while set in their mother's womb they had done nothing good or bad, nor had they merit or offense, that the one should be chosen and the other cast off, except that, in a type, as we have said, of the Synagogue and the Church, the elder is rejected and the younger taken up —. All, he says, the ships of the sea and their sailors were among the people of the Tyrian trade (or toward the west of the west — just as 'Song of Songs' and 'age of ages' and 'work of works' are said, so that a song is greater than the other songs, and an age longer than the other ages, and a work more useful than the other works, so 'west of the west' is said in order to signify the greatness of the western regions —), and fittingly the ships of the sea and their sailors and rowers, who are in aid of the Tyrian ship, do not go to the east, nor to the rising of the light, where the sun of righteousness rises, but to the 'west of the west', where the light sets and whence is the beginning of darkness.
Commentary on Ezekiel

The inhabitants of Sidon and the Aradians were your rowers; your wise men, O Tyre, became your pilots. The elders of Byblus and its prudent men provided sailors for the service of your varied equipment. All the ships of the sea and their sailors were among the people of your trade. (LXX: "Your princes who dwelt in Sidon and the Aradians were your rowers; your wise men, Sor, who were in you, these were your pilots. The elders of Byblus and its wise men were in you: these strengthened your counsel. And all the ships of the sea and their rowers became yours toward the west of the west.") He had said above: Your neighbors, who built you, have filled up your beauty; before he comes to those who dwell far off, he describes the help of the nearest provinces: 'Your inhabitants,' he says, 'or the princes of Sidon and of Aradus, which is a neighboring island, are your rowers; your wise men, O Tyre, have become your pilots' — for piloting belongs properly to the wise, as Scripture says: Those who have no piloting fall like leaves —.
Commentary on Ezekiel

'The old men or elders of Byblus and its prudent men provided sailors for the service, or strengthened the counsel of Tyre, and provided varied equipment; and all the ships of the sea and their sailors were among the people of the Tyrian trade, or toward the west of the west'.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Persians and Lydians and Libyans were in your army; your men of war hung up shield and helmet in you for your adornment (or hung up targes and helmets in you, they gave you your glory). That the Persians were most brave, whose king Cyrus, as is foretold by the prophecy of Isaiah, having overthrown Astyages king of the Medes, captured Babylon, both sacred and secular history relate; that the Lydians too were reckoned at that time among the most robust nations, whose king Croesus was captured by the same Cyrus, Xenophon writes most fully; and that Libyans came against Jerusalem with the Troglodytes and Ethiopians, we read in the volume of Chronicles; because in those times they were most flourishing and fighters famous in battle, they are recorded to have been defenders of the Tyrian city, and to have hung up shields and helmets on the battlements of the walls to terrify enemies. But the spiritual understanding sounds thus: that the 'Persians', who mean 'tempting' or 'tempted', and the 'Lydians', whom we understand as 'begotten', and the 'Libyans', who in the Hebrew language are called 'phut' and are rendered 'os' [mouth] — from 'ore' [mouth], not from 'osse' [bone] —, strive in vain to defend Tyre, since they are overcome by temptation and serve generation and lust, and only multiply empty words, not having the helmet of salvation nor the shield of faith, but only put forward glory and the din of words for its adornment.
Commentary on Ezekiel

The sons of the Aradians with your army were upon your walls round about; but the Pygmies too, who were in your towers, hung their quivers on your walls all around; they completed your beauty. (LXX: "The sons of the Aradians and your strength were upon your walls round about; guards were in your towers; they hung their quivers upon your battlements all around; they perfected your beauty.") The word 'gamadim' the first edition of Aquila translated 'Pygmies', Symmachus 'Medes', the Seventy 'guards', Theodotion 'gomadim', the Hebrew word itself; we see to this day the island of Aradus, which is entirely a city, and has opposite it the town of Antaradus, and is near to Tyre, and lies out off the Phoenician shore of the mainland. These are in the army of the Tyrian city and are the guards of its towers, and they hang their quivers all around and complete its beauty, so as to show that they are archers; or they are pygmies, that is, warriors and most ready for wars, ἀπὸ τῆς πυγμῆς, which in the Greek language is rendered 'into combat'. But if the Aradians mean 'those who put down', everyone who puts forward the knowledge falsely so called, and has in the quiver of his breast the fiery darts of the devil, with which he wounds and sets on fire the hearts of the deceived, is to be called an Aradian: for he desires to put down those who strive to climb to the heights, and he completes the beauty of Tyre, of which it is also written in Proverbs: Let not the desire of beauty deceive you, nor be captured by your eyes, and again: Like earrings in the nostrils of a pig, so is beauty to a woman of bad character.
Commentary on Ezekiel

The Carthaginians were your traders, by reason of the multitude of all riches; with silver, iron, tin and lead they filled your fairs. Not only in the present place, but also in Isaiah, where it is written: Howl, ships of Carthage, the other translators rendered the Hebrew word as 'Tharsis'; and that these are a colony of the Tyrians no one doubts; they themselves, from the regions of the west, filled the fairs of Tyre with silver, iron, tin and lead. 'Tharsis' in our language sounds 'exploration of joy'; but we ought not to understand the explorers here in a good sense, such as Moses had sent to explore the land of promise, but in the contrary sense, such as the Apostle too says that he avoids: Because of the false brothers secretly brought in, who came in to explore our liberty which we have in Christ, and of whom Joseph speaks: You are explorers; you have come to examine the tracks of the land, and his brothers, understanding that it is no small crime to explore other people's things through ambush, answered: Your servants are not explorers. These, then, multiply the fairs of Tyre not with gold nor with precious stone, but with silver, iron, tin and lead, having the charm of eloquence and weapons for assault, and in the tin the likeness of eloquence, which counterfeits silver, and in the lead the heaviest impiety, according to Zechariah, in whom a woman sits upon a talent of lead, and the Egyptians were sunk into the deep like lead. The discussion of the individual metals would be long, but we must strive for brevity.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Greece, Tubal and Meshech, they were your dealers; they brought slaves and vessels of bronze to your people. From the house of Togarmah they brought horses and horsemen and mules to your market. (LXX: "All Greece and the parts adjacent to it, they were your traders in the souls of men, and they gave vessels of bronze as your merchandise. From the house of Togarmah they gave horses and horsemen and mules as your fairs.") 'The Ionians,' he says, '— who in Hebrew are called Iauan —, and Tubal — that is, the eastern Iberians, or the Spaniards from the regions of the west, who are called by this name from the river Iberus —, and Meshech — whom we understand as the Cappadocians, whose metropolis, which was later called Caesarea by Augustus Caesar, is to this day called Mazaca in their own language —, these made the precious commerce of Tyre, bringing slaves and bronze vessels from Corinth to Tyre, and from the house of Togarmah, that is, from Phrygia, horses and horsemen and mules, of which that province once had the greatest abundance'. The Hebrews say that 'Greece', that is, 'Iauan', means 'is and is not', which refers properly to secular 'wisdom', in which, if they find something rightly, it is called 'is', if in the contrary sense, 'is not'. For they too, by the good of nature, discourse much on duties, on continence, on despising riches — which the Stoics properly claim for themselves —, and they seem to gain the souls of the men whom they have deceived; and they have bronze vessels, with which they counterfeit the likeness of gold, which they press upon the peoples of Tyre so as to trip them up with the opinion of false doctrine; from the house too of 'Thogorma', which means 'pilgrim' and 'stranger', horses will be brought to its market and fairs, and horsemen and mules, of which it is written: A horse is a deceitful thing for safety, and in another place: All who mounted horses have slumbered, and in the Psalms: Do not become like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding; for which reason Doeg too, the accuser and slayer of the priests, was also the overseer of many; and that these are from the house of the stranger and pilgrim, who do not eat the flesh of the lamb, of whom it is written: The stranger and the hireling shall not eat of it, so that all the fairs of Tyre are filled with these wares.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Many islands were the trade of your hand: they exchanged teeth of ivory and of ebony at your price. The Syrian was your trader because of the multitude of your works: drop, purple and checkered cloths and byssus and silk and chodchod they set out in your market. (LXX: "From the islands they multiplied your trade: elephants' teeth, and to those who were brought in you paid your wages. Men were your trade from the multitude of your market: in aphec, stacte, and many-threaded cloths from Tharsis, and ramoth and chodchod they gave as your fairs.") The edition of the Seventy differs much from the Hebrew in the present place; therefore a few things must be said according to each, lest, occupied with the wares of Tyre, we pass too slowly to the remaining prophecies. The sons of Dadan, the traders of Tyre, multiplied its trade from many islands, so that they gave elephants' teeth to those who came to its commerce, and had men in the fairs because of the multitude of the trade. They had, moreover, 'in aphec' — which was added in the Seventy from the edition of Theodotion, for which Symmachus rendered 'polymita' [many-threaded cloths] —, 'stacte' too — for which all the others translated 'purple', which in Hebrew is called 'argaman' —, and 'varieties from Tharsis' — for which in the Hebrew 'bus' is said, which has been translated by all as 'byssus'. But Tharsis is not found at all in the present place —. And 'ramoth', they say, and 'chodchod' they gave as your fairs — which is found so in the Hebrew, except that for 'ramoth' Aquila translated 'silks' or 'fine stuffs'; but 'chodchod' all the translators rendered just as it is set down in the Hebrew —'.
Commentary on Ezekiel

But from many islands, to pass to the ἀναγωγὴν, which are beaten by the salty and bitter waves of this age, the traders of Dadan bring teeth of ivory, promising the whiteness of eloquence, of which it is written: From the ivory houses, from which the daughters of kings delighted you in your honor; but they are not white, nor do they imitate the bride of whom it is said: Who is this who comes up made white, leaning upon her kinsman?, but are of ebony, of a black color, who cannot change their blackness, as Jeremiah says: If the Ethiopian will change his skin and the leopard his mottling. 'The Syrian' too, that is, 'aram', who means 'lofty' and swells with pride, is a trader of Tyre, and in the multitude of the Tyrian works he brings in the knowledge falsely so called, promising many varieties and 'stacte' of the best odor, and purple of royal dignity, and checkered cloths from the dialectical art, and byssus, for which the Seventy translated 'Tharsis', given over to the works of the earth, and silk, for which in the Hebrew is written 'ramoth', which means 'vision of death' — for all earthly works hasten to destruction —, and 'chodchod', whatever it is that is understood by it, setting them out in the fairs of Tyre. 'Dadan', moreover, judging from those wares which are said to be brought by its traders and islands, is to be understood either as the region of India, or, as some suppose, as that of the Edomites and of the vast desert, and it sounds 'kinship', so that we may recognize in the heretics a likeness of the divine doctrines.
Commentary on Ezekiel

The sons of Dadan were your traders. In place of which, intending I know not what, the Seventy translated 'the sons of the Rhodians', unless perhaps by the deceptive similarity of the first letter, so that instead of 'Dadan' they read 'Radan', which itself is also the largest of the Cyclades, and was once a most powerful city in the Ionian Sea and glorious in naval combat, and, because of its very safe harbor, the resort of all merchants. And since 'Rhodians' is rendered in our language 'seeing judgment', it is now said tropologically of those who discern the truth of judgment and do not themselves do it, as the Apostle says: Therefore you are inexcusable, O man, every one who judges; for in that in which you judge another, you condemn yourself, for you do the same things which you judge. But it is better to take 'Dadan' as the name of another place, as it is found in the Hebrew and among the other translators.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Therefore, according to the Seventy, the sons of the Rhodians, traders of Tyre, multiplied its trade from very many islands; according to the Hebrew, after the sons of Dadan, its traders, islands too of various nations increased its merchandise, bringing teeth of ivory from India and ebony wood — which, being of a black color, are most precious —, and exchanged them for other wares of Tyre.
Commentary on Ezekiel

'The Syrian' too was a trader of Tyre, for which in the Hebrew is set down 'aram', in whose place the Seventy translated 'men', reading 'adam' for 'aram', deceived, as above, by the similarity of the letters 'res' and 'daleth' [r and d]. And to this day there remains in the Syrians an inborn ardor for trade: they run about through the whole world out of desire for gain, and they have such a madness for trading that, now that the Roman world has been seized, they seek riches amid swords and the slaughter of the wretched, and flee poverty through dangers; men of this kind are the traders of Tyre who deal in many-threaded cloths, purple and checkered cloths, and who set out byssus too, and silk and chodchod, in the market for her. For 'purple', which all translated, the Seventy rendered 'stacte', that is, 'drop'; but what 'chodchod' signifies I have not been able to find up to the present — the Hebrews say that all the most precious wares are signified by this name, or that it is a certain kind of precious wares which the Roman tongue does not express, or that it is the common term of those who sell trinkets —.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Judah and the land of Israel, they were your dealers in first wheat; balsam and honey and oil and resin they set out in your fairs. (LXX: "Judah and the sons of Israel, these were your traders in the commerce of grain and in ointments; first honey and oil and resin they gave in your fairs.") The Hebrew word 'phanag' Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion translated just as it is set down among the Hebrews; for it the Seventy rendered 'ointments', we 'balsam'. It is told, moreover, with what supplies the land of Judea, which is now called Palestine, abounds: grain, balsam, honey and oil and resin, which are brought by Judah and Israel to the fairs of Tyre. And since the letter is plain, according to the spiritual sense we say: the land of confession and the understanding of one who sees God, which refers to the Church, ought not to bring to Tyre the first wheat, which, falling into the earth, is multiplied and is taken for the word of God: for not by bread alone does man live, but by every word of God; then balsam, which grows in the vineyards of En-gedi, or ointment, of which it is written: Like the ointment on the head, which runs down onto the beard, the beard of Aaron; and honey, of which Solomon also speaks: Finding honey, eat as much as is enough; for if you eat more, you will vomit it up, since through excessive surfeit honey turns into wormwood; oil too, from which the lamp is lit in the tabernacle of God, lest that prophetic word be applied to us: You were selling oil in Egypt; for if it is in Egypt and in Tyre, it will be turned into its contrary, and it will be said of it: But let not the oil of the sinner fatten my head; and resin too is gentle, suited to bodies, and is taken for medicine, whence it is written in Jeremiah also: Is there no resin in Gilead; or is there no physician there? Why has the healing of the daughter of my people not gone up?; this resin Jacob too had, and he sent it to his son Joseph with honey and terebinth, nuts, incense and stacte; the Ishmaelites too, who bought Joseph from the land of Israel, were carrying these things to Egypt: incense and resin from Gilead and stacte. And that we may know more clearly what it is to bring grain, balsam, honey and oil and resin to the market of Tyre, let us hear the words of the Lord, who says: Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor cast your pearls before swine; to the Canaanite woman also, who was praying for her daughter, saying: My daughter is badly troubled by a demon, the Lord answered: It is not right to take the children's bread and give it to dogs. But because she had gone out from the borders of Tyre and Sidon and was drawing near to the land of Israel, she therefore obtained what she had asked.
Commentary on Ezekiel

The Damascene was your trader in the multitude of your works, in the abundance of various riches, in rich wine, in wool of the best color. (LXX: "Damascus was your trader in the multitude of your works, out of the multitude of all your strength: wine from Chelbon and wool from Miletus.") For 'rich wine', which Symmachus translated, both in Aquila and Theodotion and in the Hebrew itself it has 'wine from Chelbon'; and again, where we have put 'wool of the best color' or 'shining', Aquila and Theodotion translated 'in wool of Soor'. It signifies, moreover, that among the other trades of Tyre, very rich wine and choice wool were brought to its fairs from Damascus, which we see to this day. But if 'Damascus' means 'drinking blood', and it is a true tradition of the Hebrews that the field in which Abel was killed by the fratricide Cain was in Damascus, whence the place too is marked with this name — rightly, too, Paul, after the killing of Stephen, the first martyr in Christ, went to Damascus to lead believers in Christ bound to Jerusalem, and, by the mercy of God, who makes the seeing and the blind, he lost the eyes of the flesh so as to receive those of the mind, and the scales of the dragon fell from his eyes, through which he had lost the light of truth, so that he went to the street which is called 'Straight', and found 'Ananias', who in our language means 'obedient' —, from this land, then, to which it was said: Cursed is the earth which opened its mouth and drank the blood of your brother, the fairs of Tyre are gathered, and rich wine or shining wool, for which 'Chelbon' means 'milky', and for 'wool of the best color', 'wool from Miletus' — or 'Soor': 'Miletus' is not found in the Hebrew, but because choice wool is brought from there, those who translated understood 'Miletus' for 'Soor' —; from which it is to be perceived that Tyre feeds on the milk of infancy, and has no garments of its own, but from elsewhere: gathered from various provinces. That 'Damascus' means 'blood of sackcloth' and 'blood of a kiss' does not suit the present place; for Hebrew names are frequently interpreted variously, according to the diversity of accents and the change of letters and vowels, especially those which have their own properties among them.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Dan and Greece and Mozel set out wrought iron in your fairs; stacte and calamus were in your trade. (LXX: "※ Dan and Iauan and Mozel in your fairs ⁚" — which in their edition were added from Theodotion —; "iron made by workmanship and a wheel is in your mixture.") From the name of the patriarch Dan both the tribe and the place in which the tribe dwelt received their name, where today is Paneas, which was formerly called Caesarea Philippi, whence the river Jordan too obtained its name: 'Ior', that is, stream, 'Dan', which flows from Lebanon; 'Iauan', moreover, sounds 'Greece', which means, as we have said, 'is and is not'; for 'Mozel' too Symmachus translated 'bringing', so that the sense is: 'Dan and Greece brought wrought iron into your fairs, and the rest'; but Aquila for 'Mozel' put 'from Uzal', from which regions we must believe that iron and stacte and calamus were carried to the fairs of Tyre. And let us say that Greece, that is, Iauan, has wrought iron, most ready for wars and constructed by the dialectical art, boasting that it brings forth all things by judgment and reason, and that it promises a vocal sound, which is interpreted in the calamus, and stacte of the best odor; or wrought iron, and a wheel which revolves in the composition of words and has the course of speech.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Dadan were your dealers in carpets for sitting. (LXX: "Dedan were your traders with choice beasts for chariots.") The Hebrew and the Seventy differ much in the present place, except for the name of the region, which is close: 'Dedan' and 'Dadan'. For there is an infinite distance between 'carpets for sitting' and 'choice beasts for chariots'; nor is there any doubt that four-horse teams, chariots and horses are taken in the bad sense if they are earthly; otherwise, of heavenly ones, Elijah too is carried off in a chariot, and is called by Elisha: Father, father, charioteer and chariot of Israel, and the eyes of Gehazi are opened, so that he sees chariots on the mountain and horses without riders, prepared for the Lord's seat; but in the carpets the beauty of words is shown, on which the dealers of Dedan ride and rest, in a composed sitting, coming to the fairs of Tyre.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Arabia and all the princes of Kedar, they were the traders of your hand; with lambs and rams and kids they came to you. For 'lambs, rams and kids' the Seventy translated 'camels and rams and lambs'. Arabia and the princes of Kedar — which today is the region of the Saracens —, as has been shown most fully in the discourse of Jeremiah which is written against Kedar, abound in these animals, namely lambs and rams and kids — and it multiplies the fairs of Tyre by this importation —, and it is also a region most fertile in camels, because of the breadth of the desert's pastures and the mildness of the air, in which this animal delights. 'Arabia', moreover, means 'evening', and 'Cedar' 'darkness', of which it is also said in the Psalms: I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar; these regions bring to Tyre camels weighed down with the heaviest burdens of sins, or lambs and rams and kids, which they sacrifice on their altars, which they have feigned out of an iniquitous, rebellious heart. But in this same prophet too, in the vision of the shepherds, we read of rams troubling the purest waters and thrusting at the sheep with their flanks and fighting with their horns; of kids too, which are accustomed to stand at the left; and of lambs, which counterfeit the lamb of whom it is written: Behold the lamb of God, behold him who takes away the sins of the world. But in the good sense: Isaiah writes that camels from 'Madian' — which means 'judgment of the Lord' — come to Jerusalem, and Ephah, and the rams of Nebaioth, and Sheba, bringing gold and frankincense — the last two of which are also offered to the Lord by the Magi —; and these camels, having laid down the burden of sins, can enter the strait and narrow way which leads to life.
Commentary on Ezekiel

The sellers of Sheba and Rema, they were your traders, with all the first spices and with most precious stone and gold, which they set out in your market. In the Psalms, where it is written: The kings of the Arabians and of Saba will offer gifts to you, in the Hebrew it has: The kings of Saba and Saba will offer gifts to you, of which one 'Saba' is written with the letter 'sen', the other with 'samech', which is like our letter. Since, then, 'Saba' means 'conversion', this must be said: that in the present place it signifies not 'conversion' but 'aversion', from which gifts are brought to Tyre, with all spices and the best odors and precious stone and gold, all of which are set out in the fairs of Tyre; for they too counterfeit the best odor, and the precious stone with which they strive to build the churches of their perversity, and the gold which they promise in meaning, and all things are perverse — for they receive nothing freely nor give freely, but trade in everything, whereas the kings of the Arabians and of Sheba offer gifts to Christ freely —; these are they who do all things for the sake of shameful gain, and they have received these gifts from him who says in the Gospel: All these have been delivered to me, and these, if you fall down, I will give you. 'Rema', or, according to the Seventy, 'Regma', I have not been able to find in any other place of the Scriptures, nor what region it is, or what it signifies, except, what is clear, also from the fact that it is joined to Saba, that it is a region neighboring this province.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Aran and Chenne and Eden were traders, Saba, Assur, Chelmad your sellers. They were your traders in many ways, in wrappings of hyacinth and of many-threaded cloths and of precious treasures, which were wrapped and bound with ropes. (LXX: "Charran and Channa and Edne, these were traders, Saba, Assur and Chalmad your dealers, bringing trade ※ in Machalim and in Galima ⁚ hyacinth, and ※ polymita ⁚ choice treasures bound with ropes.") These too are nations containing the names of various places. What was added in the Seventy from Theodotion: In Machalim and in Galima, Symmachus translated: In precious wrappings; 'polymita' too, for which Theodotion translated 'varied', we added from Aquila and Symmachus — the garments of the traders were so precious that they were carried in wrappings and bound with ropes of hyacinth —; 'Aran', or, as the Seventy said, 'Charran', sounds in our language 'holes'; 'Chenne', 'preparation'; 'Eden', 'delights', for which among the Seventy is 'Edne', which is not found in the Hebrew; what it sounds we do not know, and we ought not to seek the ἐτυμολογιὰν of a fictitious name.
