And when I come, I will put a bridle in your jaws, or bind with snares your mouth with which you spoke so grandly, and all your allies and leaders, whom they call fish, I will make cling to your wings or scales, so that, drawn out of the river, you may be cast out or set down: for you had lifted yourself up too high, in the desert; and you will fall upon the face of the field, or of your land, because Egypt is a province of plains, and your carcass will not be gathered up nor will you be brought together, that is: you will by no means be buried, but I will give you to the beasts and the birds of heaven to be devoured, so that, when they have seen these things accomplished in you by my judgment, the inhabitants of Egypt may know that I myself am the Lord; and these things will befall you because you deceived my people Israel with your help, so that they trusted not at all in God their creator but in you: you were to them a reed staff — according to Isaiah —, or a hollow rod and a most fragile reed, leaning on which they found their protection worthless, so that, as they rested their weight on you, you were broken and tore the shoulder and the hand by which you were held, and, while they felt secure in you, all their loins were shattered as they fell to the ground and received wounds instead of help'.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Let us consider, then, what the dragon's penalty is, or what his punishment. There follows: And I will put a bridle (or a snare) in your jaws — like which is that passage of Job: But you will bring the dragon with a hook and you will put a halter around his nostrils. He will trust that the Jordan may enter into his mouth; with his eye he will take it in. But he will pierce his nostrils, with a ring his lip —. Now the Lord puts a bridle in the jaws of this dragon and pierces his lips and binds them with the circle of a ring when, through churchmen who are learned in the holy Scriptures, he imposes silence on him and all the doctrines of perversity are dissolved; and he glues the fish of his rivers to his wings or scales — by which the heretics through pride hasten to the heights —, so that they too, joined with the dragon, may make one body with him; and they are coupled to him either in fellowship of error or in likeness of punishment, just as: He who cleaves to the Lord is one spirit. Nor indeed does the Egyptian dragon have one river, but many rivers, with which he waters Egypt, low and cast down and having no mountains in it, nor the waters of Siloam, which go with silence, but 'muddy' and 'miry' ones; whence also the Lord draws him out of the midst of his rivers, so that he may by no means lie upon them nor sit in them, and all the fish cling to his scales — clinging over the whole body of the dragon, according to the quality of their vices, either to the head or to the belly or to the tail and the extremities — so that, when the dragon is drawn out, the fish too which cling to him may be drawn out together.
Commentary on Ezekiel

'And I will cast you,' he says, 'into the desert, so that you will by no means find any to deceive, or certainly I will set you down from the summit of your pride, and I will set you down swiftly' — according to that saying of the Apostle: But may the God of peace crush Satan under your feet swiftly —, so that, when the dragon is crushed and set down, the fish of his river too may be set down, and the author of crimes may fall, who formerly thought that he stood and ran about through the whole world; and let him fall upon the face of his own earth, to which he was cast headlong from heaven, so that he may by no means any longer be gathered in the churches of the heretics, nor be brought together or buried in those who believed him, once they have been freed from him, but may be given to be devoured by the beasts of the earth and the birds of heaven: the beasts, of which it is written: Do not hand over the soul that confesses to you, and the birds of heaven, which eat the seed beside the way and are interpreted by the Savior to be devils — for not only the prince of wickedness but also his disciples are named devils, according to what is said of Judas: Did I not choose you twelve? and one of you is a devil —; and they are called birds of heaven because they promise themselves lofty things; so that, after the dragon with his fish has been set down and cast out, and handed over to be devoured by the beasts of the earth, which have nothing of gentleness in them, and by those who are carried about by every wind of doctrine, then the inhabitants of this world may understand that he himself is the Lord; and the whole cause of the punishments is that he promised help to the house of Israel in vain and was to it a rod or reed staff, hollow and empty, having nothing of fullness in it, because he could not say: But we have all received of his fullness, since Scripture has commanded: You shall not appear in the sight of the Lord your God empty (or hollow); and that we ought not to ask help from Egypt, Scripture testifies elsewhere too: Woe to those who go down into Egypt for help.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Of a reed staff of this kind Rabshakeh too vainly reproaches Hezekiah king of Judah, saying: Behold, trusting in this reed rod, and a broken one, upon Egypt; whoever leans on it, it goes into his hand: so is Pharaoh king of Egypt and all who trust in him; and he indeed was lying about a righteous king in recalling these things — he who is interpreted as 'much with a kiss': for he was drunk from the golden cup of Babylon, and therefore he was thrusting his own things upon the people, while it was confessing the Lord —; here, however, Pharaoh is reproached for having been to the house of Israel a rod or reed staff, promising them help that was vain and fragile and soon to be shattered. But that we may be able to know which is the reed staff on which the house of Israel ought not to trust, we shall be able to understand it from the contrary staff and rod of the Lord, of which it is said to the Lord: Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me; this rod Aaron also had, which devoured the Egyptian dragons, and when he struck the banks of the Nile and gnats were produced in all Egypt; Moses too, according to the Seventy: Stretched out this rod and lifted it to heaven, and the Lord brought the south wind upon the land all that day and all night, and in the morning the wind lifted and brought locusts upon all the land of Egypt; of this rod, I think, it is also written in the book of Numbers that it blossomed and budded into a nut or almond; this the Apostle had, saying: What do you wish? Shall I come to you with a rod?; and those who celebrated the Passover held staffs in their hands, without which, as they support the weakness of the human body, they could not eat the flesh of the lamb; this is the rod from the root of Jesse, upon which the seven spirits rested. But not such is Pharaoh, nor the staff of Egypt and the reed rod, which deceives those who take hold of it and tears their shoulders, that is, their strength; and whoever leans upon it, his loins are loosened, and he cannot stand nor, girded in the reins, celebrate the Passover; which befits those whose hearts and reins God searches.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Therefore thus says the Lord God: Behold, I will bring a sword upon you, and I will kill from you man and beast; and the land of Egypt shall be a desert (or destruction and solitude), and they shall know that I am the Lord. Because he said (or you said): the river is mine, and I made it (or the rivers are mine, and I made them); therefore behold, I am against you and against your rivers, and I will make the land of Egypt into solitudes, laid waste by the sword (or destroyed) from the tower of Syene (or from Migdol and Syene) to the borders of Ethiopia. The foot of man shall not pass through it, nor shall the foot of beast walk in it, and it shall not be inhabited for forty years; and I will make the land of Egypt deserted in the midst of deserted lands, and its cities in the midst of overthrown cities: they shall be desolate for forty years, and I will scatter (or sow) the Egyptians among the nations, and I will winnow them into the lands. For thus says the Lord God: After the end of forty years I will gather Egypt (or the Egyptians) from the peoples (or from the nations) among whom they had been scattered, and I will bring back the captivity of Egypt, and I will settle them in the land of Pathros, in the land of their birth (or in the land from which they were taken); and they shall be to you for a kingdom (or a lowly principality). Among the other kingdoms it shall be the lowliest, and it shall no longer be lifted up over the nations, and I will diminish them so that they do not rule over the nations (or so that they are not many among the nations). Nor shall they any longer be to the house of Israel for confidence (or for hope), teaching iniquity, so that they flee and follow them (or they recall them to the memory of iniquity, so that they follow them), and they shall know that I am the Lord God. Join what follows to what precedes: 'Because you were a reed staff to the house of Israel, and were not only broken in its hand but — according to Isaiah — pierced its hand, and now you have torn its shoulder and were yourself shattered, and loosened the loins of those leaning on you, therefore I will bring upon you the sword of enemies, and I will lay waste beasts together with men, and the land of Egypt will be reduced to solitudes, and a second time the Egyptians will know that I am the Lord. Nor will I be content with this end, but because he burst out into such great blasphemy as to say that the rivers and all the abundance of Egypt were his, therefore I will take away both him who had called himself creator and the rivers which he had boasted were created by himself, and I will reduce the land of Egypt to a very long solitude, laid waste by the sword from the tower of Syene to the borders of Ethiopia'. For 'tower', which in Hebrew is called 'magdal', the Seventy put the name of a place, so as to write 'magdolum' [Migdol]; and the tower of Syene remains to this day, a fortress subject to Roman rule, where the cataracts of the Nile are, and up to which place the Nile is navigable from our sea.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Now the cloud of allegory must be discussed, and with the same brevity we shall try to avoid the length of this explanation too. The word is to the dragon, who had said: The rivers are mine and I made them, that the Lord himself is bringing upon him the sword of which it is written in Isaiah: My sword has become drunk in heaven: now it will descend upon the earth, to destroy from him man and beast, whatever seems to have either reason or simplicity; and to destroy not absolutely, but as to the dragon, so that they may perish to the dragon and live to God; and that the land of Egypt may become destruction, according to the sense given above, in which it perishes to the dragon, and after destruction be reduced to solitude, ceasing to have the worst of guests; and then men and beasts and the destroyed land will know that he himself is the Lord — in that sense which is written in Psalm 77 (78): When he slew them, then they sought him: For everyone who seeks will find, and it is God's mercy that the abundance of this world should perish —, and that the streams of Egypt may be dried up, nay rather that their land may be in solitudes and be laid waste by the sentence of the Lord from the tower of 'Soene' [Syene], which means 'circle', so that it has nothing straight in it, up to the land of the Ethiopians, who are called lowly, so that, namely, all pride which had raised itself against the knowledge of God may be destroyed, and be humbled unto its own salvation.
Commentary on Ezekiel

He says, therefore, that all Egypt is to be ravaged up to the borders of Ethiopia, to which the farthest region of Egypt is joined, so that the foot of man does not pass through Egypt nor are beasts found in it, and it is not inhabited for forty years — for the Egyptians are spared, and, because they were once hosts to Israel, their sentence is shorter in time: Tyre kept its sabbaths for seventy years and so was restored to its former state; the captivity of Judea too and the overthrow of the temple completed seventy years, until Cyrus king of the Persians: For the mighty shall mightily suffer torments.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Nor may the foot of man, that is, anything rational, pass through Egypt, nor the foot of beast walk in it — so that it may not hold any of the simple, whom Pharaoh, letting the men go, wished to keep in Egypt, while Moses opposed him and wished to free the beasts too from the captivity of Egypt —. And it shall not, he says, be inhabited for forty years — which number is always one of affliction and punishment: whence Moses and Elijah and the Savior himself fasted forty days and nights, and for forty years the people was in the wilderness, so that afterwards, circumcised at Gilgal, it might be freed from the reproach and disgrace of Egypt; in the mystery of this number this same prophet too slept forty days on his right side for the tribe of Judah, and the people is announced as about to serve in Egypt four hundred years, which make forty decades or four ἑκατοντάδας [hundreds]; the rains of the flood too bring shipwreck on the world for forty days: for it was just that he who, through the four elements of the world, of which all things are said to consist, had offended God while he loved and cherished them, should be punished in that very number; and that Israel, which had sinned against the sabbath, should endure a punishment of seven decades, that is, of seventy years —; and the land of Egypt is made deserted, and its cities in the midst of the overthrown lands and cities, which were not built of stones but of brick and straw, so that Egypt, which had been badly joined together, may be scattered and winnowed into the lands, namely so that the grain may be separated from the straw; and, when the end of forty years is completed, there may be a restoration of Egypt, and its captivity be brought back and settled in the land of 'Phatures' [Pathros], which means 'trampled bread', where that bread which had said: I am the bread that came down from heaven, was trampled by heretical perversity; so that, when they have come to the Church, they may dwell in the trampled bread, and by no means be lifted up into pride, but be a lowly kingdom.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And when he says: I will make the land of Egypt deserted in the midst of deserted lands, he means the Philistines, the Edomites and the Moabites and all the other regions against which the prophet's oracle stands above —; then he will scatter or sow the Egyptians among the nations and winnow them into the lands, and, because The Lord is merciful and compassionate, patient and of many mercies, after forty years there is the restoration of Egypt, and the whole captivity will be brought back to its ancient soil and settled in the metropolis, which is called Pathros, where it arose and from which it set out, only on condition that, for its own good, it loses its ancient pride and is a lowly kingdom, indeed the lowliest of all nations, and is no longer lifted up against the nations nor has rule over them, but, reduced to fewness, by no means deceives the house of Israel by confidence in itself, nor teaches them iniquity, or recalls them to the memory of iniquity, in that, having forsaken the help of God, they sought the support of Egypt; and all these things will happen so that a third time the Egyptians may know that he himself is the Lord. These things we have touched on in brief discourse, laying the foundations of the history.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And so that, even when they have been restored to their former state, they may cast themselves down through humility because they lived in Egypt and built cities of brick, and among the many kingdoms of the Church may be lowly, and may know against whom they have sinned; and that Egypt may no longer be lifted up over the churches spread through the whole world, but be reduced to fewness, and few may remain in it among the nations, according to what is written: Give them, O Lord. What will you give them? Give them a barren womb and dry breasts, so that they may by no means rejoice and exalt themselves in the multitude of the deceived, but be reduced to a few: For many are called, few chosen. And may they no longer deceive the house of Israel, that is, the Church, nor promise them a vain hope and confidence, teaching iniquity, so that they flee the discipline of the Church and follow Egyptian pleasures. And these things will happen so that a third time the Egyptians may know that he himself is the Lord; which seems to me to be said for this reason: that the first knowledge of the Egyptians may be in the flesh, the second in the soul, the third in the spirit: first upon the earth, second when the life of this world is ended, third after the resurrection.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And it came to pass in the twenty-seventh year, in the first and on one day of the month, the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon made his army serve a great service against Tyre; every head made bald and every shoulder rubbed bare, and wages were not paid to him, nor to his army, over Tyre for the service with which he served me against it. Therefore thus says the Lord God: Behold, I will give Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon in the land of Egypt, and he will carry off its multitude, and plunder its booty, and seize its spoils, and it will be wages for his army, and for the work for which he served against it. I have given him the land of Egypt because they labored for me, says the Lord God. In that day a horn shall sprout for the house of Israel; and to you I will give an open mouth in their midst, and they shall know that I am the Lord. The question is asked how, after the tenth year of the preceding discourse, the twenty-seventh year is immediately set down, and in what follows the tenth and the twelfth, and in the final description of the temple the twenty-fifth; but the solution is easy: for since both the preceding prophecy and this one which is now spoken are woven together concerning Egypt, although it was made at different times, nevertheless, because it is prophesied concerning one province, they are joined to each other; which we also frequently read in Jeremiah, that the times are described in reversed order: for in certain places the deeds of Zedekiah are related first, and afterwards those of Jehoiakim, who was before him; in the Psalms, however, because it is lyric song, the order of history is not sought.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And lest we seem to pass anything over, according to the spiritual understanding we inquire where we have read this number, that is, the twenty-seventh: in the book of Genesis Scripture testifies that in the six hundredth year of Noah's life, in the second month, on the twenty-seventh day of the second month, the waters of the flood were brought upon the face of the earth, and afterwards in the seventh month of the same year, which is near to the sabbath, and on the twenty-seventh day of the same seventh month, the waters of the flood ceased, and the ark of Noah rested upon the mountains of 'Ararat', which means 'of Armenia'; from which we understand that the number is a middle one and can be applied to either side: since in it both the wrath of God begins with the flood, and his clemency is shown in the seventh month on the same number of days; and because among the Hebrews the month, which among us is divided by the Kalends and Nones and Ides, is reckoned according to the course of the moon — whence also by the Greek word μήνη, that is, 'moon', it took its name from the month —, this has been said: that on the twenty-seventh day of the moon a little light remains, lest his wrath be entirely without mercy; but when the whole orb of the moon is filled, then both the Passover is celebrated and all the greatest solemnities. This we have set down briefly, so that we may know that in this number good and evil things are contained alike: good things for Nebuchadnezzar, whose labor is repaid with wages, evil things for the Egyptians, whose devastation is announced.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Let us speak first, then, according to the letter. When Nebuchadnezzar was besieging Tyre and could not bring rams, engines and mantlets up to the walls — because it was surrounded by the sea —, he ordered the countless multitude of his army to carry stones and earth for a mound and, having filled up the sea in between, or rather the very narrow strait, he made the neighboring shore continuous with the island; when the Tyrians saw this now all but completed, and the foundations of the walls were being shaken by the battering of the rams, whatever precious things the nobility had in gold, silver, clothing and various furnishings, it put on ships and carried off to the islands, so that, when the city was taken, Nebuchadnezzar found nothing worthy of his labor; and because in this respect he had obeyed the will of God, some years after the captivity of Tyre Egypt is given to him; and Tyre was much more savage than Egypt: for the former attacked Jerusalem, the latter promised vain help — and it is one thing to deceive hope through weakness, another to fight against the people of God —. This, then, is what he says: 'Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, in the siege of Tyre, made his army serve me, to fulfill my will: Every head made bald and every shoulder rubbed bare of those carrying baskets of earth and stones, by which shoulders are rubbed and the head is made bald; and yet neither he nor his army found anything worthy in Tyre. And since he served me in this and fulfilled my will against Tyre, therefore I will give him the land of Egypt'; which some say was fulfilled under Nebuchadnezzar, others under Cambyses son of Cyrus, who laid waste Egypt as far as Ethiopia, so that he killed Apis and destroyed all their images, for which reason they think he was turned to madness and was pierced through with his own dagger in a fall from his horse — Herodotus narrates this history most fully, where all Egypt too is described by districts and villages and forts, and the source of the Nile and the peoples of that nation and the measurement of the land in circuit up to the desert of Ethiopia, and the shores of the Great Sea, and the borders of Libya and Arabia are shown —.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Let these things have been said of the prophecy according to the letter, or rather according to the truth; but from the fact that Nebuchadnezzar received the wage of a good work, we understand that even in the case of the heathen, if they have done anything good, it is not passed over without reward by the judgment of God; whence also through Jeremiah Nebuchadnezzar is called the dove of God, because he served God's will against a sinful people. And I will bring, he says, my servant Nebuchadnezzar; from which it is clear that we are condemned by comparison with the Gentiles, if they do by natural law the things which we neglect even when written; of which the apostle Paul argues most fully to the Romans.
Commentary on Isaiah

For in another prophecy too, which is seen to be against the Egyptians, the same Scripture weaves in: Son of man, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon has made his army serve a great service against Tyre: every head made bald, and every shoulder rubbed bare, and no wage has been paid to him, nor to his army, for Tyre (Ezek 29). By this he signifies that a mound was heaped up over a long time by the army of Babylon, so that he tried beforehand to do what Alexander did afterwards, joining the island to the mainland (Quintus Curtius, book 4).
Commentary on Isaiah

We read in the histories of the Assyrians that the besieged Tyrians, when they saw no hope of escape, embarked on ships and fled to Carthage, or to other islands of the Ionian and Aegean sea. Hence too it is said in Ezekiel: No wage has been paid to him, nor to his army, for Tyre (Ezek 29): because all the wealth of the city had been carried away, and all the nobles had left it empty.
Commentary on Ezekiel

The cause of the Lord's anger against Egypt is this: that it deceived the people of God by its help, so that it would not hope in the Lord and would provoke him to wrath: 'In that day,' he says, 'on which Egypt has been taken, the horn of the house of Israel will sprout' — no doubt signifying the royal line; which some refer to Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, who was born of the stock of David through Jeconiah, others to the last time, when they think that Elijah too will come; but we, understanding the horn of the Lord as concerning Christ, touch lightly on the present history —. 'And when,' he says, 'O prophet, this has first been fulfilled, then your mouth will be opened, and your prophecy will by no means hang on a doubtful promise but will be seen accomplished in deed, so that those who have heard may know that I am the Lord, for whom to have said is to have done'.

n: Day of vengeance, (Calmet) when the Lord shall judge, (1 Corinthians v. 2.) and Egypt shall fall a prey to the most powerful nation of the Chaldeans. (Worthington)
Ethiopia. Hebrew, "Chus," denoting part of Arabia, or rather Ethiopia.

Lydia. Hebrew, "Phut," near Egypt. (Calmet) --- These troops were paid. (Haydock) --- Chub, in Mareotis. --- Covenant: the Jews or auxiliaries. Septuagint add, "the Persians and Cretans." (Calmet) --- There were Persians in Africa who followed Hercules. (Pliny, [Natural History?] v. 8.)
Messengers; the Chaldeans. (Calmet) --- The Nile was navigable as far as Syene. (St. Jerome)
Dry. The canals were obstructed (Calmet) which rendered cavalry useless. (Herodotus ii. 108.)

Memphis, the capital of Lower Egypt, (Calmet) where the idol or bull (Haydock) Apis was fed. (Calmet) --- Here Amasis overcame Apries. (Herodotus ii. 168.) --- The Chaldeans made war on the gods as well as on the people. --- Prince Amasis was tributary to Babylon. Some of this probably regards the times of Cambyses and Ochus. (Usher, the year of the world 3478 and 3653.) (Calmet) See chap. xxix. 14. (Haydock)

Taphnis, or Tanis, famous for the miracles of Moses. (Calmet) --- Alexandria. In the Hebrew No, which was the ancient name of that city, which was afterwards rebuilt by Alexander the Great, and from his name called Alexandria. (Challoner) --- Septuagint, "Memphis or Diospolis;" (Calmet) or Thebes, capital of Higher Egypt; (Bochart) though it seems rather a maritime town, Nahum iii. 8. (Calmet)
Pelusium. Hebrew Sin, (Haydock) "muddy," has the same import as pelos. (Calmet) --- The place is now called Damietta. (Haydock)
Darkened: war and misery shall ensue. --- Sceptres, by dethroning Apries. --- Pride; overflowing of the Nile. See Jeremias xlix. 19.

Year, in which Jerusalem was taken. Pharao lost a battle. His country was afterwards invaded, (Calmet) and his subjects rebelled, ver. 21. (Haydock) --- Part of the kingdom had been already subdued, 4 Kings xxiv. 7. (Worthington)

f: Commentary on Ezekiel

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, prophesy and say: Thus says the Lord God: Howl, woe, woe for the day, for the day is near, and the day of the Lord draws near, a day of cloud; it will be the time of the nations. And a sword will come upon Egypt, and there will be terror in Ethiopia, when the wounded have fallen in Egypt and its multitude has been carried off and its foundations destroyed. Ethiopia and Libya and the Lydians, and all the rest of the common throng, and Chub, and the sons of the land of the covenant with them will fall by the sword. Thus says the Lord God: And those who prop up Egypt will collapse, and the pride of its dominion will be destroyed; from the tower of Syene they will fall in it by the sword, says the Lord of hosts. And they will be laid waste in the midst of desolate lands, and its cities will be in the midst of deserted cities; and they will know that I am the Lord, when I have set fire in Egypt, and all its helpers have been crushed. On that day messengers will go out from my face in triremes to crush the confidence of Ethiopia, and there will be terror among them on the day of Egypt, for without doubt it will come. Thus says the Lord God: And I will make the multitude of Egypt cease by the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon. He and his people with him, the mightiest of the nations, will be brought to destroy the land; and they will unsheathe their swords against Egypt, and will fill the land with the slain. And I will make the channels of the rivers dry, and I will deliver the land into the hand of the most wicked, and I will lay waste the land and its fullness by the hand of foreigners. I the Lord have spoken. Thus says the Lord God: And I will destroy the images, and I will make the idols cease from Memphis, and there will no longer be a leader in the land of Egypt, and I will put terror in the land of Egypt. And I will destroy the land of Pathros, and I will set fire in Tahpanhes, and I will execute judgments in Alexandria; and I will pour out my indignation upon Pelusium, the strength of Egypt, and I will slay the multitude of Alexandria. And I will set fire in Egypt; Pelusium will be in pain like a woman in labor, and Alexandria will be laid waste, and in Memphis there will be daily distresses. The young men of Heliopolis and of Bubastus will fall by the sword, and they themselves will be led captive. And in Tahpanhes the day will grow black, when I have broken there the scepters of Egypt and the pride of its power has failed in it; a cloud will cover her, and her daughters will be led into captivity. And I will execute judgments in Egypt, and they will know that I am the Lord. (LXX: "And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, prophesy and say: Thus says Adonai the Lord: O day, for the day is near, and the way of the Lord is near, a day of cloud; it will be the end of the nations. And a sword will come upon the Egyptians, and there will be confusion in Ethiopia, and the wounded will fall in Egypt, and they will carry off its multitude, and its foundations will be cut down. Persians and Cretans and Lydians and Libyans, and all the mixed peoples, and some of the sons of my testament will fall by the sword. Thus says Adonai the Lord: And the supports of Egypt will fall, and the insolence of its strength will come down; from Migdol to Syene they will fall in it by the sword, says Adonai the Lord. And it will be made desolate in the midst of desolate regions, and its cities will be in the midst of deserted cities; and they will know that I am the Lord, when I have set fire upon Egypt, and all who help it have been crushed. On that day messengers will go out from my face, 'siim', hastening to destroy the hope of Ethiopia, and there will be confusion among them on the day of Egypt, for behold, it will come. Thus says the Lord God: And I will destroy the multitude of the Egyptians by the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, of him and of his people with him: pestilent men who have been sent from the nations to destroy the land; and they will all unsheathe their swords against Egypt, and the land will be filled with the wounded. And I will make their rivers deserted, and I will deliver the land into the hand of the most wicked, and I will destroy the land and its fullness by the hands of aliens. I the Lord have spoken. For thus says the Lord Lord: and I will make the nobles fail from Memphis and the princes from the land of Egypt, and they will be no more, and I will put terror in the land of Egypt. And I will destroy the land of Pathros, and I will set fire upon Tanis, and I will execute vengeance in Diospolis; and I will pour out my fury upon Sain, the strength of Egypt, and I will destroy the multitude of Memphis. And I will set fire upon Egypt; and Sais will be thrown into confusion with confusion, and in Diospolis there will be a breach, and waters will be poured out. The young men of Heliopolis and of Bubastus will fall by the sword, and the women will be led captive. And in Tahpanhes the day will grow dark, when I have broken there the scepters of Egypt, and the insolence of its strength will perish there; and a cloud will cover her, and her daughters will be led captive. And I will execute judgments in Egypt, and they will know that I am the Lord.") After the twenty-seventh year of the captivity of King Jehoiachin, he will return to the present time when he had begun to prophesy against Egypt — that is, to the tenth year and the tenth month, on the eleventh day of the month —, and he will say that he was commanded by the Lord to speak to all the nations and, together with them all, specially to Egypt. What then are the things he speaks?: 'Howl, woe, woe for the day, for the day is near, and the day of the Lord draws near, not glowing with a bright sun, but covered with clouds, and bringing a Babylonian storm; and when the sword has begun to lay Egypt waste, there will be terror in Ethiopia, which is neighbor to Egypt, lest the Babylonian blade reach even to itself: for the wounded will fall in Egypt, and its multitude will be carried off, and everything will be destroyed down to the foundations, so that, if anyone is found in Egypt from Ethiopia and Libya and Lydia and, in general, from the various peoples and 'Chub' — which Symmachus renders as 'Arabia' — and from the sons of the land of the covenant, that is, from the people of the Jews, he will fall by the sword with them — for which nations the Seventy put: Persians and Cretans and Lydians and Libyans, and all the mixed peoples, and the sons of my testament will fall by the sword with it —'.
Commentary on Ezekiel

We have set down these things like elementary lessons for little children, so that through letters, syllables and nouns and the joining of words they may arrive at the reading of prose or verse. Now let us approach the tropology, and let us display the vast sea of discussion on a small panel, as it were, of a painting. The Word of the Lord, which was always in the Father, came to the prophet and calls him not by his own name but 'son of man', which in the holy Scriptures is always taken in a good sense, at least in the singular number — as in this same prophet and in Daniel and in the Gospel —; otherwise, in the plural number, it is read in the opposite sense — as in that verse: Sons of men, their teeth are weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword, and again: Sons of men, how long heavy of heart? The lion indeed will roar, and who will not fear? The Lord has spoken, and who will not prophesy? —. Howl, he says, woe, woe for the day, for the day is near, and the day of the Lord draws near, a day of cloud; it will be the time (or the end) of the nations; the consummation is twofold: either the general one of all, when the end of the world has come, or the particular one of each individual, when the time of death has pressed upon him; and it is called 'near' because, compared with eternity, all time is short — whence Jacob too, of the hundred and thirty years he had lived: Few, he says, and very evil are my days, and the psalmist, discussing the frailty of the whole human race, says: Our days pass away like a shadow; reflecting on this, we shall neither be lifted up by power nor brood over riches nor rejoice in good fortune, knowing that all things are soon to be taken away —; and fittingly it is called the 'day' 'of the Lord', when the whole way of life of this world will be destroyed and, error removed, the one truth will appear; 'and a day of cloud and mist' — for no one, fearless and uncertain of the sentence, awaits the judge without dread —, and 'it will be the time, or the end, of the nations' — not of the one Egyptian nation, but of all, so that it may become clear that the prophecy concerns all the nations —.
Commentary on Ezekiel

There follows: A sword will come upon Egypt — the 'sword' turning and flaming: the divine word, which divides the good from the evil and consumes the most wicked with its fire; and 'upon Egypt': of this world —, so that there is terror in Ethiopia: those who dwell beyond Egypt in the night of error and in darkness, and whose blackness is turned to whiteness either with difficulty or not at all. And the wounded will fall in Egypt, those who had stood badly in wickedness. 'And the multitude of Egypt will be carried off' — For wide and spacious is the way that leads to death —. And its foundations will be destroyed, so that nothing of its former firmness may remain in Egypt, but, the most wicked foundations abandoned, the foundation of Christ may be laid, on which the Church may be built — every indeed planting which the heavenly Father has not planted will be rooted up; whence Jeremiah too is commanded to destroy what had been built, so that he may build better things —.
Commentary on Ezekiel

'There will perish in Egypt also the Ethiopians, Libyans, and Lydians — or, according to the Seventy, Persians, Cretans and Lydians and Libyans — and Chub, that is, the Arabs, and all the rest of the common throng — whom the Seventy translated as hybrids and mixed peoples —'; all of whom, according to the diversity of vices and the interpretation of the names which we set out in the vision of Tyre, we can understand as different nations — whence the Apostle too: You, he says, Gentiles in the flesh, who are called the foreskin: for he would never have said Gentiles in the flesh unless there were others in the spirit; and in another place: Behold Israel according to the flesh —; whence we must take great care not to return in heart to Egypt, from which we once went out, and be found among the other nations, and perish by the sword — of which it is said in what follows: The young men of Heliopolis and of Bubastus will fall by the sword —, especially since it is added: And the sons of the land of the covenant (or of my testament) will be struck down together by the blade — of whom it is written: Woe to those who go down to Egypt for help, trusting in horses and chariots —; but if men of the other nations are slaughtered in Egypt, how much more the sons of the covenant and testament of God, who, despising the bread of angels, remembered the melons and onion and garlic and cucumbers of Egypt!
Commentary on Ezekiel

Then 'the supports and props of Egypt will collapse', which held it up in wickedness: the subtleties of the dialecticians and the argumentation, the tricks, of the philosophers; 'the insolent and proud dominion will also be destroyed', of those who speak all things through arrogance and count the simplicity of the Church as nothing; for 'from the tower of Syene they will fall in it' — which lies at the farthest limits of Egypt, bordering on Ethiopia and the Blemmyes, where the Nile is unnavigable, and there is the roar of the cataracts, and everything is pathless and full of serpents and venomous creatures —; but if, as we said above, 'Magdolus' means 'magnificence' and 'Soene' 'circle', it is clear that the wealth of Egypt and its insolent strength and magnificence, that is, boasting and exaltations, perish by force as far as the circle of Egypt, where nothing is stable but rolls in an uncertain fall, and comes to ruin.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And so that we might know that all these nations had been in aid of Egypt, the following passage shows it: 'And those who prop up Egypt will collapse — or the supports of Egypt, that is, its allies —, and all the pride of its dominion — or the insolence of its strength — will be destroyed and brought down from the tower of Syene — which we have said is situated at the farthest borders of Egypt; or 'from Migdol to Syene', as the Seventy translated —. All the cities of Egypt will be deserted, so that they may acknowledge the Lord when the fire of the Chaldeans has laid everything waste and its helpers have been crushed.
Commentary on Ezekiel

'Then the Egyptian cities will be laid waste and the land will be deserted and no congregation will remain that has any firmness, so that, at the end of things, they may know that he himself is the Lord, when he has sent fire into Egypt', which the Lord desires to burn, so that the hay, wood, stubble that have been built upon the foundation of Christ may be burned up, 'and all the helpers of perverse doctrines may be crushed' — from which it is to be understood that the knowledge falsely so called, and those of whom it is written: Scatter, O Lord, the nations that want wars, are called the allies and helpers of Egypt —.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And messengers will have come — according to Aquila and Theodotion 'siim', which Symmachus translated 'hastening', and we rendered as 'triremes': for so we received it from the Hebrews — so that all the confidence of Ethiopia may be crushed, and, when the neighboring province has been made desolate, terror may seize those nearest'.
Commentary on Ezekiel

'On that day', he says, 'messengers will go out from the face of God' — of whom it is written in the Gospel: Their angels always see the face of my Father who is in heaven; and in the parable of the sowing 'the reapers, the angels', that is, 'they are messengers', are sent: To gather all stumbling blocks and cast them into the furnace of fire: where there is weeping of eyes and gnashing of teeth —, and they will hasten to fulfill the command, 'to frighten off, or crush, the confidence of Ethiopia', those who have reached the highest peak of malice; 'and, in the overthrow of Egypt, Ethiopia may be crushed and tremble, because the day of the Lord is one of vengeance and retribution', by which the darkness of sins is put to flight and the light of virtues remains.
Commentary on Ezekiel

But so that we might know what this sword was that would lay Egypt waste and terrify Ethiopia, there follows more plainly: And I will make the multitude of Egypt cease by the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, who will not only come, but will come accompanied by many nations, so that all Egypt will be filled with the blood of the slain.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And I will make, he says, the multitude of Egypt cease by the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, to whom they were handed over for him to punish — for he is the enemy and avenger who also received a wage because he had served in the siege of Tyre — the multitude of Egypt: so that the many may cease to be in Egypt, who are always in it — but if anyone should object, asking how that is said in Deuteronomy: In seventy souls your fathers went down into Egypt, but now you have become like the stars of heaven in multitude, it is easily resolved: for he did not set down an example of an earthly multitude but of a heavenly one, which shines with virtues and is full of lights —; against which multitude of Egypt 'the mightiest' of the nations are brought, to destroy the land — for whom the Seventy translated 'pestilent men', which I do not know how it suits those who are brought by the Lord, unless perhaps according to that example: A sending by most wicked angels —; and they will unsheathe their swords against Egypt and fill the land with the slain, or the wounded, so that they may feel themselves slain and wounded, and that Egypt has been destroyed to such a degree and has come to nothing that all the rivers of eloquence by which the Egyptian rush and reed of errors were watered dry up, and they are delivered into the hand of the most wicked, who torment them, and the fullness of the land of Egypt, which had grown evilly, is wiped out by the hand of those alien to God — for not good but evil angels are set over the torments —. These things must be, 'so that they may know that the Lord has spoken' — which is frequently added so that those who hear may know that the words are not the prophet's but the Lord's, whose commands cannot be void —.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And so great will be the wrath of the Lord that the channels of the rivers — that is, the διωρύγες [canals] of the Nile — will be dried down to the ground, and the fullness of Egypt will be made desolate by the hand of pestilent men — or of the most wicked men —.
Commentary on Ezekiel

'For my words cannot be void; and my indignation will advance to this point: that the images of Egypt are destroyed and the idols cease from Memphis', which to this day is the metropolis of Egyptian superstition — or the nobles and princes from Memphis and from the land of Egypt —.
Commentary on Ezekiel

There follows: And I will destroy the images (which the Seventy translated abominations), and I will make the idols (or the nobles) cease from Memphis, and a leader (or princes) in the land of Egypt; they will be no more: for it belongs to the most merciful Lord to overthrow evil works, so that no likeness that falsely counterfeits the image of truth may remain in Egypt; and that the nobles too may perish from 'Memphis', which means 'from the mouth', from which they fashioned all the idols, so that, with the heads and masters of the idols cut off, there may be no prince in Egypt, and 'all Egypt may be filled with terror and destruction'; of whose cities it is said: And I will destroy the land of Pathros, and I will set fire in Tahpanhes (or in Tanis), and I will execute judgments in 'No' (which the Seventy translated 'Diospolis'); and I will pour out my indignation upon Sain, the strength of Egypt; 'Phatures' means 'trampling of bread', 'Tanis' 'a lowly command', 'Diospolis' — in place of which the Hebrew has 'No' — 'rest', 'Sain' 'temptation'; by these names are shown the various conventicles of heretics and of all lies, who trample on and despise the bread of the Church, and follow a lowly command that does not lead to heavenly things, and give themselves over to pleasures, and are at rest — such as the rich man clothed in purple of whom we read in the Gospel —, and are slaves to temptations — one of whom sought from the Lord to have power to tempt Job —. All these the Lord destroys and sets on fire; and he will pour out his indignation upon it, and he scatters the strength of Egypt, so that, reduced to nothing, they may no longer entice the people of God and make them hope in their help, so that, truth forsaken, they seek a lie and are wounded by their protection as by a staff of reed.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And so great a terror will possess all Egypt that the whole land of Pathros will perish, and fire will lay waste Tahpanhes — or, as the Seventy translated, Tanis —. And I will execute, he says, judgments in 'Alexandria', which is so called today; but it has the ancient name 'No', which Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion translated as it stands in the Hebrew; in its place the Seventy, intending I know not what, said 'Diospolis', which is a small city of Egypt; but we have put 'Alexandria' for 'No' — by 'anticipation', which in Greek is called πρόληψις, according to that line of Vergil: and he came to the Lavinian shores: not that at that time, when Aeneas came into Latium, they were called Lavinian, but because they were later named Lavinian, so that the passage might become clearer to the reader's understanding —.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And I will pour out, he says, my indignation upon 'Sain', which we rendered as 'Pelusium'; and it is called the strength of Egypt because it has a very safe harbor and the trade of the sea is carried on there most of all — whence the poet too calls the lentil Pelusian, not because this kind of legume is grown there, or chiefly there, but because the greatest quantity of it is brought there from the Thebaid and all Egypt along the stream of the Nile —. And I will slay, he says, the multitude of 'Alexandria', which again is set down in the Hebrew as 'No', for which the Seventy translated not 'Diospolis', as above, but 'Memphis'. And, to show that the city was already populous at that time: I will destroy, he says, the multitude of 'No'.
Commentary on Ezekiel

After this it is said: And I will slay (or destroy) the multitude of 'Memphis' — in place of which the Hebrew has 'No', which above the same Seventy translated 'Diospolis', which means 'rest' —: for there are many who seek rest and want to lie on ivory beds and eat suckling lambs; or — according to the Seventy, who translated 'Memphis' —: there are many who say to others: Allow me to remove the speck from your eye, when they themselves have beams.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And I will set fire, that is, the king of Babylon, in Egypt, who, like fire, is to ravage everything. Like a woman in labor 'Sain' will be in pain, that is, 'Pelusium' (or will be thrown into confusion with confusion), and in 'Alexandria' (that is, in 'No') there will be a breach, and waters will be poured out (for which again the Seventy translated 'Diospolis'). Now it is the custom of the Egyptians, because of the flooding of the Nile, to build high embankments along the banks of the Nile; and if these have been broken through the negligence of the guards or by the excessive volume of the waters, the waters do not irrigate the fields lying below but overwhelm and ravage them; by these it is signified that Egypt was to be occupied by the army of the Chaldeans just as it is usually covered and ruined when the waters of the Nile flood and rise beyond measure. In place of the flooding of the waters and the bursting and breaching of the embankments, the Hebrew has: And there will be daily distresses in Memphis, so that where the Nile divides, and where the temple of Apis is and the oracles give answers to those who consult them, there daily distresses come about.
Commentary on Ezekiel

'And fire is set in Egypt', to consume wordiness and pleasures with its burning. 'All temptation will be in pain, and in Diospolis — which again in the Hebrew is set down as 'No' — there will be a breach', so that the waters are poured out, and every most wicked congregation is scattered and perishes here and there; or, according to the Hebrew: 'In Memphis there will be daily distresses', so that they may render account for every idle word and understand that nothing of their sayings escapes the judgment of the Lord.
Commentary on Ezekiel

'The young men also of Heliopolis — which in Hebrew is called 'On' — and of Bubastus, another city, will fall by the sword, so that the cities themselves, that is, their inhabitants, or their women, are led into captivity — the sex that lies exposed to outrage —.
Commentary on Ezekiel

The young men also of Heliopolis and of Bubastus will fall by the sword — 'Heliopoleos' is called 'On' in Hebrew, which means 'pain'; and 'Bubastus', in the Egyptian language, means 'trial of the mouth' —; all these, who could not bear the pain of the world but pursued the pleasures of Diospolis and trusted in their fluency of speech and, disputing against the other doctrines, had had experiences of victory, will fall by the sword of the word of God; and those who are called not young men at all but, from weakness of mind, women, will be led captive; or the cities themselves, through pain and the boasting of the mouth, will be brought into captivity.
Commentary on Ezekiel

But in Tahpanhes, which is a royal city, the scepters of Egypt will be broken, that is, the whole royal line; and when its power has failed, its princes slain, then the day will grow black and everything will be filled with gloom and darkness, so that the city itself is covered with a cloud of sorrow and mourning, and its daughters, that is, the remaining towns, are led into captivity; so that, after I have executed judgments in Egypt and shown myself judge to all, then the Egyptians may know that I am the Lord'.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And in Tahpanhes, he says, the day will grow black; 'Taphnae' means 'yielding to the mouth', 'of the devil' being understood; those who have yielded to him will lose the light of truth and exchange day for night, and will perceive that the scepters of Egypt and all its dominion have been broken in Tahpanhes, so that the insolent strength, or the pride of its power, fails in it, and the rays of the sun of righteousness are blinded by a cloud, and not women at all, but daughters, are led into captivity.
Commentary on Ezekiel

'And let the Lord execute not one judgment but many judgments in Egypt' — for just as there are various mansions of the good with the Father, so also there are various judgments of the punishments of Egypt — so that, when all these things have been done, the Egyptians may know that he himself is the Lord, whose judgments are true, justified in themselves.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And it came to pass in the eleventh year, in the first, on the seventh of the month, the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, I have broken the arm of Pharaoh king of Egypt, and behold, it has not been bound up so that health might be restored to it, that it might be tied with cloths and packed with linen bandages (or that it might receive a poultice) and, its strength recovered, might be able to hold a sword. Therefore thus says the Lord God: Behold, I am against Pharaoh king of Egypt; and I will shatter his arm, strong but broken (or arms strong and set in order), and I will cast the sword down from his hand, and I will scatter (or I will sow) Egypt among the nations, and I will winnow them into the lands. And I will strengthen the arms of the king of Babylon, and I will give my sword into his hands; and I will break the arms of Pharaoh and the slain will groan with groanings before his face (or, as is contained in the Seventy: And he will bring a sword upon Egypt and will plunder its booty and despoil its spoils. There follows:) And I will strengthen the arms of the king of Babylon, and the arms of Pharaoh will fall; and they will know that I am the Lord, when I have put my sword into the hand of the king of Babylon and he has stretched it out over the land of Egypt. And I will scatter Egypt among the nations, and I will winnow them into the lands, and they will know that I am the Lord. He returns to the order of the prophecy: for after the twenty-seventh year he now sets down the eleventh; and this question is contained in the earlier passages too: for although the word of the Lord against Tyre came in the eleventh year, which was set down first, in what follows he speaks to Pharaoh in the tenth year, and again sets down the twenty-seventh, as we said, and now the eleventh — to pass over the other things contained in the order of the psalms: how the third psalm — the psalms in which David changed his face before Abimelech, and on Doeg the Edomite, and when he was found in the cave, and Psalm 50 (51), of penitence, in whose title it is shown that he went in to Bathsheba the wife of Uriah, are earlier psalms than the third, in which he is noted as fleeing from the face of his son Absalom; but in the Psalms the answer is easy: that it is lyric poetry, and in a work of this kind one does not look for the order of history but for songs on the individual deeds —. In history, however, this must be said: that the things said about one matter at different times ought not to be divided in the telling but enclosed in the narrative of one passage; for example, so that the things said about Egypt at one time and another may be learned in one sequence of reading. Though we have said this, the question nevertheless remains why in this same place the word of the Lord came to Pharaoh first in the eleventh year, and afterward in the twenty-seventh, and then in the tenth year, when surely according to order the tenth year should have been noted first, the eleventh second, the twenty-seventh third, at the head of the individual prophecies; to which we can answer this: O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How inscrutable his judgments and untraceable his ways!, and in another place: The abyss and wisdom, who will search out?. We can, however, say this: that in the prophets too the order of history is not kept, at least not in all but in certain places, for they do not narrate past things but foretell future ones, as the will of the Holy Spirit has been; but in history, such as the five books of Moses and the volumes of Joshua and of Judges, Ruth also and Esther, Samuel and Malachim [Kings], the book of Chronicles and Ezra, with Nehemiah likewise joined to it, an inverted narrative is nowhere found. Let it suffice to have said this about the order of the years.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Now let us see what the prophecy against Pharaoh, or about Pharaoh, is. He says that he has broken his arm, and that it has not been bound up nor tied nor packed with linen bandages nor received a poultice — according to what is written: Not to apply a poultice, nor oil, nor bandages —; had this been done, surely, its strength recovered, he could hold a sword and go forth to wars. Therefore the merciful and compassionate God shatters his arm again, or his arms, so that the sword may fall utterly from his hand and Egypt be scattered among the nations and winnowed into the lands — but in the arm understand strength and might, as Scripture says: Crush the arm of the sinner and the evil one —; and this is crushed in our adversaries when they persecute us indeed but cannot overwhelm us; and for the salvation of the servants of God the Babylonian king often rises up against Pharaoh, so that a more powerful one overwhelms the powerful and the evil are handed over to the worse; and the arms of the most wicked are strengthened by God, so that he who has been set free may know that he himself is the Lord; and it is an advance in virtue to know that he himself is the Lord — on the contrary we can say: The sons of Eli, sons of pestilence, not knowing God, and in the good sense it is written of the kings who did what was right in the sight of God that they knew the Lord —. But what is said in the Seventy: And I will crush his arms, strong and 'set in order', which in Greek is said 'tetagmena', has been corrupted by the fault of the copyists; for they translated not 'tetagmena' but 'tetamena', that is, not 'laid down' but 'stretched out'; in place of which the other translators, according to their custom, put 'lofty'.

n: Year, about a month before the fall of Jerusalem.

Assyrian. The ruin of this great empire (Calmet) might have admonished the king of Egypt of his frail condition. (Haydock) --- About thirty-eight years before (Calmet) Ninive had been taken, and its king (Sarac or Chinaladan) slain by his own general, Nabopolassar, and by Astyages, of Media. They divided the empire between them, and the father of Nabuchodonosor fixed his residence at Babylon. (Usher, the year of the world 3378.) --- Cedar. Septuagint, "cypress." --- Top; the king of Ninive. (Calmet) --- Egypt's monarch thought himself invincible; yet would fall like the Assyrian. (Worthington)
Roots. Various nations paid tribute to the Assyrian, (St. Jerome; Calmet) while he sent his troops, like rivulets, to keep all in subjection. (Theodoret)

I have delivered. Here the time past is put for the future; i.e., I shall deliver. --- The mighty one, &c., viz., Nabuchodonosor, who conquered both the Assyrians and Egyptians; (Challoner) or rather his father, Nabopolassar, subdued the former, ver. 3. (Haydock)
Strangers; revolted Assyrians. See Psalm xvii. 46.
Branches. The nations continued, but submitted to another master.
Pit. The new king would appoint fresh governors.

Waters, as if they bewailed his fate. (Calmet) --- Those whom the king of Ninive had exalted, and the people, who wished not to submit to a foreigner, would no doubt lament the slaughtered monarch, now silent (Haydock) in the grave. (Theodoret)

Comforted. The ghosts of princes who had been subject to Serac, seeing his fall, bore their own misfortune with greater content. In the grave there is no distinction of master and slave. (Calmet) --- Surviving princes expected some emolument from the change. (Haydock)
Arm; those in power. Septuagint, "his seed." Hebrew Zora, (Haydock) means both.

Famous king of Assyria, or of Egypt. --- Pharao. (Calmet) --- Mutato nomine de te Fabula narratur. (Horace, 1. Sat. 1.) --- Though Egypt be like the most potent kingdoms, it shall likewise fall. (Worthington)

f: Commentary on Ezekiel

Let these things be said for the present according to the history; most understand them as things that will happen at the consummation of the world, and that King Pharaoh, that is, the power to which Egypt is subject, is compared to the most mighty king of the Assyrians, that is, the Antichrist; and if he falls, surely the other rulers too of this darkness and the princes of the world will fall the more easily. Let us speak, therefore, of the particulars, touching on everything briefly, so that we may seem not so much to discuss and explain obscure things as to have given material to those who wish to explain them. And first it must be discussed why in the eleventh year, the third month, on the first day of the month, the word of the Lord came to Ezekiel, saying: Son of man, say to Pharaoh king of Egypt and to his multitude. To one who is about to speak to Pharaoh, the word of the Lord comes in the eleventh year; for he had not yet come to the twelfth, which is the number of full and consummate virtue — whence also there are twelve sons of Jacob, from whom the twelve tribes are afterwards named; and the names of twelve prophets are contained in one volume; and the apostles are twelve, in whose number, because one, Judas, was a traitor, Matthias is chosen in his place; and the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, twelve years old, is raised up by the Lord; the αἱμορροοῦσα [the woman with the flow of blood] too received health in the twelfth year —, but because Pharaoh is rebuked and afterwards lamented, therefore the third month and one day are joined to the number of eleven years — whence in what follows, in the twelfth year, in the twelfth month, on the first of the month, the word of the Lord comes to Ezekiel, saying: Son of man, take up a lament over Pharaoh king of Egypt and you shall say to him; for he who is lamented is lamented for this reason, that he may understand how great goods he has lost; and yet, because he was Pharaoh, and his arm had not yet been bound up nor had he recovered his former strength, therefore, in the twelfth year and month, twenty-nine days still remain before the number of twelve years is completed — ; on the first day of the month, then, the word of the Lord comes, and he is commanded to speak to the king of Egypt and to his 'multitude' — in which it is remarkable that the four translators did not say 'people' but 'multitude': For many are called but few chosen, and in the Law it is written: You shall not be with the multitude in evil —.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And it came to pass in the eleventh year, in the third, on the first of the month, the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, say to Pharaoh king of Egypt and to his people: Whom have you become like in your greatness? Behold, Assyria like a cedar (or cypress) in Lebanon, beautiful in branches and thick with leaves, and lofty in height, and among the dense leaves (or in the midst of the clouds) its top was raised up; the waters nourished him, the deep raised him up, its rivers flowed round about its roots, and it sent out its streams to all the trees of the region. Therefore its height was raised above all the trees of the region (or of the field), and its shrubs (or branches) were multiplied ※ and its branches (or shrubs) were raised up ⁚ because of many waters. And when it had stretched out its shade, all the birds of heaven made nests in its branches, and under its leaves all the beasts of the forests brought forth young, and under its shade dwelt the assembly of all the nations; and it was most beautiful in its greatness and in the spreading (or multitude) of its shrubs (or branches), for its roots were beside many waters. The cedars (or cypresses) were not loftier than it in the paradise of God, and the firs (or pines) did not equal its top, and the plane trees (or firs) were not equal (or like) to its leaves (or branches); no tree of the paradise of God (or in the paradise of God) was likened to it and to its beauty, since I made it beautiful, and with many and dense leaves: and all the trees of pleasure (or of delights) that were in paradise emulated it. Therefore thus says the Lord God: Because it was lifted up in height, and set its top green and dense (or in the midst of the clouds) — its heart was lifted up in its height —, I delivered it (or him) into the hand of the mightiest (or the prince) of the nations; doing he will do to it (or and he will bring about its destruction): according to its impiety I cast it out. And strangers will cut it down, and the most cruel of the nations (or the pestilent of the nations); and they will throw it down upon the mountains, and in all the valleys its branches will fall, and its shrubs will be broken on all the crags (or plains) of the earth, and all the peoples of the earth will withdraw from its shade, and will leave it. On its ruin all the birds of heaven dwelt (or rested), and in its branches were all the beasts of the region. Therefore all the trees of the waters will not be lifted up in their height, nor will they set their loftiness among the wooded and leafy places (or in the clouds), nor will all that are watered by waters stand in their loftiness, for all have been delivered to death, to the lowest land, in the midst of the sons of men, to those who go down into the pit. Thus says the Lord God: On the day when he went down to the underworld I proclaimed mourning (or it mourned), I covered him with the deep and held back its rivers and restrained many waters; Lebanon was crushed (or darkened) over him, and all the trees of the field were shaken (or failed). At the sound of its fall I shook (or were shaken) the nations, when I led him (or it) down to hell with those who were going down (or go down) into the pit; and all the trees of pleasure (or of delights), choice and splendid in Lebanon, all that were watered by waters, were consoled in the lowest land. For they too with it (or him) will go down (or went down) to hell to those slain (or wounded) by the sword, and the arm (or seed) of each of those dwelling under its shade in the midst of the nations (or perished of their life). To whom have you been likened, O renowned and lofty one among the trees of pleasure? Behold, you have been brought down with the trees of pleasure to the lowest land; in the midst of the uncircumcised you will sleep with those who were slain by the sword; so Pharaoh and all his multitude, says the Lord God. As is my custom, I have blended both editions, where, however, they differed very greatly, so that a double setting-out of the text would not increase the size of the books. And first it must be known that whatever is said about the king of the Assyrians in future time is recorded in the Seventy as already past, and he speaks thus either to the tree or to the prince of the Assyrians, so that it is understood of one person in the masculine as well as in the feminine gender, while the tree is referred to the Assyrian and the Assyrian is named in the tree; nor is any mention made of the Babylonian king in the present discourse, lest he, placed in Chaldea, should seem to provoke the wrath of the masters and rulers against the captive people; but it is said of the king of the Assyrians, who had already at that time been captured by the Chaldeans, and all the strength of the Assyrians lay subject to the Babylonian empire; whence also the Assyrians take captive the ten tribes, that is, Israel, while the Chaldeans overcome the two, that is, Judah and Benjamin, and overthrow the city of Jerusalem. The divine word, then, being about to speak against Pharaoh king of Egypt and his people, used such an opening against him: Whom have you become like in your greatness? Behold, Assyria like a cedar in Lebanon and the rest; and the sense is: 'Do not wonder if you are to be conquered by the Babylonians and to perish, and to lose your empire, and all the wealth of Egypt is to be destroyed, since Assyria, much stronger than you, has been destroyed when the same Chaldean prevailed'; and he describes the power of the Assyrian king under the figure of a tree, a 'cedar' according to the Hebrew, a 'cypress' according to the Seventy, set on Mount Lebanon, which is beautiful in branches and dense with leaves and raised up right to the clouds, which grew so great for this reason, that it is watered not by waters but by deeps, that is, by most abundant waters — for the deep is a multitude of the sound of waters —, so that all the birds made nests in its branches, and under its leaves all the beasts of the forests brought forth young; and lest we should doubt what the birds of heaven were, and what the beasts of the woods, he put it more openly: And under its shade dwelt the assembly of very many nations. The cedars, he says (and cypresses), the firs (or pines) and the plane trees (or cypresses) were not equal to its branches; and, so as not to speak of all the trees one by one: All, he says, the trees of the paradise of God were not likened to it and to its beauty, by which some understand that it is said not of the Assyrian king, but of the adverse power which in the discourse on Tyre is said to have been made among the cherubim and adorned with precious stones, and afterwards by its own fault to have fallen down to earthly things, which in Isaiah too is called 'Lucifer falling', and is marked out by the Lord in the Gospel: I saw Satan like lightning falling from heaven; but let us, in order to follow the history for the present, understand all these things as said ὑπερβολικῶς [hyperbolically], because the Assyrian was of such great power and so oppressed all the nations that he compared himself to the might of the angels; and all things are said μεταφορικῶς [metaphorically] to the Assyrian under the very lofty 'cedar' or 'cypress', and his slaying is called 'cutting down'.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And it is said to the king of Egypt: Whom have you become like in greatness (or height) of yours? — because he too exalted himself and is subject to that sentence: Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled —, but yet he is not like the height of the one who was like a cedar, or cypress, in Lebanon: Beautiful in branches and thick with leaves, and lofty in height, and raised his head right up to the clouds — to which, according to David, the truth of God reaches, and which are commanded not to rain a shower upon Israel —.
Commentary on Ezekiel

His beauty too is proclaimed, which was changed into ugliness by a depraved will — so that it is said of him: The Lord will break the cedars of Lebanon —, and he, lofty and set on Lebanon, the highest of mountains, would fall the more heavily the more sublime he had been; and holy Scripture, wishing to show his height, calls him a great top which the waters nourished — not the waters of Siloam: Which go with silence, but the waters of Rezin and the waters of Egypt, of which it is written: What is it to you, that you should drink the water of Geon (or Sior, which means 'turbid' waters)? —. The deep also exalted him — the deep over which darkness was borne at the beginning of the world, and into which in the Gospel the demons beg not to be sent —; the rivers of that same deep were round about his roots — of which it is said: What have you to do with the way of the Assyrians, that you should drink the waters of the rivers?, and in another place: Behold, the Lord will bring upon you the water of the river, strong and abundant, the king of the Assyrians and all his glory —; the deep also sent out its streams to all the trees of the region, so as to water not only the prince of this world but also his allies.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Therefore he was lifted up and grew up above all the tallest trees, and his shrubs were multiplied, and he possessed the empire of the whole world, saying: All these things have been delivered to me; and his branches were lifted up, which had been watered by the waters of the deep.
Commentary on Ezekiel

He stretched out, or spread, his shade, so as to subject all to his sway. In its branches all the birds of heaven made nests — For everyone who commits sin is born of the devil and is counted among the number of his branches; and those birds made nests in his branches which ate the seed beside the way in the Gospel, or, since All have sinned and are in need of the mercy of God, of whom it is said: All have turned aside, together they have become useless, for this reason they made nests in his branches —; there follows: And under its leaves all the beasts of the forests brought forth young, those which have lost the gentleness of Christ, and under its shade dwelt the assembly of very many nations, so that there was no one who was not touched by his shade — except the one who said: Behold, the prince of this world comes, and will find nothing in me. Through one indeed man sin entered into the world, and through sin death, and so death passed through to all men, in which we all sinned; and in Adam we all die; and we have all sinned and are in need of the glory of God —; and yet in that very dwelling the condition is different: some dwell in his branches like birds, promising themselves knowledge in philosophy and in the doctrines of heretics, others like beasts, wild, savage and cruel, others like a multitude of very many nations, so that he signifies those mixed up in various vices and sins.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Now Assyria was most beautiful in its greatness and in the spreading of its shrubs, because its root had been watered by many waters, so much so that in the paradise of God none of the cedars and cypresses was higher, nor did firs and pines equal its loftiness, or plane trees were not equal to its leaves; and for this reason none of the trees planted in paradise had been made equal to it, because: No tree of the paradise of God was likened to it and to its beauty — for they were by no means lifted up through pride, but knew their humility, nor did they try with a sacrilegious mind to claim likeness to God for themselves —, and what follows: And all the trees of delights that were in paradise emulated it, we expound thus: 'The trees of paradise emulated the multitude of its branches' — For many are called but few chosen, and: Wide and spacious is the way that leads to death —; for it longs to have as many for salvation as Assyria had for perdition.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Whence, because Assyria was lifted up in height, and set its loftiness green and dense (or raised its top right up to the clouds), and its heart was lifted up, so that he said: I will be like the Most High, therefore he was delivered into the hand of the mightiest of the nations — which let us understand as another detestable power, to which he is delivered for punishment: for he is the enemy and the avenger; so that Assyria is understood as the Antichrist, and the mightiest of the nations, to whom he was delivered, as Satan, according to that saying of the Apostle: Whom I have delivered to Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme —, who: Doing will do to him whatever has been commanded him by the Lord: and this cypress was cast out of the paradise of God on account of its impiety.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And what follows: I delivered it into the hand of the mightiest of the nations, he calls the Babylonian king, so that he may understand that his conquering the Assyrian was not of his own might but of divine power. According to its impiety, he says, I cast it out, so as secretly to warn the Babylonian that he ought not to be cruel nor oppress the people of God which had been delivered to him, lest he suffer things like those of the Assyrian, who was cruel and impious.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And strangers and the most cruel of the nations will cut it down (or, according to the Seventy, the pestilent), which he would never say while placed in Chaldea, lest he stir up their madness against his own nation; it is also thrown down upon the mountains, and in all the valleys its branches fall and are broken on the crags, and it is abandoned by all the peoples, that is, by the birds of heaven and the beasts of the field, and it will come to such great destruction that all the trees which were thought lofty in comparison with the Assyrian tree cease, by its example, to be lifted up any longer and raised on high, nor do they stand in their height, but, once it has been cut down, all are cut down together by fear; and what had been said by metaphor becomes clearer: All, he says, have been delivered — kings is understood — to death, to the lowest land, that is, to hell, in the midst of the sons of men, by no means among trees, to those who go down into the pit, by which there is no doubt that he means the infernal regions.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And strangers and cruel men will cut it down (or the pestilent among the nations) — so that that which is written may be fulfilled: When the pestilent man is scourged, the fool will become wiser, and again: Already the axe is laid to the roots of the tree —, and they will cut it down upon the mountains, so that it falls in its pride. In all moreover the valleys its branches will fall, so that all who were in his retinue are led down to Tartarus and withdraw from its shade and leave it, so that the birds of heaven and the beasts of the earth, which before had been under it and were covered by its shade, afterwards become partakers of its punishment.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And when the other trees of the forests, or of paradise, see that Assyria the cypress has fallen by the sentence of the Lord, they will not be lifted up in pride, nor will they think themselves anything, nor will they consider the watering of their waters their own riches: because all the branches and the birds of heaven and the beasts of the earth which were under the rule of Assyria are led down to death, to the lowest land — of whom it is written: In his sight all who go down into the earth will fall, and in another place: They will go into the uttermost parts of the earth —, and they will be by no means with the angels, but with the sons of men: Who go down into the pit (or into the ditch) everlasting.
Commentary on Ezekiel

After the cutting down of the Assyrian tree, or on the day when the Assyrian went down to the underworld, the Lord proclaimed mourning, and again by metaphor speaks of him, that he was covered with the deep — according to that which is written: I came into the depth of the sea, and the tempest overwhelmed me —, and that all the rivers, namely all the nations, ceased to water him any longer; and that Lebanon was saddened, or darkened, over her, that is, the tree, or over him, that is, the Assyrian.
Commentary on Ezekiel

But when he has gone down into the uttermost part of the earth and has become the portion of foxes, by which he is to be torn, then there will be mourning, either of all his allies or of the holy powers, who will grieve that he has gone down to the underworld; whence the Lord says: I covered him with the deep, by whose waters he had before been nourished, and I held back its rivers, that is, the deep's, and restrained many waters, so that they would not water him but rather overwhelm him; Lebanon was saddened over him, in which he had been exalted, and all the trees of the field were shaken, dreading a like cutting down.
Commentary on Ezekiel
