And lest we should think the discourse is about a tree, there follows: At the sound of its fall I shook the nations — for what fall of a single tree can be so great that all the nations are shaken at its sound? —, when I led it, he says, down to hell — according to the letter, a tree cannot be led down to the underworld — with the others who were going down into the pit, that is, to the underworld; and were consoled in the lowest land, namely in the heart of the earth, all the trees of pleasure (or of delights, which in Hebrew is called 'eden', so as to signify wooded glades and forests), choice and splendid, which were in Lebanon and were watered by waters. For those trees too with it, that is, with the Assyrian, will go down to hell to those slain (or wounded) by the sword — trees are not wounded by swords but felled, nor do they go down to hell —, and the arm, he says (or seed, since among the Hebrews the word 'zara' signifies both), rests in its shade in the midst of the nations, not of the forests at all, but of the nations.
Commentary on Ezekiel

At the sound of its fall I shook the nations, so that no one would be ignorant of his destruction and of his being led down to the underworld with his other allies; and all the trees of pleasure, that is, of paradise, received consolation, while they see evil things repaid to the evil and good things to the good — and these are the trees of Lebanon, watered by the waters of the rivers of the Lord, with which that tree too which fell had been watered; or all the trees which once were good and were watered by waters and dwelt on the height of Lebanon will receive consolation when they see their prince suffer like torments —; for they too will go down to hell to those slain by the sword of the Lord, and all the strength of the trees will dwell under its shade, that is, in punishment, in the midst of all the nations which will be held by the bars of hell.
Commentary on Ezekiel

At the end an apostrophe is made to the Assyrian himself or to Pharaoh: To whom have you been likened, O renowned and lofty one among the trees of pleasure? 'No one', he says, 'was your equal, but you surpassed all kings in power, and yet with the other kings who were in your retinue you have been brought down to the lowest lands, that is, to the underworld' — as Scripture says: They will go into the uttermost parts of the earth, they will be delivered into the hands of the sword, they will be portions for foxes —. In the midst, he says, of the uncircumcised you will sleep with those who were slain by the sword: he shows what the trees were, what the cedar or cypress, wounded by swords and lying with the uncircumcised; and, to join the last things to the earlier, since he had said above: Whom have you become like in your greatness? Behold, Assyria like a cedar in Lebanon, beautiful in branches and leaves and the rest, he now adds: So is Pharaoh, and all his multitude, says the Lord: 'As', he says, 'the Assyrian, the cedar and cypress, was cast down when the Babylonian cut it down, so also Pharaoh and his people, that is, the tree itself and its branches, will be cut down by the Babylonian'.
Commentary on Ezekiel

After this the discourse is turned to Pharaoh himself, to whom it had been said at the beginning: Whom have you become like in your height?, and it is said to him: To whom have you been likened, O renowned and lofty one among the trees of pleasure? — to the Assyrian, of course, who fell —: 'You too were renowned and lofty among the trees of Eden — that is, of delights and of paradise —, and behold, you have been led down like the Assyrian, with all the trees that were once in delights, to the lowest land and to the underworld; and you will sleep not in rest but in punishments, in the midst of the uncircumcised — that is, the unclean — and with those who fell by the sword of the Lord'; and so that we may know who it is to whom he said: O renowned and lofty one among the trees of pleasure, he puts it more openly: He is Pharaoh and all his multitude (or, according to the Seventy: So is Pharaoh and all his multitude), so that, as the Assyrian above was cut down and fell, so also the Egyptian may be overthrown.

n: Twelfth. He counts from the captivity of Jechonias, as Sedecias reigned only eleven years. (Worthington)

Dragon, or crocodile; two of the most terrible creatures. --- With the horn is not expressed in Hebrew and the crocodile has nothing like a horn. It has four feet, with which it makes the water muddy. (Calmet)
Net. Septuagint, "hook," chap. xxix. 4. (Calmet) --- Some take the crocodile with a net, ver. 3. (Elian. Hist. x. 21.)
Corruption. Septuagint, "blood." But romuth (Haydock) means rather "worms." (Syriac) (Calmet)

Out, like a candle, by death; extinctus. (Haydock) --- The glory of Egypt was so great, that at its fall the light of heaven seemed diminished. (Worthington) --- Great desolation is thus intimated. --- When, &c., is not in some Latin copies, nor in Hebrew, &c. (Calmet)
Anger, as they will not know why I have treated thee so severely: or rather, they shall be afraid for themselves, ver. 10. (Calmet)
Invincible, when they wield God's sword. Cyrus easily conquered them. (Haydock) --- Hebrew, "strong,." Septuagint, "pestiferous."
Oil. It is very transparent. It seems the Nile was rendered muddy by cattle, &c.
Fulness, or all of it shall be desolate.
Month: probably the twelfth, ver. 1.
Down: announce this catastrophe. (Calmet) --- Apries was slain by order of Amasis. (Diodorus 1.) (Jeremias xliv. 30.)

Most. Septuagint, "giants shall say to thee: Remain in the depth of the pit. Whom dost thou excel? descend," &c. (Haydock) --- They vary much in this chapter from the Hebrew. (St. Jerome) --- Helpers; Lybians, &c., chap. xxx. 5. These shall come to compliment the king. (Calmet) --- After a battle, those of the same nation were buried together, ver. 22. (Theodoret) --- The Egyptians had tombs like houses, in which there were separate holes or apartments (Calmet) as in large vaults. (Haydock)
Shame. They are buried without any distinction.

Not. Some copies of Septuagint omit the negation. Others render the Hebrew, "Have they not slept?" &c. These nations were deprived of military honours, dying like cowards; and therefore their swords were not placed with them in the grave. (Calmet) --- It was customary to inter such things as the deceased had liked the most. (Serv. in Virgil's Æneid x. Arma quibus lætatus habe tua, &c. Simon (1 Machabees xiii. 29.) placed arms and representations of ships on the pillars at Modin, in honour of his kindred. If Elam, &c., had not received such distinction, why should the Egyptian repine? Were they any better? (Calmet) --- The country and king of the Elamites, Assyrians, and other infidels, shall be destroyed. (Worthington)
Midst. This threat would make great impression on the Egyptians, who were particularly solicitous to be buried with their fathers.

Edom. Septuagint add, "and all the Assyrian princes." Some copies omit Edom. (Haydock) --- This nation had laid aside circumcision, which Hircan forced them to resume. They had been present at the siege of Jerusalem, chap. xxxv. (Calmet)
Hunters of men, like Nemrod, the first king of Assyria. (Haydock)

My. Hebrew, Septuagint, "his," (Calmet) alluding to the ravages of Nechao; (Grotius) though the Hebrew may also signify my, as the Jews read Egypt, and Palestine, the land of the living, were filled with terror. After the latter had been chastised, Pharao might dread (Calmet) a worse fate; (Haydock) and the multitudes slain before him, might afford him some (Calmet) wretched consolation. (Haydock) --- It is evident that these nations believed the existence of separate spirits, and had not given in to the errors of the Sadducees, or of the Metempsychosis. (Calmet)

f: Commentary on Ezekiel

And it came to pass in the twelfth year, in the twelfth month (or the tenth), on the first day of the month, the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, take up a lament over Pharaoh king of Egypt, and you shall say to him: You have been likened to the lion of the nations, and to the dragon that is in the sea; and you tossed with your horn in your rivers, and you troubled the waters with your feet, and you trampled their rivers (or your rivers). Therefore thus says the Lord God: I will spread my net over you in a multitude of many peoples, and I will draw you out in my dragnet (or I will draw you out on a hook); and I will cast (or I will draw) you onto the land, upon the face of the field I will throw you (or the plains will be filled with you), and I will make dwell (or sit) upon you all the birds of the sky, and I will glut the beasts of the whole earth with you; and I will put your flesh upon the mountains, and I will fill the hills (or the valleys) with your gore (or with your blood). And I will water (or the land will be watered) with the stench of your blood (or with your dung) upon the mountains, and the valleys will be filled with you; and when you have been extinguished I will cover the sky, and I will make its stars grow black: I will cover the sun with a cloud, and the moon will not give its light; all the lights of the sky I will make mourn (or they will grow dark) over you, and I will put darkness upon your land, says the Lord God. And I will provoke the heart of many peoples, when I bring your destruction (or your captivity) among the nations upon a land (or in a land) which you do not know. And I will make stand astonished (or there will be saddened) over you peoples (or many nations), and their kings will tremble over you with exceeding horror, when my sword begins to fly over their faces, and each one will be suddenly dumbfounded for his own life on the day of his ruin (or awaiting their own ruin from the day of your ruin). For thus says the Lord God: The sword of the king of Babylon will come to you; by the swords of the mighty (or of giants) I will cast down your multitude (or your strength) — all of them invincible nations (or pestilent ones from all the nations) —, and they will lay waste (or destroy) the pride (or the insolence) of Egypt, and its multitude will be scattered (or all its strength). And I will destroy all its beasts that were beside many waters (or from many waters), and the foot of man will trouble them no more, nor will the hoof of beasts trouble (or trample) them; then I will make their waters most pure (or so that their waters may at length be at rest), and I will lead their rivers like oil (or so that they flow like oil), says the Lord God, when I have made the land of Egypt desolate (or ruined): and the land will be deserted of its fullness (or with its fullness) when I strike (or scatter) all its inhabitants, and they will know that I am the Lord. It is a lament, or they shall lament him; the daughters of the nations shall lament him; over Egypt and over its multitude (or all its strength) they shall lament him, says the Lord God. We mingle both editions, only in those places in which they disagree; otherwise, where there is one sense, we follow the Hebrew. In many copies, moreover, according to the Seventy 'the twelfth year' and 'the tenth month' is set down, but according to the other translators 'the tenth year' and 'the twelfth month', so that either Jerusalem has already been taken, and Pharaoh's joy, with evils hanging over him, is taken away, or at any rate it is about to be taken, and he should grieve more over his own miseries than rejoice at the captivity of others; and meanwhile, briefly laying down certain foundations of the history, let us run through what the Hebrews understand concerning this passage.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Pharaoh is compared to a lion — not of one nation but of many nations — or to a dragon in the sea, so that he possesses land and waters; he was lifted up into 'pride' by the watering of the rivers — which he calls 'horn' — and, by the multitude of his army, passing through all the waters, he was able to trouble them.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Let it suffice to have said these things in passing on the simple letter, so that we may come to the spiritual understanding. Nor do I think one must labor greatly to know who Pharaoh king of Egypt is, since we have spoken of it more fully above: namely that power to which Egypt was entrusted, whether one province or the Egypt of the whole world, which was not created a lion but by its own vice was likened to the lion of the nations — for Man, indeed, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared to the senseless beasts, and was made like them; of this lion Peter also speaks: Our adversary the devil goes about like a roaring lion, and in Psalm 9 (10) it is written: He lies in wait in secret like a lion in his den; he lies in wait to seize the poor, and Jeremiah says by the Holy Spirit: A lion from the forest has struck them —; but that the devil is called a dragon — for which Aquila translates Leviathan, setting out the name of the dragon — I have shown in the earlier explanation with many testimonies, he who had said: The rivers are mine and I made them. This dragon, then, tossed very many nations with his rivers as with horns; which we can understand of Marcion, Valentinus, Arius and Eunomius, and the other leaders of heresies, who imitate churchmen saying to the Lord Savior: In you we will toss our enemies with the horn, and they do not toss them unto salvation, to lift them from earth to heaven, but to cast them into the deep. Then follows: And you troubled the waters with your feet — according to that saying of the Apostle: But he who troubles you will bear the judgment —; for he does not wish to drink the waters of Siloam, which go in silence, but the 'turbid' and 'muddy' waters of Egypt, which, before they were trampled by the dragon's feet, were pure and flowed in their own order, but after they were troubled by his feet, lost the order of their course — for the heretics do not use testimonies of the Scriptures that cohere with one another, but they trouble everything —; and, because he himself is the enemy and the avenger, the Egyptian dragon not only troubles other people's waters with his feet, but tramples his own rivers, so as not to spare those whom he has once brought under his power — which the righteous man, desiring to avoid it, prays: Let not the foot of pride come against me; and in another place, having been trampled, he asks not to be trampled again: Have mercy on me, O Lord, for man has trampled me; and the enemy man is the devil, of whom another psalm also speaks: That man may no more be magnified upon the earth —.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Therefore he says that he will spread his net over his multitude and draw him out with his dragnet — or hook —, and cast — or stretch — him out upon the land, him who like a serpent had been wound in many coils, so that he may be devoured by all the birds of the sky. And when not only the birds but all the beasts of the earth have torn him, the rest of his flesh will fill the mountains and valleys and plains, so that all things swarm with worms — and he says this by way of metaphor, so that, after the birds of the sky and the beasts have been glutted with his flesh, that is, his army and the whole multitude, the remaining part may be turned into worms and gore —:
Commentary on Ezekiel

Therefore thus says the Lord God: I will spread my net over you, in a multitude of many peoples; the Lord's net, woven by the plan of the Old and New Testament, is cast over the dragon — who dwells in the multitude of peoples, and delights in crowds and multitude —, so as to draw him out in his dragnet, or on his hook — this is the dragnet that is cast into the sea of this world and draws out many fish, some to be chosen and others to be thrown away; or this is the hook of which it is written in Job: But you will draw out the dragon with a hook and put a halter around his nostrils, for which Aquila translates: Drawing out Leviathan with a hook, and with cords you will bind his tongue —; and the dragon — or Leviathan — is drawn out of the sea with the hook — or the Lord's dragnet —, so as to be cast — or stretched out — upon the land, and all his coils, in which he used to hide his snares, may be opened and brought out into public and thrown down upon the land, and he may lie prostrate who had set his mouth in heaven and boasted that he was like the Most High; hence there follows: And I will make dwell (or sit) upon you all the birds of the sky, and I will glut the beasts of the whole earth with you — according to what is written: You gave him as food to the peoples of the Ethiopians —, who are called either birds or beasts of the earth: birds, which, as we have said, snatch the seed beside the way; beasts of the whole earth, made savage by vices; which can be referred to heretics and Gentiles;
Commentary on Ezekiel

and what follows: And I will put your flesh upon the mountains, and I will fill your hills with your gore (or I will fill the valleys with your blood), has this sense, that we should understand the birds of the sky and the beasts of the earth as the peoples of the deceived and the cruelty of the Gentiles, and refer the mountains to the leaders of heresies — such as Valentinus and Marcion were —, and the hills to their successors who are glutted with the dragon's gore, or the valleys which are filled with the dragon's blood to all the lower sort of believers; or certainly the mountains are the hostile powers that roam about in the air, and the valleys those which penetrate the underworld and have been consigned to eternal punishments.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Further, what is said: And I will water the land with the stench of your blood upon the mountains (or the land will be watered with your dung upon the mountains), and the valleys will be filled with you, signifies this, that all the pride and arrogant swelling of the heretics is filled not so much with living and pure blood as with putrid and stinking blood — according to what is written: Make them like the dung of the earth, from which the holy man is delivered by the Lord: Who raises the needy from the earth, and lifts the poor from the dung, to set him with princes, with the princes of his people —; and the valleys, sunk into the depths, as we said above, signify either the underworld or the lowly mind of the heretics, who do everything for the sake of pleasure and earthly wealth;
Commentary on Ezekiel

and what is joined: And when you have been extinguished I will cover the sky, and I will make its stars grow black: I will cover the sun with a cloud, and the moon will not give its light; all the lights of the sky I will make mourn (or grow dark) over you, and I will put darkness upon your land, says the Lord God, if we follow the letter, cannot be understood at all: for when, after Pharaoh — or the dragon — was slain, did the sun and moon and stars not give their light, and the sky was covered with darkness — according to that poetic line: And the impious ages feared eternal night —? This, then, must be said: that when Pharaoh has been extinguished — who transformed himself into an angel of light, of whom it is written in another place: The light of the impious will be extinguished —, the sky, or the heavens, will be covered with darkness — of which Paul also speaks: And the spiritual things of wickedness in the heavenly places —; and the Lord made its stars grow black, whether the dragon's or the sky's — concerning whom Jude the apostle also writes: Wandering stars, for whom the gloom of darkness is reserved forever —; the sun too is covered in a cloud: the sun of iniquity — which is the opposite of the sun of righteousness —, and with a cloud: either by the Lord Savior himself — who descends into Egypt upon a light cloud, weighed down by no burden of sins —, or by the prophets and apostles — of whom we read: I will command the clouds that they rain no rain upon it, and in the Psalms: Your truth reaches to the clouds —; and when the sun of iniquity has been darkened, the moon — which we take to be the church of the heretics, and which was thought to receive its light from the sun of iniquity — will not give its light, nor will it deceive believers with the knowledge falsely so called;
Commentary on Ezekiel

'Then,' he says, 'the heavens will be wrapped in darkness: the sun and the moon and the other lights will not give their light, but over you all things will grow black, and nothing will be joyful for you.
Commentary on Ezekiel

all the lights also, and whatever of doctrine seems to be among the heretics, will be blinded when the dragon has been extinguished, or they will mourn the loss of their prince, so that the Lord himself covers the land of the heretics with darkness, namely ignorance of the truth, so that the blind lead the blind into a ditch and the inhabitants of the land are sent into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.
Commentary on Ezekiel

After this it is said: And I will provoke the heart of many peoples, when I bring your destruction (or your captivity) among the nations upon a land which you do not know, so that those who formerly served Pharaoh are angered against him, seeing that his captivity has been led away to another land, which the dragon did not know. Nor ought we to doubt that the lands which Pharaoh does not know are good, namely when the captivity of Pharaoh is exchanged for another captivity — of which it is said to the Savior: Ascending on high, he led captivity captive; he received (or, according to the Apostle, gave) gifts among men —.
Commentary on Ezekiel
And at your destruction all peoples and all their kings will tremble with exceeding horror, seeing my sword flying this way and that and sparing no one, and in your ruin they dread a like ruin.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And I will make, he says, many peoples stand astonished over you, so that those who formerly admired Pharaoh's power may afterwards marvel at him for having fallen from his summit; the kings of the peoples, too, will tremble over him with exceeding horror — whose kingdoms the devil showed to the Lord, and of whom it says in the psalm: The kings of the earth stood up, and the princes gathered together —; and this will come about when the sword of the Lord begins to fly over their faces, understood as those of the kings, or of the peoples — and the sword of the Lord is to be understood as the word of God, living and effective, and sharper than any two-edged sword, which flies and darts about and dazzles the eyes of those who behold it and frightens their faces —, so that, astounded at the ruin of Pharaoh, they may see themselves cast down in him; and indeed the sword of the Lord — of which it is written: Behold, this one is set for the fall and rising of many — raises those who lie fallen and by humility changes those wrongly lifted up.
Commentary on Ezekiel

But so that you may know what this sword is, hear it more plainly: The sword of the king of Babylon will come to you; by the swords of the mighty (or of giants) I will cast down all your multitude — which giants are the invincible nations that were held in the army of the Babylonian king —; these will lay waste (or will destroy) the pride of Egypt and all its multitude, and nothing will remain in Egypt, but together with the men the beasts and brute animals too will be carried off alike.
Commentary on Ezekiel

But the sword of the king of Babylon will come upon the Egyptian dragon, so that by the swords of the mighty — or of giants — the Lord may cast down his multitude, which followed the king of Egypt: Invincible, he says, (or pestilent ones from the nations) are all these, so that the evil are handed over to worse ones to be punished — of whom it is written: A sending by most evil angels, and the Apostle: Whom I have handed over, he says, to Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme, or for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved —.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And when by ministers of this kind the pride of Egypt has been cast down and its multitude scattered, all its beasts that were beside many waters will perish, and the foot of man will trouble them no more — for if Blessed is he who sows upon the waters, where ox and ass tread, conversely unhappy is he who will be able any longer to hold the simple by his terror, so that the foot of man does not tread in them, whereby the Egyptian waters seem not to have in them even a sign of wisdom and reason —; nor will the hoof of beasts trouble them, so as to make them 'turbid and muddy' instead of most limpid and shining.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And so great will be the desolation in Egypt that its waters will be troubled neither by the foot of man nor by the hoof of beast, but all things will be quiet; and the waters of its rivers will flow like oil, most pure and shining, with no one passing through them nor troubling their streams' — and this will come about because of the desolation of Egypt, which will be reduced to a desert, stripped of all its multitude, when the Lord has struck its inhabitants, so that those who remain may understand that he himself is the Lord —.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Then the waters that had been troubled by the dragon's dominion will be rendered most pure, not by another but by the Lord himself, so that their rivers are rendered like oil and are the nourishment of the true light; and these things will come about when the Lord has made the land of Egypt desolate and has destroyed its fullness and all its inhabitants have been struck, so that by this progress they may be able to know that he himself is the Lord.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Therefore it is a lament for Pharaoh, and the daughters of the nations round about will lament him, and not only over him, but also over his multitude which, as the Lord laid it waste, was blotted out.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And what is joined: It is a lament, and they shall lament him; the daughters of the nations shall lament him; over Egypt and over its multitude they shall lament him, says the Lord God, makes it plain that the souls of all the nations which had formerly been oppressed by him, or of those nations which by no means dwelt in Egypt but in the region of the living, lament the slain dragon and all his multitude: not in hope of salvation, but because from so great a power, by his own vice and pride, he has been cast down into eternal punishments.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And it came to pass in the twelfth year, on the fifteenth of the month, the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, sing a dirge over the multitude of Egypt, and drag it down, it and the daughters of the mighty nations, to the lowest land with those who go down into the pit. Than whom are you more beautiful? Go down, and sleep with the uncircumcised. In the midst of those slain by the sword they shall fall; the sword has been given; they have dragged her away and all her peoples. The mightiest of the strong will speak to him from the midst of hell, they who went down with his helpers; and they have slept uncircumcised and slain by the sword. There is Assyria and all her multitude, round about her are their graves, all of them slain, and they who fell by the sword; whose graves have been set in the uttermost parts of the pit, and her multitude is round about her grave; all of them slain and falling by the sword, who once had spread dread in the land of the living. There is Elam and all her multitude round about her grave; all these slain and falling by the sword, who went down uncircumcised to the lowest land, who set their terror in the land of the living, and they have borne their shame with those who went down into the pit. In the midst of the slain they have set his bed, among all his peoples; round about him is his grave, all these uncircumcised and slain by the sword; for they had spread terror in the land of the living, and they have borne their shame with those who go down into the pit; they have been set in the midst of the slain. There is Meshech and Tubal and all her multitude, round about her are her graves, all these uncircumcised and slain, falling by the sword, who set their dread in the land of the living; and they will not sleep with the mighty who fell, and the uncircumcised, who went down into hell with their weapons and set their swords under their heads, and their iniquities were in their bones, because they became the terror of the mighty in the land of the living. And you therefore will be crushed in the midst of the uncircumcised, and you will sleep with those slain by the sword. There is Edom and all her kings and her leaders, who were given up with their army with those slain by the sword, and who have slept with the uncircumcised, and with those who went down into the pit. There are all the princes of the north and all the Sidonians (or 'hunters'), who were led down with the slain, trembling, and confounded in their strength, for they have slept uncircumcised with those slain by the sword, and they have borne their confusion with those who go down into the pit. Pharaoh saw them and was comforted over all his multitude which was slain by the sword, Pharaoh and all his army, says the Lord God, for I have set his terror in the land of the living; and he has slept in the midst of the uncircumcised with those slain by the sword, Pharaoh and all his multitude, says the Lord God. (In this place the edition of the Seventy translators disagrees greatly both in order and in translation, and some things in it have been added from Theodotion; hence we have found it necessary to set it down too, by no means sparing length, and serving the diligence of the studious reader. LXX: "And it came to pass in the twelfth year, on the fifteenth of the month, the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, lament over the multitude of Egypt, and the nations will lead her daughters down dead into the depth of the earth, to those who go down into the ditch." — Moreover, under asterisks there has been added: ※ From the most beautiful water go down, and sleep with the uncircumcised ⁚. Again the sequence follows: — In the midst of those wounded by the sword they shall fall with him, and all their strength will sleep. And the giants will say to you: Go down into the depth of the ditch. Than whom are you better? Go down, and sleep with the uncircumcised in the midst of those wounded by the sword. There is Assyria and all her congregation. — And what is joined: ÷ All the wounded have been set there, and his grave is in the depth of the ditch, and his congregation came to be ⁚, is not found in the Hebrew, but was added by the Seventy. Again it is said: — Round about his grave, all the wounded who had fallen by the sword. — And again from the edition of Theodotion there has been added under asterisks: ※ Who had set graves for them in the sides of the pit, and the congregation came to be round about his grave; all these wounded and falling by the sword ⁚. After which the Seventy set down: — Who set their fear in the land of life. There is Elam and all her strength round about her grave; all wounded and falling by the sword, and who go down uncircumcised into the depth of the earth, who set their terror in the land of life, and they received their torment with those who go down into the ditch, in the midst of the wounded. There have been set Meshech and Tubal and all their strength, round about his grave, all his wounded, all uncircumcised and wounded by the sword, who set their terror upon the land of life; and they did not sleep with the giants, who had fallen from of old, who went down into hell with the weapons they used for wars and set their swords under their heads, and their iniquities came to be in their bones, because they had terrified giants in their life. And you in the midst of the uncircumcised ※ will be crushed, and ⁚ will sleep with those wounded by the sword. There is Edom, ※ her kings and all ⁚ the princes of Assyria, who gave his strength to the wound of the sword; these have slept with the wounded, with those who went down into the ditch. There are all the princes of the north, all the magistrates of Assyria, who go down wounded with their terror, and confounded in their strength; they have slept, uncircumcised too, with those wounded by the sword, and they have carried off their torment with those going down into the ditch. Pharaoh will see them and will receive comfort over all their strength ※ wounded by the sword, Pharaoh and all his strength ⁚, says the Lord God, for I have set his dread upon the land of life, and he will sleep in the midst of the uncircumcised with those wounded by the sword, Pharaoh and all his multitude, says the Lord God.) I am not unaware that so great a discrepancy between the two editions will be tiresome to the fastidious reader; but what am I to do with my slanderers, who, if I take away anything from the translation of the Seventy translators, cry out that I am sacrilegious and without the fear of the Lord — especially those who, though they disagree with me in the truth of the faith and follow the errors of the Manichaeans, stir up the minds of the unlearned on this very point, if they can show that anything of the old has been changed against established custom, preferring to err rather than to learn anything true from a rival. Meanwhile, according to the history the sense is plain. For in the same twelfth year, and in the same month, as we think, but not on the first of the month, as above, but on the fifteenth day, a lament is taken up not over Pharaoh, but over the strength — or multitude — of Egypt, which is dragged down from its pride with all its daughters — or those of the mighty nations — to the lowest land, that is, into the depth of hell. And it is said to the king of Egypt: 'Than whom are you better, that you should deserve to escape death? — for since Assyria and Elam — that is, the Persians —, and Meshech — who are interpreted as the Cappadocians —, and Tubal — whom some take to be the Iberians, others the Italians —, the Edomites also and the princes of the north and the Sidonians, with all their armies by whose help they struck horror into all the nations, have died and been slain by the sword, and have set their swords under their heads — which saying is to be taken ἐμφατικώτερον [more emphatically, as an expressive figure] —, will you alone be able not to endure the same things? Rather, when you see so great a multitude of sleepers with you among the dead below, and your grave surrounded by the memorials of princes once most mighty, you will have consolation, reckoning your torments lighter through the fellowship of very many —'. Let it suffice for the present to have said these things briefly according to the simple sense.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Now, with the same brevity, so far as the difficulty of the explanation permits, let us gather the chief points of the spiritual understanding. Above, the word of the Lord came to the prophet on the first day of the month; here, on the fifteenth — now on the first day, that is, on the calends, is the beginning of the month; on the fifteenth, when the whole orb of the moon is filled; and if it was the first month, it is the first day of Unleavened Bread, but if the seventh, of Tabernacles, when the tents are pitched, which feasts are among the very greatest among the Hebrews —; and the lament is made over the strength of Egypt, so that he who is strong in evil may cease to be so and take on weakness, and when he is weaker, then he may be stronger. For the 'strength' of Egypt, the Hebrew has 'multitude' — For wide and spacious is the way that leads to death, and many enter by it, just as, on the contrary, it is said to Israel: But you are few among all the nations; for virtue is always rare, and: Narrow and strait is the way that leads to life, and few are those who enter by it —. And that Egypt is lamented, and its dead daughters — 'her' daughters according to the Seventy, or those 'of the mighty nations' — are led down to the lowest land into the deepest pit — or ditch —, signifies the souls dwelling in the Egypt of this world — which have lost him who says: I am the life, and, dead in sins, are dragged down to the underworld by their weight, as the sinner says: For my iniquities have gone over my head; like a heavy burden they weigh upon me; these are the ones of whom it is also written in another place: They go into the lower parts of the earth; they will be given over into the hands of the sword; they will be portions for foxes. He who, indeed, digs a ditch, falls into it; whence we also read: He opened a pit and dug it out, and he will fall into the ditch which he made —.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And what follows: Than whom are you more beautiful? Go down, and sleep with the uncircumcised, the word is properly addressed to Pharaoh king of Egypt — or, as was added in the Seventy from Theodotion, to Egypt itself: From the most beautiful water go down, and sleep with the uncircumcised; which pertains especially to him who, reborn in the baptism of Christ, hearing with the Church: Who is she that comes up made white, leaning upon her kinsman?, afterwards, defiled either by fornication or by other vices, is cast out of the Church, and it is said to him: From the most beautiful water go down, and sleep 'with the uncircumcised', that is, 'with the unclean', according to that sense which the Apostle sets down: We are the circumcision, who serve God in the spirit, and glory in the Lord, and put no confidence in the flesh —.
Commentary on Ezekiel

All these will fall with Pharaoh in the midst of the wounded — or the slain —, by that sword which is the opposite of the sword which the Lord came to send upon the earth: for just as the sword of Christ separates the good from the evil — as he says: I came not to send peace upon the earth, but a sword —, so the sword of the heretics cuts down all peoples and leads the wounded down to the underworld; these are the giants, most mighty and rebellious and setting their mouth on high, and the more they raise themselves up to the heights through pride, the more they are dragged down to the depth of the ditch and the uttermost parts of hell, all of whom have been slain by the sword.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And so that either Pharaoh or the whole strength of Egypt, which has been dragged down to the underworld, might know whom he had as companions in punishment, the following word shows: There is Assyria and all the multitude (or synagogue) of her; for the prince of the heretics is the devil — whose congregation is truly a synagogue, of which it is said in the Revelation: Who are the synagogue of Satan —.
Commentary on Ezekiel

But the following short verses, which are marked in front with an obelus, I think should be passed over, and what is found in the Hebrew should be stated: Round about her are their graves, namely of those deceived by him, who are all wounded (or slain) by the sword, and therefore have fallen; whose graves have been set in the uttermost parts of the pit — and that hell is called a pit is plainly shown by that psalm in which the penitent says: I have been likened to those who go down into the pit; which we ought by no means, according to the proper sense of the Latin word, to understand as that which in Greek is called λίμνη [lake] — such as the lake of Tiberias, and lakes Larius and Benacus, and many others —, but as what we are accustomed to call cisterns; which pits, because they chill the waters and take from them all the warmth of the spirit, sinners and all heretics dig; and, so far as my memory goes, Scripture testifies that none of the saints dug a pit — that is, a cistern — but all sinners — among whom was Uzziah, the leprous king, who also fell through his pride, of whom it is written that he was a man brooding over the works of the soil, and that he built many towers of pride in the corners, and that he dug pits —; on the contrary it is said to the righteous man: Drink waters from your own vessels and from the springs of your wells, and again: Let the fountain of your water be your own, whence the Lord also says: They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and have dug for themselves pits (that is, cisterns) which cannot hold water —. There follows: And her multitude is round about her grave; all these surround the Assyrian, and their multitude is very great, all of whom have been wounded and slain and are falling by the sword — for none of them can stand with Moses, or hear: You who stand in the house of the Lord; but all have been wounded and slain and are falling —: who once had spread dread in the land of the living; and dread to those who were set over the churches, lest in the land of the living they should make peoples of the dead and deceive all the simple — whence Paul also said: But I fear lest, as the serpent deceived Eve in his malice, your minds be corrupted through the simplicity that is in Christ; but this fear is softened by hope in the Lord, as the man of the Church says: The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? The Lord is the protector of my life; of whom shall I be afraid? —.
Commentary on Ezekiel

After this it is said: There is Elam, and all her multitude round about her grave, no doubt the Assyrian's. 'Elam' is rendered into our tongue as 'their ascent'; for all who, despising the humility of Christ, have ascended to the pride of the devil and have thought themselves to be something in the knowledge falsely so called, are to be named Elamites, who go round the grave of the Assyrian king and have been slain and wounded by the sword; and although they set their mouth on high, yet they went down unclean and uncircumcised to the lowest land, so that the more loftily they had been raised up, the more heavily they might fall; these set their terror not once but a second time in the land of the living — for who among the churchmen is safe from the terror of Elamites of this kind and has not lost someone of his flock? —; and beautifully the Church of Christ is called the land of the living, so that, on the contrary, the conventicles of the heretics may be believed to be the land of the dead.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And they have borne, he says, their shame (or their torment) with those whom they dragged down with them into the pit and the depth of hell, whose bed is in the midst of the slain; namely of those whose throats they cut with their blade, and they are surrounded by peoples of this kind; these peoples are the peoples of the Assyrian king, and although they boast that they are circumcised, yet they are uncircumcised and slain by the sword, and a third time they have spread terror and dread in the land of the living; hence they have borne their torment and punishment in the midst of those whom they deceived by their frauds.
Commentary on Ezekiel

There also is — that is, beside the Assyrian — Meshech and Tubal and all her multitude, round about her grave, all uncircumcised and slain and falling by the sword, who had set their dread in the land of the living. For 'Mosoch and Thubal', Symmachus and Theodotion translated 'their bed', to show that the beds of the heretics, or rather their everlasting ditches, are the punishments of the Assyrian king; 'Mosoch' means 'madness', 'Thubal' 'conversion' — not to good from evil but from good to evil — or 'all things', to show that all heretics are mad and with equal zeal are turned to worse things; nor is it surprising if those who are mad and heaped together for evil have a multitude, since they are companions of the Egyptian king, who rejoices in multitude; all these have been slain by the sword, who set their dread, not once nor a second time, but a third time, in the land of the living, of which we have spoken more fully above.
Commentary on Ezekiel

There follows: And they will not sleep with the mighty (or the giants) who fell, and the uncircumcised, who went down to hell with their weapons and set their swords under their heads, and their iniquities were in their bones, because they became the terror of the mighty in the land of the living. 'These,' he says, 'who stood out as leaders of the heretics, have come to such a summit of malice and of torment, that they do not deserve to bear like punishments even with the mighty and the giants who fell from the beginning; who, having by no means done penance for their error, went down to the underworld with their weapons, rebels against God and his Church, carrying their spirit with them' — of whom it is written: Sons of men, their teeth are weapons and arrows —, 'and they set,' he says, 'their swords under their heads, resting in a hostile spirit, and, as their supreme victory, embracing the darts of their opinions, to such a degree that their iniquities were in their bones — that is, their strongest fabrications —, and holding fast the doctrines of their error: Because they became the terror of the mighty in their life (or in the land of the living)', which is said for the fourth time, that by their perversity they terrified even the mightiest, and those who had knowledge of the Scriptures and who were of the region of the living, while they go down to hell with their weapons and set their swords under their heads and their iniquity reaches to their bones.
Commentary on Ezekiel

After this it is written: 'And you therefore will be crushed in the midst of the uncircumcised' — which is said either to Pharaoh or to the strength, or multitude, of Egypt, that it too is crushed, according to what is written: But may God crush Satan under your feet swiftly — 'and you will sleep,' he says, 'with those slain by the sword, in perpetual sleep'.
Commentary on Ezekiel

There, with the Assyrian and with the Egyptian multitude, will be Edom and her kings, all who have served earthly works or delighted in blood — for 'Idumaea' [Edom] sounds both 'earthy' and 'bloody' —; all the kings and all the princes — of whom the Apostle also frequently speaks: 'brooding over earthly works and daily shedding the blood of those whom they have deceived by their fraud' — have slept with the uncircumcised and unclean and with those who went down into the pit, of whom we have spoken above.
Commentary on Ezekiel

In the same company will also be the princes of the north, from which evils blaze up upon the earth — and from which, whether in Jeremiah or in this same prophet, that pot full of flesh and bones is set alight —, and not only the princes of the north, but every magistrate of 'Assur' — for which in the Hebrew is more truly set down all the 'Sidonians', whom we have rendered as 'hunters', according to what is written: Our soul has been snatched like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters (for which in the Hebrew is set down of the Sidonians); which Sidonians — or hunters — will be led down to the underworld trembling, who once trusted in their own strength; and they will sleep unclean, and they will bear their confusion — or torment —, having the everlasting remorse of an evil conscience, so that their fire is not quenched and their worm does not die.
Commentary on Ezekiel

When Pharaoh has seen all these, he will be comforted, either still having his former malice and seeing that he has many companions of his punishment, or at any rate he was comforted seeing that they too are confounded in their punishments and their terrors, over all his multitude which was slain by the sword: that is, Pharaoh's, or that of all his companions, and especially of the Assyrian king and Meshech and Tubal and the Edomites, and of the princes of the north and of the Sidonians; for these had set their terror in the land of the living — which is said for the fifth time, so that we ought to beware of and flee all nations of this kind, which have deceived us in all our senses, and know that they are dreadful and cannot easily be avoided unless we keep our heart with all vigilance —. 'He has slept,' he says, 'Pharaoh himself too, with his companions slain by the sword', which companions are his multitude, going by the wide and spacious way to everlasting punishments.

n: Take. Before (chap. iii. 17.) God made the choice, (Calmet) as he does here, ver. 7. He confirms the authority of those who are appointed to govern. --- Meanest. Literally, "last," (Haydock) which seems to denote such as are chosen without regard to their dignity or obscurity in life, Genesis xlvii. 2., and 3 Kings xii. 31. (Calmet) --- Pastors are not excused from admonishing the people for fear of danger or despair of reclaiming them, as each one is bound to do his duty. (St. Jerome) (Worthington)

Iniquity, not regarding the admonitions of his pastor; (chap. iii. 18.; Calmet) or rather of conscience, when the guide proves faithless and silent, as in this instance. (Haydock) --- The people were persuaded that none suffered except for some fault, ver. 10.; Jeremias xxxi. 30., Daniel xiii. 52., and Genesis xliv. 16. The author of the Book of Job takes great pains to remove this mistake. God sometimes sends crosses for a trial, (Calmet) and to increase the merit of his servants; though it be very true, (Haydock) "no one is miserable except he deserve it." (St. Augustine)
Surely die a temporal, (Theodoret) or rather an eternal death. (St. Jerome)

Live? They suppose their case to be desperate, as their fathers had sinned, chap. xviii. The prophet shews that none are punished except for their own faults, (Calmet) and that "each one has free-will to be saved or to be lost." (St. Jerome)

Desire. The sinner's damnation is not an object of God's pleasure, chap. xviii. 23. (Calmet) --- He has an antecedent will to save all. He knocks at the door of our heart, (Apocalypse iii. 20.) and if man do what depends on him, nothing will be wanting on the part of God. (St. Thomas Aquinas, [Summa Theologiae] i. 2. q. 109. and 112.) (Worthington)

Hurt him. God effaces all past crimes: yet a relapse makes them as it were revive, and is pardoned with more difficulty, Matthew xviii. 35. Some read, "In what day the converted sinner groans, he shall be saved," as if they had taken in part of Isaias xxx. 15.

Equitable; as we are much more inclined to vice than to virtue. This argumentation is inconclusive, as God owes nothing to man; and what good the latter does, is an effect of his grace. The propensity to evil is no excuse, as man is still free. He is judged according to the dispositions in which he is found at the hour of death; yet we must not infer, that those who have spent their lives in sinning will be no worse treated than the person who dies guilty of a single crime.

Twelfth. Roman Septuagint, "tenth." Syriac, "eleventh year,...in the twelfth month;" which Theodoret thinks more probable, as the city was taken in the ninth of the fourth month of that year. Yet even so, it is strange that the news should not arrive before. Some think (Calmet) that the messenger came also to announce what happened after the death of Godolias. (Sanctius) --- Captivity. Here it is evident that the prophet dates from that event, chap. i., &c. (Haydock) --- As he prophesied on the very day when the city was besieged, (chap. xxiv. 2.) so ([chap. xxiv.] ver. 26.) he foretold that one should come three years after to inform him of the capture. (Worthington) --- Then the people would believe him, (ibid.[chap. xxiv.] ver. 27.; Calmet) and he would open his mouth boldly, ver. 22. (Haydock)

Places. He has answered those who despaired, ver. 10. Now he turns to the presumptuous, who expected to be treated like Abraham, though they did not imitate his virtues. (Calmet) --- They perhaps entertained these sentiments before the death of Godolias, thinking to establish themselves in the land. Afterwards the prophet Jeremias could not prevail on them to remain, though God promised them security.

To them. Grabe marks to ver. 27., Thus saith, &c., as wanting in the Septuagint, though not in the Alexandrian copy. St. Jerome reckons eight verses or lines omitted. (Haydock) --- The Complutensian and Theodoret read them with some variations. --- The blood. It must be carefully extracted, Genesis ix. 4., and Leviticus vii. 26. --- Uncleannesses; idols, in which you trust.
Swords, thinking to live thereby, (Genesis xxvii. 40.) and to be secure. But I will disarm you. The pestilence shall find out those in the rocks, ver. 27.
Walls, the resort of idle people. (Calmet)

In to a religious meeting. (Chaldean) Perhaps they came on the sabbath to his house. Yet they made a just and song of his instructions. (Calmet) --- They heard them with pleasure, but did not reform their lives. (Haydock)
Coming. The desolation of Jerusalem, (Haydock) and what I have foretold, hath already taken place; or, the news will presently arrive: as it did the following morning, ver. 21. (Calmet)

f: Commentary on Ezekiel

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, speak to the sons of your people, and you shall say to them: A land, when I bring the sword upon it, and the people of the land take one man from the last of them (or one man from among them), and set him over themselves as a watchman, and he sees the sword coming upon the land, and sounds the trumpet and announces it to the people; but whoever he is who hears the sound of the trumpet does not take heed for himself, and the sword comes and takes (or seizes) him: his blood shall be upon his own head; he heard the sound (or voice) of the trumpet and did not take heed for himself, his blood shall be upon him. But if he guards himself, he has saved his soul. But if the watchman sees the sword coming, and does not sound the trumpet, and the people do not guard themselves; and the sword comes and takes a soul from among them: that one indeed has been taken in his iniquity, but his blood I will require from the hand of the watchman. And you, son of man, I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel. Hearing therefore the word from my mouth, you shall announce it to them from me. If, when I say to the wicked: Wicked one, you shall die by death; you have not spoken so that the wicked may guard himself from his way, that wicked one shall die in his iniquity, but his blood I will require from your hand. But if, when you announce to the wicked that he should turn from his ways, he has not turned from his way, he shall die in his iniquity, but you will deliver your soul. Again the word of the Lord comes to the prophet — the word which had for a time been silent, because the prophet cannot, nor can human frailty, sustain within itself an unceasing and continuous prophesying —, and it speaks the same things that are contained in the earlier passages: 'Son of man, I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel, and hearing the word from my mouth, you shall also threaten them from me; in that I shall say to the unrighteous: You shall die by death, and you did not announce it to him, nor did you speak so as to announce it to the unrighteous, that he might turn from his ways and live, that unrighteous man shall die in his iniquity and his blood I will require from your hand. And you, if you announce it to the unrighteous, and he has not turned from his iniquity and from his way, that unrighteous man shall die in his iniquity, and you will deliver your soul'; if you examine these words carefully, you will understand that they are indeed similar, but not the same, since they disagree in a great many points — and this we ought to observe in all the holy Scriptures: where there seems to be some similarity of meaning, not everything is said identically, but a great many things are either taken away or added, and the difference between the individual words has its reason —. And meanwhile, before we come to higher things, the sense must be briefly explained: 'If a watchman has been appointed among the people to announce the sword of the Lord and the wrath that is coming, and, when he announces it, the people are unwilling to hear, the watchman will be free, and he who has been overwhelmed by the sword will himself bear the guilt of his own blood; but if he has heard, he has saved his soul; if, however, the watchman has not sounded the trumpet and the people, not knowing that the sword is coming, have by no means taken heed for themselves, the people indeed will die in their iniquity; yet I will require the blood of the dying from the watchman's hand'; and so that the prophet Ezekiel might know that this general discussion pertained above all to himself: 'And you,' he says, son of man, not by the land and by the people of the land, as I said above, but by me you have been appointed watchman for the house of Israel: If therefore, when I say to the wicked: Wicked one, you shall die by death, you have not spoken to him so that he may guard himself and be delivered from destruction, he indeed will die in his iniquity, which he had committed before and from which, had you announced it, he could have been delivered: but his blood I will require from your hand. But if you declare it to the wicked, and command him to turn from his most evil ways, and he is unwilling to do this, he indeed will die in his iniquity, but you have delivered your soul from the destruction of negligence'.
Commentary on Ezekiel

We can, however, discuss this passage in a threefold way: so that the land which appoints a watchman for itself is either, according to the letter, the land of Judea, or, according to the spiritual understanding, the Church, which often chooses a watchman from the last of its people — namely that one whom the Apostle too, writing to the Corinthians, takes as judge —, or certainly the soul of the believer, which sets the mind and reason over the people and crowd of its thoughts — so that it may not admit every incitement of the thoughts, but may judge and discern which things it should pursue and which it should flee —. The watchman of the land of Judea can be understood as either the king or the prophet; but the watchman of the Church as either the bishop or the presbyter, who has been chosen by the people and, knowing and foreseeing through the reading of the Scriptures what is to come, is to announce it to the people and correct the one who goes astray. Hence we must greatly fear lest we approach this office unworthy, and, having been taken up by the people, give ourselves over to negligence and sloth, and, what is worse than these, serving delicacies and the belly and leisure, think that we have received an honor, not a ministry: For the Son of man did not come to be ministered to, but to minister, and he washed the feet of the disciples, to show that all the filth and vices in the disciples ought to be washed away and cleansed by the teacher; nor let us at once reply: 'What use is it to speak, if the hearer is unwilling to do what you have taught?', for each one is judged by his own intention and office: you, if you have not spoken; he, if he has been unwilling to hear; of negligent teachers Solomon speaks: Wisdom hidden and treasure hidden, what profit is there in either?; something of the kind is signified also in the Gospel: that for one who has caused one of the least of the Church to stumble, it would be better that a donkey's millstone be tied to his neck and he be cast into the deep, than that, set in the watchtower, he should harm very many.
SERMON 46:20

Do you see how dangerous it is to keep silent? He dies, and rightly dies; he dies in his own wickedness and sin; his own heedlessness kills him. Yes, the one who says "I live, says the Lord," would like to find a living shepherd. But since he has been heedless, not being warned by the one who was given charge and made a watchman for this very purpose of warning him, he will die justly, and the other will be justly condemned.… It is our business not to keep quiet; it is your business, even if we do keep quiet, to listen to the words of the shepherd from the holy Scriptures.
DIALOGUE WITH HERACLIDES

And: "From the hand of the watchman I will require your blood." What blood does God demand from the hand of the watchman, if not that of which the sinner is deprived? So the heart of the foolish one is destroyed, according to the saying: "Listen to Me, you who have lost heart!" — because the sinner is deprived of the blood and vital force of the soul.
City of God 1.9

For this reason, overseers or rulers are set over the churches to reprimand sin, not to spare it. Nor is a person fully free from blame who is not in authority but who notices in those persons he meets in social life many faults he should censure and admonish. He is blameworthy if he fails to do this out of fear of hurting feelings or of losing such things as he may rightfully enjoy in his life but to which he is unduly attached.
Commentary on Ezekiel

From these words we learn: that a man, though unrighteous and wicked, can be saved from his wickedness if he hears the words of the teacher and repents; and no less, that the teacher incurs peril if he is unwilling to teach, whether from fear of peril or from despair of the sinner, since he is guilty of the blood of one who could have been delivered and rescued from death, had he not fallen through the teacher's silence; and that in both free will is preserved, since it lies both in the teacher's will either to keep silent or to speak, and in the hearer's choice either to hear and do and be saved, or to despise and perish by his own contempt. Nor does it immediately follow that, because a prophet foretells something, what he foretold comes — for he does not foretell it so that it may come, but so that it may not come —; nor, because God speaks, must what he threatens necessarily happen; rather he threatens for this reason: that the one whom he threatens may turn to repentance, and that what is to come if the words of the Lord are despised may not happen.
Commentary on Ezekiel

You therefore, son of man, say to the house of Israel: Thus you have spoken, saying: Our iniquities and our sins are upon us, and we are wasting away in them; how then shall we be able to live? Say to them: As I live, says the Lord God; I do not want the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn back from his way, and live; and turn from your most evil ways; and why will you die, house of Israel? You therefore, son of man, say to the sons of your people: The righteousness of the righteous shall not deliver him on whatever day he sins, and the wickedness of the wicked shall not harm him on whatever day he turns from his wickedness; and the righteous shall not be able to live in his righteousness on whatever day he sins. Even if I say to the righteous that he shall live by life, and, trusting in his righteousness, he commits iniquity; all his righteous deeds shall be consigned to oblivion, and in his iniquity which he has wrought, in it he shall die. But if I say to the wicked: You shall die by death, and he repents of his sin, and does judgment and righteousness, restores the pledge, and gives back what he has robbed, walks in the commandments of life, and does nothing unjust, he shall live by life, and shall not die: all the sins which he has sinned shall not be imputed to him; he has done judgment and righteousness, he shall live by life. And the sons of your people have said: The way of the Lord is not of equal weight; and it is their own way that is unjust. For when the righteous withdraws from his righteousness and commits iniquities, he shall die in them; and when the wicked withdraws from his wickedness and does judgment and righteousness, he shall live in them. And you say: The way of the Lord is not right. I will judge each one of you according to his ways, house of Israel. If we read carelessly, it seems to us to be the same prophecy as the one above, in which it is said: Do I willingly desire the death of the unrighteous, says the Lord, and not rather that he turn from his evil way and live?, and at the end of the same prophecy: Turn and return from all your wickednesses, and they will not be to you a torment of iniquity; for there the word is addressed to those who wish to repent and would blot out their sins with righteousness, so that they may turn with confidence and repent with a full heart; here, however, he speaks to those who, because of the greatness of their sins, or rather of their wickednesses, despair of salvation and say: Our iniquities and our sins are upon us, and we are wasting away in them; how then shall we be able to live?; and the sense is: 'Since death has once been set before us, and no medicine can restore health to our wounds, what need is there to toil and be worn out in vain, and not to pass the present life in desperation, so that at least we may enjoy this one, since we have lost the future one?'; to them God answered that he does not want the death of the wicked, but that he turn back and live, and he makes an apostrophe to the despairing wicked: Turn from your most evil ways; and so that we may know who the wicked are to whom he speaks, the following word shows it: Why will you die, house of Israel? — but the life and death signified in this place is not this one by which all of us, by the law of nature common with the beasts, either live or are dissolved by death, but that of which it is written: I will please the Lord in the land of the living, and: The soul that sins, it shall die —.
Clement's First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 8

The ministers of the grace of God have, by the Holy Spirit, spoken of repentance; and the Lord of all things has himself declared with an oath regarding it, "As I live, says the Lord, I desire not the death of the sinner, but rather his repentance;" [Ezekiel 33:11] adding, moreover, this gracious declaration, "Repent, O house of Israel, of your iniquity." [Ezekiel 18:30] Say to the children of my people, Though your sins reach from earth to heaven, and though they be redder than scarlet, and blacker than sack-cloth, yet if you turn to me with your whole heart, and say, Father! I will listen to you, as to a holy people. [2 Chronicles 7:14] And in another place He speaks thus: "Wash you and become clean; put away the wickedness of your souls from before my eyes; cease from your evil ways, and learn to do well; seek out judgment, deliver the oppressed, judge the fatherless, and see that justice is done to the widow; and come, and let us reason together. He declares, Though your sins be like crimson, I will make them white as snow; though they be like scarlet, I will whiten them like wool. And if you be willing and obey me, you shall eat the good of the land; but if you refuse, and will not hearken unto me, the sword shall devour you, for the mouth of the Lord has spoken these things." [Isaiah 1:16-20] Desiring, therefore, that all His beloved should be partakers of repentance, He has, by His almighty will, established [these declarations].
ON PURITY 10

Come now, you tightrope walker, walking on a tightrope of purity and chastity and every sort of sexual asceticism, you who, on the slender cord of a discipline like this, far from the path of truth, advance with reluctant feet, balancing the flesh by the spirit, moderating your desires by the faith, guarding your eyes through fear, why do you watch your step so anxiously?
ON PRAYER 7:1

Having considered God's generosity, we pray next for his indulgence. For of what benefit is food if, in reality, we are bent on it like a bull on his victim? Our Lord knew that he alone was without sin. Therefore he taught us to say in prayer, "Forgive us our trespasses." A prayer for pardon is an acknowledgment of sin, since one who asks for pardon confesses guilt. Thus, too, repentance is shown to be acceptable to God, because God wills this rather than the death of the sinner.
Treatise III. On the Lapsed 36

He who has thus satisfied God, who by repentance for his deed, who by shame for his sin has conceived more of both virtue and faith from the very sorrow for his lapsing, after being heard and aided by the Lord, will cause the church to rejoice, which he recently had saddened, and will merit not only the pardon of God but a crown.
HOMILIES ON 2 TIMOTHY 3

And yet God is gracious and merciful. He is called a God "of mercies and a God of comfort"; good as none else is good, and kind, and gentle, and full of pity, Who "willeth not the death of a sinner, but that he should be converted and live." Whence then, whence is that Day so full of agony and anguish? A stream of fire is rolling before His face. The books of our deeds are opened. The day itself is burning as an oven, the angels are flying around, and many furnaces are prepared. How then is He good and merciful, and full of lovingkindness to man? Even herein is He merciful, and He shows in these things the greatness of His lovingkindness. For He holds forth to us these terrors, that being constrained by them, we may be awakened to the desire of the kingdom.
LETTER 122.1

Nothing makes God so angry as when people from despair of better things cleave to those which are worse; and indeed this despair in itself is a sign of unbelief. One who despairs of salvation can have no expectation of a judgment to come.
Homily 1, on Psalm 1

This is really what the Prophet Amos says: 'For three crimes and for four, I will not revoke my word, says the Lord.' Moreover, he says this same thing eight times. Now, this is what he actually is saying: you have entertained sin, I have pardoned you; you have done evil, I have forgiven you; you have not repented of your sins, I have excused you: did you also have to teach evil? What the Scripture implies is this: For three sins and for four, I shall not be angered against you, says the Lord.
SERMON 40:2

You though, standing there, having made no decision to put yourself right—let me speak like this as though to a single person. Whoever you are, you do not want to put yourself right; what are you promising yourself?
Forty Gospel Homilies, Homily 33

Let us consider the grace of merciful God, and let us condemn the multitude of our own guilt. Behold, he sees sinners and endures them, tolerates those who resist, and yet daily calls them mercifully through the Gospel. He desires our confession from a pure heart, and has forgiven all that we have done wrong. The mercy of the Redeemer has tempered for us the severity of the law. For in it was written: If anyone does this or that, let him surely die. If anyone does these or those things, let him be overwhelmed with stones. Our Creator and Redeemer appeared in the flesh, promising not punishment but life to the confession of sinners; he receives the woman confessing her wounds, and sends her away healed. He bent the hardness of the law toward mercy, because those whom the law justly condemns, he himself mercifully frees. Hence it is also well written in the law that the hands of Moses were heavy; therefore taking a stone, they placed it underneath, upon which he sat; and Aaron and Hur supported his hands. Moses indeed sat upon a stone, when the law rested upon the Church. But this same law had heavy hands, because it did not mercifully bear with sinners, but struck them with severe punishment. Aaron means mountain of strength, and Hur means fire. Whom therefore does this mountain of strength signify, if not our Redeemer, of whom it is said through the prophet: "In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the top of the mountains"? Or who is figured by fire, if not the Holy Spirit, of whom the same Redeemer says: "I came to cast fire upon the earth"? Therefore Aaron and Hur support the heavy hands of Moses, and by supporting them render them lighter, because the Mediator of God and men, coming with the fire of the Holy Spirit, showed us through spiritual understanding that the heavy commandments of the law, which could not be borne while held carnally, are tolerable for us. For he rendered the hands of Moses light, as it were, because he turned the weight of the law's commandments to the power of confession. He indicated this promise of mercy for us who follow, when he says through the prophet: "I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he be converted and live." Hence again under the figure of Judea it is said to every sinful soul: "If a man puts away his wife, and she departs and marries another man, will he return to her again? Will not that woman be polluted and contaminated? But you have fornicated with many lovers; nevertheless return to me, says the Lord." Behold, he gave the example of a shameful woman. He showed that after such shame she cannot be received back. But he overcomes by mercy this very example that he set forth, when he says that a fornicating woman can by no means be received back, and yet he himself waits to receive the fornicating soul. Consider, brothers, the weight of such great tenderness. He says what cannot be done, and demonstrates that he himself can do this even against custom. Behold, he calls, and those whom he declares to be defiled, he also seeks to embrace, those by whom he complains he has been abandoned. Let no one therefore waste the time of such great mercy, let no one cast away the offered remedies of divine tenderness.
Treatise XI. Exhortation to Martyrdom 5:8
We must press on and persevere in the faith and virtue and in the consummation of heavenly and spiritual grace, that we may be able to arrive at the palm and the crown.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And from the particular admonition with which he was speaking to the house of Israel, he passes to a general discussion: that past acts of righteousness do not save the righteous man if he has become taken up with new crimes, and old sins do not destroy the sinner or the wicked if he has amended his old errors by works of righteousness, and that God in both cases judges not past things but present ones: 'If I say,' he says, 'to the righteous: You shall live by life, and promise him the rewards of righteousness, and he, trusting in this, sins, all his former righteous deeds will be consigned to oblivion and he will die in his present iniquity; nor has my sentence changed, since I cannot render to the same man, now a sinner, what I had promised to the righteous man; on the contrary, if I threaten the sinner and the wicked — and say: Yet three days and Nineveh shall be overthrown —, and he repents and amends his old error by good works, so that he does judgment and righteousness, restores the pledge, and gives back what he has robbed, walks in the commandments of life, and does nothing unjust: ought he not to live by life, which is Christ, and by no means die, since the threat made to the sinner ought not to punish the righteous man?' — something of the kind the divine word says to Jeremiah when he goes down into the potter's house and hears that God's promises or threat aim at this: either to call men forth to salvation or to deter them from sin — 'hence those who say: The way of the Lord is not fair, are convicted of this, that it is their own judgment that is unfair, since they have a most evil eye and judge by no means the new things but the old'. By all these things it is shown that neither ought the sinner to despair of salvation if he repents, nor the righteous to trust in his righteousness if he has carelessly lost what he had acquired with great labor. We pass quickly over what is plain, in order to linger over what is more obscure; but in what points the present prophecy differs from the earlier one, and in what it says similar things, a comparison of the two will be able to show. Moreover, what it is to do judgment and righteousness, to restore the pledge, to give back what was robbed, to walk in the commandments of life, and the rest, we have said above in this same prophet.
LETTER 54.6
In the lives of Christians we look not to the beginnings but to the endings. Paul began badly but ended well. The start of Judas wins praise; his end is condemned because of his treachery.
Forty Gospel Homilies, Homily 34

But behold, while we search out the secrets of the heavenly citizens, we have digressed far from the order of our exposition. Let us therefore sigh toward those of whom we speak, but let us return to ourselves. For we ought to remember that we are flesh. Let us be silent meanwhile about the secrets of heaven, but before the eyes of our Creator let us wipe away the stains of our dust with the hand of repentance. Behold, divine mercy itself promises, saying: There shall be joy in heaven over one sinner doing penance; and yet through the prophet the Lord says: In whatever day the just man shall sin, all his righteousnesses shall be in oblivion before me. Let us consider, if we can, the dispensation of heavenly loving-kindness. To those who stand, if they should fall, he threatens punishment; but to the fallen, that they might desire to rise, he promises mercy. He terrifies those, lest they presume upon their good works; he comforts these, lest they despair in their evils. You are just—fear wrath, lest you fall; you are a sinner—trust in mercy, that you may rise.
Forty Gospel Homilies, Homily 34

If you are righteous, fear his wrath lest you slip; if you are a sinner, believe in his mercy so that you can arise. But see, we have already fallen, we are not strong enough to stand, we lie prostrate in our evil desires. He who created us to be upright still waits, and he appeals to us to rise. He opens up his heart of love and seeks to get us back to himself again through repentance.
Commentary on Ezekiel

This is according to the letter; but according to the ἀναγωγὴν [anagogy, the higher sense]: if 'Hiezechiel' [Ezekiel] means 'strength of God' — and Christ, moreover, is the power of God and the wisdom of God! —, this is to be understood: that, Jerusalem having been taken and overthrown, whoever has been able to escape the faithlessness of the Jews — such as were the apostles and the remnant that was saved —, he himself announces to Christ that all the ceremonies of the Jews have been overthrown — which certain people think must be observed even to this day, not hearing that saying of the Apostle: You have fallen from grace, you who are justified in the law. And I marvel at the obstinacy of men in wishing to defend in word what they do not dare to fulfill in deed, unless perhaps Jewish wolves are hiding under the skin of sheep, that is, of Christians. Why does a defender of the Synagogue make his voice resound in the churches of Christ? —. Jerusalem, therefore, having been taken and overthrown, the mouth of the Lord is opened through the apostles and apostolic men — who can say: My mouth is opened to you, O Corinthians, and: A great and effective door has been opened to me, and that saying: I opened my mouth and drew in the spirit —, a mouth which will never be able to keep silent, nor to hear — along with Israel: Hear, Israel, and be silent —, but will resound in the whole world and will lay open the Gospel of Christ to the nations. Hence, according to this sense, the 'twelfth year' refers to the twelve tribes, and the 'tenth month' to the time of the Jewish propitiation, which in Greek is called ἱλασμὸς, and the 'fifth day of the month' to the fleshly senses — all of which, Jerusalem having been taken and the Gospel succeeding, we have shown to have been abolished and to have passed away —, and 'in the evening', that is, at the consummation of the world, to the hand of the Lord having come upon the true Ezekiel, who had sung of the future ruins of the city through the prophets and in the morning showed that they had been fulfilled.
Commentary on Ezekiel
