The history of the Kings relates that under Rehoboam the son of Solomon the twelve tribes were divided, and that two, that is, Judah and Benjamin, with the Levites and priests, followed Rehoboam, who reigned in Jerusalem: and his kingdom was called Judah; but that the other ten tribes — who said: We have no part in David, nor inheritance in the son of Jesse — submitted their necks to Jeroboam the son of Nebat, of the tribe of Ephraim, who was the son of Joseph, and served him: and that they were called, from the greater part of the people, by the ancient name Israel; and that for a long time the kingdom of Judah and Israel waged conflicts against each other and obeyed their own kings, and that first the ten tribes were taken captive by the Assyrians, and, after some time, those which were called Judah were led captive by the Chaldeans into Babylon; and that the tribe of Judah was restored to its ancient land after seventy years, but the ten tribes, which were called Israel, serve as captives to this day in the mountains and cities of the Medes. The present prophecy, therefore, promises these things from the mouth of the Lord: that both realms are to be joined together, that is, the kingdom of Judah and the kingdom of Israel, and that the rod of Ephraim, who was begotten of the stock of Joseph, is to be taken up with the remaining tribes which are associated with him, and joined to the rod of Judah, so that they are no longer called Judah and Israel but are called by one name, Judah, and, under the figure of the prophet, who goes before as a type of the Lord Savior, are held not by two hands but by the one hand of Christ.
Commentary on Ezekiel

For he says that he takes the sons of Israel from the midst of the nations to which they were led captive, and will lead them back into the land and into the mountains of Israel — of which we read above —, and that they are to be called one nation and ruled by the authority of one king, so that they are no longer defiled with their idols and abominations; but that, when they have been freed from the dwelling places of captivity in which they had sinned, they are to be cleansed of all vices and will be the people of God, so that the Lord is their God.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And my servant, he says, David shall be king over them — of whom the angel also speaks in the Gospel, saying that he will reign over the house of Jacob and of his kingdom there will be no end —; and he will be of such clemency that he is called not only king but also shepherd, so that the name of shepherd may soften the proud name of power; and they, after they have become one nation and have dwelt in the land and on the mountains of Israel, will walk in all the judgments of the Lord and keep his precepts; and they will dwell not in another land but in that which he gave to his servant Jacob, in which their fathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob and the other saints dwelt; and not only will they themselves dwell there, but also their sons and grandsons — according to that line of Vergil: And the sons of sons and those who will be born of them —; and they will dwell there not for a short time, but for ever.
Commentary on Ezekiel

'But do you wish' he says 'to know who this king and shepherd is? He is the one of whom I spoke above: My servant David: Who, though he was in the form of God, did not think it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and became obedient to the Father unto death, even the death of the cross. And when they are under such a king, I will strike with them a covenant of peace': not, as in the old testament, a covenant of contests and wars, but a pact of peace: Which surpasses all understanding — of which the Savior speaks to the apostles: My peace I give to you, my peace I leave to you, and the prophet says: His place was made in peace —. And when he has founded and established them in the Church — so that they can say: He set my feet upon a rock —, then they will be multiplied, either in the number of believers or in the multiplication of virtues.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And I will put, he says, my sanctification (or sanctuary) in the midst of them for ever, which the Jews interpret of the temple that was built under Zerubbabel — but how will what is said, 'for ever', be able to stand, when that temple, which was built by Zerubbabel and afterwards restored by many, was burned by Roman fire? —. All these things are to be referred to the Church and to the times of the Savior, when his tabernacle was set in the Church, where he has become our God and we his people. And it is the advancement of all, that they may know that he is the Lord; and that he himself sanctifies Israel, not according to the flesh but according to the spirit, when his sanctification has been set in the midst of believers for ever.

n: Gog. This name, which signifies hidden, or covered, is taken in this place either for the persecutors of the Church of God in general, or some arch persecutor in particular; such as Antichrist shall be in the latter days. See Apocalypse xx. 8. And what is said of the punishment of Gog, is verified by the unhappy end of persecutors. --- Magog. Scythia or Tartary, whence the Turks and other enemies of the Church of Christ originally sprung. (Challoner) --- These are supposed to be the princes of some northern and barbarous country, (Worthington) peopled by the son of Japhet. (St. Jerome) --- St. Augustine (City of God xx. 11.) observes, that as the Church is spread everywhere, so also are persecutors. But Christ will overcome them all. (Worthington) --- This prophecy is very difficult. It seems literally to refer to Cambyses, who invaded Judea about seventy years after the temple had been destroyed, and perished by the hand of God, at Ecbatana, upon Mount Carmel. It is very usual with the prophets to give fictitious names; as the king of Tyre is called a cherub, and Jerusalem Ooliba. Cambyses ruled over Scythia, in Iberia; styled Gogarene, by Strabo (xi.). (Calmet) --- The proper Scythia withstood all the attempts of his successors, and defeated Darius. (Haydock)
Jaws. Thus Cambyses treated the son of Psammenites. God has the most absolute dominion over all monarchs, ver. 7.

Visited, or rather "shall visit" Judea. (Chaldean) (Grotius) --- Cambyses invaded Egypt twelve years after the Jews had returned, and came upon them two years later, designing to plunder them, at the instigation of their malevolent neighbours. He had sustained great losses in Egypt, and was arrived at Carmel when news was brought that the false Smerdis had declared himself king. See Herodotus iii. 61.

Midst. Literally, "navel." Hebrew, "Thabor," intimating a mountain rising in a plain, Judges ix. 7. (Calmet) --- Alluding to this intended blunder of the Jews lately returned, he speaks of Antichrist and of all heretics, who seek to pervert or suppress Catholics rescued from the power of the devil, by the sacraments of Christ. (Worthington)

Tharsis. Septuagint, "Carthage, and all their villages." The merchants or naval forces of Cambyses spurred him forward, (see Psalm lxxvii. 6.) as well as the Arabs, Cuthites, &c., 1 Esdras iv. 8. (Calmet)
Latter. Antichrist shall persecute the Church at the end of the world. (Worthington) --- After Cambyses had punished Egypt, his turn came, and all his designs were baffled.
Prophets. See Isaias xiv., and xvi. 21., and xxvi. 1., and Jeremias xxx. 3., and 23., and Joel ii. 30., and iii. 1., &c.
Israel. The Jews shall be full of dismay, (ver. 20.) as the tyrant will vent some threats; (Calmet) or this commotion was in his own army. (Haydock)

Sword. The Jews were not in a condition to make resistance. (Calmet) --- Cambyses had his brother Smerdis slain. But another was set on the throne; whereupon, mounting his horse in a fury, he wounded himself with his sword in the thigh, which mortifying, caused his death after twenty days. (Herodotus iii. 21., &c.) --- The historian does not mention what became of his army; but it seems to have perished by discord, as was very common among such a collection of nations. See Judges vii. 22., and Judith xv. 1., and 1 Kings xiv. 20., and 4 Kings ii. 21. (Calmet) --- They were now without a head. (Haydock) --- In the whole universe, God will at last destroy Antichrist and all his adherents. (Worthington)
Pestilence. His wound might be thus described. --- Blood. Thus was he punished for shedding that of innocent people. (Calmet)

f: Commentary on Ezekiel

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, set your face against Gog and the land of Magog, the prince of the head (or Ros) of Meshech and Tubal, and prophesy concerning him, and you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I am against you, Gog, the prince of the head (or Ros) of Meshech and Tubal, and I will turn you about, and I will put a bridle in your jaws, and I will lead out (or I will gather) both you and all your army, horses and horsemen, all of them clothed with breastplates, a great multitude seizing spear and shield and sword (or bucklers and helmets and swords). Persians and Ethiopians and Libyans with them, all with shields and helmets; Gomer and all its troops, the house of Togarmah, the sides of the north (or from the farthest parts of the north) and all its strength, and many peoples (or nations) with you. Prepare and equip yourself and all your multitude that is heaped together to you, and be for them a command (or and you shall be to me for a guard). After many days you will be visited; in the last of the years you will come to the land which has turned back (or been perverted) from the sword and has been gathered out of many peoples to the mountain (or land) of Israel, which had been continually deserted: this one has been led out from the peoples, and all of them will dwell confidently. And going up you will come like a storm and like a cloud, to cover the land, you and all your troops and many peoples (or nations) with you. Thus says the Lord God: On that day words will go up according to your heart, and you will think a most wicked thought, and you will say: I will go up to the land (or upon the land) without a wall (or cast off), I will come to those who are at rest and dwell securely (or in peace); all of them dwell without a wall, they have no bars and gates; to seize spoils and fall upon plunder, and to lay your hand upon those who had been deserted and were afterwards restored, and upon the people which has been gathered out of the nations, which has begun to possess and to be the inhabitant of the navel of the earth. Sheba and Dedan and the merchants of Tarshish (or the Carthaginians) and all its lions (or villages) will say to you: Is it to take spoils that you come? Behold, to seize plunder you have gathered your multitude, to carry off silver and gold, to take away household goods and property, and to seize boundless booty. Therefore prophesy, son of man, and you shall say to Gog: Thus says the Lord God: Will you not, on that day when the people Israel dwells confidently (or in peace), know (or rise up)? And you will come from your place from the sides (or from the farthest parts) of the north, you and many peoples with you, all of them riders of horses, a great company and a mighty army. And you will go up against my people Israel like a cloud to cover the land. In the last days you will be (or it will be), and I will bring you upon my land, so that all the nations may know me, when I am sanctified in you before their eyes, O Gog. Thus says the Lord God: You then are he of whom I spoke in ancient days, by the hand of my servants the prophets of Israel, who prophesied in those days and times (or years), that I would bring you upon them. And it shall be on that day, on the day of the coming of Gog upon the land of Israel, says the Lord God, that my indignation will go up in my fury. And in my zeal, in the fire of my wrath I have spoken, that on that day there shall be a great commotion upon the land of Israel, and the fish of the sea and the birds of the sky and the beasts of the field (or of the plain), and every creeping thing that moves upon the ground, and all the men who are upon the face of the earth shall be moved before my face; and the mountains shall be overturned (or split) and the enclosure walls shall fall (or the valleys), and every wall shall collapse to the ground. And I will call together against him on all my mountains a sword (or every terror of the sword), says the Lord God; the sword of each one (or of each man) shall be directed against his brother. And I will judge him with pestilence (or death) and blood and violent rain and immense stones (or of hail); fire and sulphur I will rain upon him, and upon his army (or upon all who are with him), and upon the many peoples who are with him, and I will be magnified and sanctified and I will be known in the sight of many nations, and they shall know that I am the Lord. First the foundations of the history must be laid, and it must be known that this is the last word of the Lord to the prophet Ezekiel; for after it we cannot in any way find anything similar, except what is written in the twenty-fifth year of the exile of Jeconiah: The hand of the Lord came upon me, and brought me there, that is, into the land of Israel, when the building of the temple is described and the order of its ceremonies is related.
Commentary on Ezekiel

The eleventh book of the explanations on Ezekiel will contain, in its last part, the prophecy against Gog and Magog, and it will come as far as the beginning of the city set on the mountain, Jerusalem, and of the temple situated in it. If, with the Lord helping and expounding his own mysteries, I am able to bring it all the way to the end, I shall have to hesitate long and much whether I ought to set my hands to the spiritual temple or openly confess my ignorance, especially since, both among the Jews and among us, there is a great silence over its interpretation: some judge that it is to be built in time to come; others, with a good intention indeed but an unskilled one, know that the things said are spiritual, and yet do not know how those spiritual things themselves ought to be expounded. And in the meantime, so that the care of the present work may hold us, know also, O virgin of Christ Eustochium, that you must pray for us. In a most difficult prophecy I will briefly point out this: that a man of our own age, by no means undistinguished, writing to the emperor, said concerning this nation: This Gog is the Goth; by what reasoning everything that is written in it can be fitted to him is not mine to expound, but theirs who think so.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Next it must be observed that the face of the prophet is set, or made firm, against Gog the land, or of the land, of Magog; for there is need of firmness and of much consideration of the countenance, so that we may be able to know the things that are said, according to that apostolic saying: But we all, contemplating the glory of the Lord with unveiled face, are re-formed into the same image, from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord. Accordingly the Jews and our own Judaizers think that Gog is the Scythian nations, savage and innumerable, which stretch beyond the Caucasus mountain and the Maeotic marsh and near the Caspian Sea as far as India — and that these are to be stirred up by the devil after the reign of a thousand years —, and that they are to come into the land of Israel to fight against the saints, with many nations gathered together with them: first Meshech, whom Josephus interprets as the Cappadocians; then Tubal, whom the same man supposes to be the Iberians or Spaniards, and the Hebrews the Italians, having with them in their army Persians, Ethiopians and Libyans; also Gomer and Togarmah, whom they interpret as the Galatians and Phrygians; also the Sabaeans and Dedan and the Carthaginians, or Tarshish; and that this is what John too sets down in his Revelation: And when the thousand years are finished, Satan will be loosed from his prison, and he will go out to seduce the nations in the four corners of the earth, Gog and Magog, to gather them for war: whose number is as the sand of the sea. And they went up over the breadth of the earth, and surrounded the camp of the saints and the beloved city. And fire came down from God out of heaven and devoured them; and the devil who seduced them was cast into the lake of fire and sulphur, where the beast and the false prophet were, and they will be tormented day and night for ages of ages; not understanding that the whole volume of John, which is headed with the title of Revelation, is mystical, and that we need revelation so that we may be able to say with the prophet: Unveil my eyes, and I will consider the wonders of your law. Others, however, abandoning the earthly sense and the Jewish and old-wives' fables, which are harmful and drag down into the depths those who acquiesce in them, climb up too far to the heights and invent much worse trifles, so that they describe the wars of the devil and of all his army in the heavenly Jerusalem, and under the ἐτυμολογίαις [etymologies] of the individual nations interpret the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places. Leaving all these things to the reader's judgment, we shall try not so much to condemn the views of others as to affirm the Church's explanation. 'Gog' is called in the Greek tongue δῶμα, in the Latin 'roof'; 'Magog', moreover, means 'from the roof' — so all pride, and the knowledge falsely so called which raises itself against the knowledge of the truth, is shown by these names —; these are the roofs of which Isaiah too speaks in the vision against the valley of Zion: What has happened to you now, that you all go up onto the empty roofs?; and by 'roof' we shall interpret the princes of the heretics, and by 'from the roof' those who have taken up their doctrines; and fittingly, after the many mystical prophecies in this volume, the last prophecy is against Gog and Magog — for if It is the time of judgment, according to Peter, that it should begin from the house of God, and according to this same Ezekiel, who says: And begin from my saints, and: The last enemy, death, is destroyed, in Isaiah too the first word is directed against Judea, in which is the confession of the Lord, and the last against the four-footed beasts which are in the desert; rightly here too the last word is directed against Gog and Magog, who assail the city of God, which the rush of the river makes glad, and which says in Isaiah: I am a strong city which is besieged, and of which it is written in the Gospel: A city set on a mountain cannot be hidden, and more fully in the psalm: Jerusalem, which is built as a city whose sharing of it is in the selfsame. Mountains are round about it, and the Lord is round about his people —. Moreover, as to the fact that in the army of Gog or Magog, who according to the Seventy, Symmachus and Theodotion is prince of Ros, Meshech and Tubal, Aquila translates the first nation, 'Ros', as 'head', and we too have followed him — so that the sense is: The prince of the head of Meshech and Tubal; and in truth neither in Genesis, nor in any other place of Scripture, nor even in Josephus, who in the first book of the Antiquities sets out the names of all the Hebrew nations, have we been able to find this nation, from which it is clear that 'Ros' signifies not 'a nation' but 'head'; this too must be briefly noted, that in Ezekiel Gog is said to be the prince of the land of Magog, whereas Revelation records that both Gog and Magog are nations which go out from the four corners of the earth; and that just as from Jacob, who was afterwards called Israel, the whole people of the Hebrews received the name Israel, and from Aram Syria, from Mesraim Egypt, whose names are written in Genesis, so too from the prince Gog all who are subject to him are called Magog —; 'Mosoch', however, means 'madness', and 'Thubal' 'whole' or 'all things': so the 'prince' and 'head of proud madness and of all evils' — according to what is written: The world is set in the evil one — are called 'Gog' and 'Magog' — nations which, hostile and adverse to the saints, go out from the corners of the earth, abandoning the straight line and the arrangement of the camps of God which is related in Numbers, and not knowing that testimony: Many will come from the east and the west and the north and the south, and will recline with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of God, and in another place: I will say to the north: Bring; and to the south-west wind: Do not hinder, bring my sons from a distant land and my daughters from the end of the earth, all who are called by my name; but not such are the corners of the earth from which Gog and Magog go out: beside such corners the harlot stands in Proverbs, who hastens to deceive the foolish young men passing by through the streets, that is, through the broad and spacious way which leads to death: the scribes and Pharisees too pray at the corners of the streets so as to be seen by men, who have received their reward —.
Commentary on Ezekiel

What, then, is the threat against Gog? 'I will turn you about (or I will convert), and I will put a bridle in your jaws: first I will make you waver from your opinion and be converted, and I will put a bridle in your jaws — of which it is written: With bridle and bit bind fast the jaws of those who do not draw near to you —, so that the untamed horse, wanton and rushing headlong over precipices, may be subjected to the bridle of the Lord' — to whom the prophet says: You will mount upon your horses, and your riding is salvation, and to Job it is said through clouds and whirlwind: Did you surround the horse with strength? Such were the horses and horsemen whose multitude John saw in heaven —. So he says to Gog: I will lead out (or I will gather) you and all the army (or strength) of yours; he who is led out and gathered from dispersion is drawn back to salvation — according to what is promised in the law: If your dispersion be from the height of heaven to its height, from there I will gather you —.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Of his horses too, and horsemen clothed with breastplates — who imitate the armor of the Apostle and boast that they have the breastplates of righteousness — there is an excessive multitude, and all of them seize shield and sword against the Church, and they are most savage nations, hostile to Israel: Persians, Ethiopians and Libyans — whose wars against the people of God are related in the holy Scriptures —; Gomer too and the house of Togarmah, who come from the sides of the 'north' — which is a most cold wind and is called by the name 'dexter' [right-hand] —, and all the strength of Magog and all the peoples that are subject to him, will come with him to battle.
Commentary on Ezekiel

To him it is said by way of εἰρωνείαν [irony]: 'Prepare and equip yourself, and heap together to yourself all your multitude, which obeys your commands; but know that after many days you will be visited' — according to what is written: I will visit their iniquities with the rod and their sins with stripes —.
Commentary on Ezekiel

'In the last', he says, 'of the years you will come'; whence John too says: My little children, it is the last hour, and the people of the Gentiles is hired at the eleventh hour to work in the vineyard; to whose land — that is, the land of the meek and the land of the saints, which brings forth fruit a hundredfold and sixtyfold and thirtyfold — Gog comes to storm it, the land which has turned back, or turned away, from the sword — for it knows that it is written: Scatter, O Lord, the nations that desire wars —, and abides in peace, and has been gathered from many peoples and nations so that, having despised the error of the nations, it might come to the mountains of Israel, that is, the patriarchs and prophets, who were once continually deserted, without the law and the precepts of God, to which it is afterwards said: More are the children of the deserted one than of her who has a husband; these are the deserted and waterless places in which the devil could find no place, because they had been called to salvation, and afterwards, taking with him seven other demons more wicked than himself, he returned to his house, that is, to the nation of Israel. This, he says, has been led out from the peoples, land being understood, or: This one has been led out from the nations, so that the people of believers may be understood, which has dwelt in peace; and it trusts in the Lord.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And Gog, going up with all his army, will come like a storm and like a cloud, to cover the land of the believers — for which of the heretics, whose prince is the devil, does not come like a storm against the Church, and hasten to overwhelm and cover with the cloud of his words all the simple among the believers? —; whence it is said to him: 'As far as lies in you, you will cover all things, you and all your troops and many peoples with you'; and fittingly Gog, going up, has no willing rain, no early and late shower to gladden the parched fields, but storm and darkness, so as to confound all things with gloom and error.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Therefore the Lord God speaks these things to him: At that time, that is, in the last days, words will go up upon your heart, and you will think a most wicked thought — as Scripture says: If the spirit of one who has power should wish to go up upon you, do not abandon your place; but on the contrary God goes up into the heart of the holy man, of whom it is written: He has set ascents in his heart —; and Gog says: I will go up to the land without a wall (or cast forth) — that is, the land which is destitute of the help of God and not fortified by the argumentation of the dialecticians, I will come to those who are at rest, dwelling securely (or in peace) — for our king is peaceable, and his place is in peace —; all of them, he says, dwell without a wall, they have no bars and gates.
Commentary on Ezekiel

This the devil, the prince of the heretics, says: that the Church has no fortifications, nor the worldly wisdom which is foolishness with God, so that he may seize the spoils and fall upon the plunder of the Church, and lay his hand upon those who had been deserted when they did not have the knowledge of God and afterwards, restored through Christ, come to the Father — he says in the Gospel: Father, I have revealed your name to men —; and so that we may know that the people which had been deserted and afterwards restored signifies the Christian people, there follows: And upon the people which has been gathered out of the nations, which people has begun to possess the inheritance of Christ and to be the inhabitant of the navel of the earth — of which it is written: He has worked salvation in the midst of the earth. Truth, indeed, has sprung from the earth; which says in the Gospel: I am the way and the truth and the life —.
Commentary on Ezekiel

While he thinks and says these things and hastens to snatch the possession of the Church, the nations which had been converted from their former error to salvation: Sheba and Dedan and the merchants of Tarshish — of Carthage or of the sea — who amid the waves of this world seek merchandise by good works, and all their villages or lions — or lions' whelps, as is contained in the Hebrew —, will say to him what follows — that the Seventy and Theodotion, however, put 'villages' in place of 'lions' whelps', which in Hebrew are called 'chaphir', is an evident error: for if you write it with the letter 'chi', it is called 'lion's whelp', but if with 'ce', which in Hebrew is called 'coph', it is called 'field' and 'village'; whence Capharnaum too is called 'most beautiful field' —. So Sheba and Dedan and the merchants of Tarshish will say, and all the saints who are called lions' whelps, or at any rate the villages and dwellings of the believers: 'O Gog, is it for this that you come: to snatch the spoils of the Church? and is it for this that you have gathered a multitude: that the possession of Christ may become your inheritance? or do you think that you will possess the silver and gold of the Church — which is understood of eloquence and meaning —, so as to take away its household goods and all its property, and seize the boundless booty gathered by Christ the victor?'
Commentary on Ezekiel

'Therefore, O prophet Ezekiel, who in the type of Christ are called son of man, speak to Gog and say to him: Thus says the Lord God: When, the error of the whole world having been taken away, my people Israel, which discerns God with the mind, dwells in the Church confidently or in peace, then you will know, or rise up and come from your place' — and what the place of heretical depravity is, the following word shows: From the sides of the north, which tries to chill all the warmth of the believers —.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And many peoples will come with him, all riders of horses — of whom it is written: The horse and the rider he has cast into the sea —, a great company and a mighty army; with whom: 'You will go up', he says, 'against my people Israel like a cloud and darkness, to cover my land — of which it was spoken above —. In the last days you will be, in the time of the preaching of the Gospel, and I will bring you upon my land — For there must also be heresies, so that those who are approved may be made manifest, and by the will of God the devil, the ἀνταγωνιστής [adversary], and all the dogmas of perversity have been left —, so that all the nations may know (and understand) me, when I am sanctified in you before their eyes, O Gog, that is, when through your punishments they have understood me as judge'.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And he makes an apostrophe to Gog himself: 'Are you not he of whom I spoke in ancient days, by the hands of my servants the prophets of Israel?': that is, of Moses — who says in the book of Numbers, at least according to the Seventy: A man shall come forth from his seed and shall rule over very many nations, and Gog his kingdom shall be lifted up, and his kingdom shall increase, but according to the Hebrew I found it written thus: His king shall be taken away because of Agag, and his kingdom shall be removed, because the kingdom of Israel was destroyed in Saul on account of Agag king of Amalek; and in another place: He will cleanse the land of his people —; Joel too describes the peoples to be gathered in the valley of 'Iosaphat', that is, 'of the judgment of God'; and Isaiah, and all the prophets, in whose hands and good works the word of the Lord comes about.
Commentary on Ezekiel

'When therefore you come upon the land of Israel, my indignation will go up in my fury against you. And in my zeal for my people, in the fire of my wrath I have spoken, which is to consume all the timbers of your vices: At that', he says, 'time there will be a great commotion upon the land of Israel': for at the instigation of the devil frequent persecution will arise against the Church, and when it has been lulled to rest and overcome by the protection of God, then the fish of the sea and the birds of the sky and the beasts of the field, and every creeping thing that moves upon the earth, and all the men who are upon the face of the earth, will be moved before his face; which is clearly shown of the inhabitants of the Church, of whom some like the fish of the sea, some like the birds of the sky, some like the beasts of the field and all the creeping things that move upon the earth, others as retaining the dignity of man, dwell upon the face of the earth — and that diversity of conduct is signified by various names the Apostle also writes to the Corinthians, since he says that after the resurrection some bodies are heavenly, others earthly, one the body of a fish, another of a bird, another of beasts, another of creeping things, and another of men, who have kept their original name; in the Acts of the Apostles too, that sheet which is shown three times to the apostle Peter by its four corners signifies the variety of believers which was also contained in the ark of the flood —.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Then, from the face of the Lord and from the sight of his majesty, the mountains which raised themselves against the knowledge of God will be overturned, and the hedges or valleys will fall, which either have sunk to the depths through lowness of understanding or at any rate promise some fortification so as to imitate the Church of God — of whose hedges it is said: Whoever breaks down a hedge, a serpent will bite him —, and every wall will collapse to the ground: for when the strength of the Church's word appears, all the fortifications of the heretics will collapse.
Commentary on Ezekiel

'And I will call together against him, that is, against Gog, the prince of the heretics, a sword on all my mountains, so that the princes of his army may be destroyed by the sword for the Lord'; then heresy will fight against heresy, and their fighting among themselves is our victory.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And I will judge, he says, him with death (or pestilence) and blood and violent rain and immense stones (or of hail): and Gog is judged by his own death, and by the blood which he shed, and by violent rain, the words of a learned and perfect man, and by immense stones which overwhelm him with the testimonies of the Scriptures, or of hail, which make his heat grow cold — All, indeed, who commit adultery, their hearts are like an oven —. Fire, he says, and sulphur I will rain upon him, by which the punishment of eternal judgment is shown; and not only upon him who was the author of perversity, but also upon all his army and multitude and upon the many peoples who are with him — for the heretics have many companions, or rather the devil, their prince, is surrounded by an infinite multitude —.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And when all error has been taken away and the princes of the heretics have been punished and destroyed, the Lord is magnified, and sanctified in the believers, and becomes known in the eyes of the many nations which have believed in his faith, and both from their own blessedness and from the punishments of the adversaries they will know and recognize that he himself is the Lord. These things we have interpreted as we were able, obeying that precept: You shall turn aside neither to the right nor to the left, but: You shall walk on the royal road; but if anyone finds fault with what is ours, let him either bring forward better things for us to follow, or, if he wishes to say nothing, let him leave perfect knowledge to God, provided only that he knows that it is by no means our powers, but our intention, that is to be judged.

n: Arrows. Cambyses thought himself the most skilful at shooting. This was the usual weapon of the Persians (Calmet) and Parthians. (Haydock)
Fall. In every part some shall resist Antichrist, who shall be overpowered. (Worthington) --- Cambyses died at Carmel.

Islands; in the naval forces, or in the places of his dominion where discord shall prevail. (Calmet) --- Cambyses resolved to attack Ethiopia, the people near the temple of Ammon, and the Carthaginians: but his troops refused to go against the latter, and many were smothered in the sands, or starved to death in the other expeditions. (Just. i.; Lucan x., &c.)

Years; for a long time, ver. 12. Little fuel is necessary there. Mariana (Hist. xi. 24. A.[The year of the Lord] 1212.) mentions, that the arms of the Moors supplied Spain four years with fuel. (Calmet)
Prey. The Jews relate that Zorobabel went out to oppose these nations, and took so much plunder as to be able to begin the temple. (Theodoret)

East of the Mediterranean and of Carmel, the high road from Assyria to Egypt, (Genesis xxxvii. 2.; Calmet) where the Romans had a station at Legion. (Eusebius) --- Called, or shall be, Isaias vii. 14., and lx. 14. (Calmet) --- Valley. Septuagint, "Gai, the grave of Gog." Protestants, "the valley of Haman-Gog," ver. 16. (Haydock) --- Antichrist will not be burnt with material fire. But Catholics shall resist him zealously, and gain the victory. (Worthington)
Land, to prevent infection, and to comply with the law, Numbers xix. 16.

Day. It does not occur in the calendar. Yet Comestor and [Denis] the Carthusian mentions Cambysa, the day when Bethulia was delivered, Judith xvi. 31. The history of Judith may perhaps relate to the defeat of this prince. The embellishments will not injure the truth. The Jews immediately after his death recommence the building of the temple, (1 Esdras iv.; Aggeus i. 14.) which they are forced to discontinue, till Hystaspes confirmed the decree of Cyrus. This was the grand object of their desires, and therefore the day when Cambyses fell was ever memorable to them. (Calmet, Diss.) --- So will that be for Christians, when Antichrist shall be no more. (Menochius)

Buriers. These might be foreign slaves, or Jews, who followed this employment. (Calmet) --- They would be habitually (Haydock) unclean, and their company would be carefully avoided. Those who sought after the dead remains, contracted no uncleanness. (Calmet)

Amona. Hebrew hamon, (Haydock) means "a multitude." (Calmet) --- Septuagint, "a place for many graves:" poluandrion. (Haydock) --- So many would be buried there, that the place might justly receive such a name; though we find no such city in the neighbourhood. (Calmet) --- Rabbath, of Ammon, was sometimes so called. (Haydock)
That are. Hebrew, "and of meries, (a species of oxen, in Syria.; Bellon. ii. 50.) all of them from Basan," beyond the Jordan, a most fertile country. Septuagint, "all calves fattened."

Sword. I could as easily have protected them against the Chaldeans as against this prince, if their sins had not been in the way. (Calmet) --- These bring on the ruin of God's people more than the power of the enemy. (Worthington)

Israel. All who please may now return. Hystaspes was very favourable to them. He married Esther, raised Mardochai to great power, and sent Esdras into Judea with ample privileges. Many returned under him, Artazerxes, and Alexander [the Great]. --- Jealous. I will restore the people to favour, and will protect them (Calmet) like a husband. (Haydock)

There, except such as refused to return. They have entire liberty. This and what follows was not fully accomplished till the propagation of the gospel. God wished all to embrace it; and though Israel has been partly blind, they will enter the Church after the Gentiles, Romans xii. 26. (Calmet)

f: Commentary on Ezekiel

But you, son of man, prophesy against Gog and say: Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I am against you, Gog, prince of the head (or Ros) of Meshech and Tubal; and I will turn you about (or gather you) and lead you astray (or lead you down), and make you go up from the sides (or from the uttermost parts) of the north, and bring you upon the mountains of Israel. And I will strike (or destroy) your bow in your left hand (or from your left hand), and your arrows from your right hand, and I will cast you down upon the mountains of Israel. And you will fall, you and all your troops, and the peoples (or nations) that are with you; to the wild beasts, to the birds and to every winged thing and to the beasts of the earth I have given you to be devoured: on the face of the field (or plain) you will fall, for I have spoken, says the Lord God. And I will send fire on Magog, and on those who dwell in the islands confidently (or and the islands will be inhabited in peace), and they will know that I am the Lord. And I will make my holy name known in the midst of my people Israel, and I will not pollute (or it will not be polluted) my holy name any more, and the nations will know that I am the Lord God, the holy one of Israel. Behold, it comes, and it has been done (or you will know that it will be), says the Lord; this is the day of which I have spoken. And the inhabitants of the cities of Israel will go forth, and will kindle and burn the weapons, the shield and the spears (or the targes and the pikes), the bow and the arrows, the hand staves and the pikes (or lances), and they will kindle them with fire seven years. And they will not carry (or will not take up) wood from the regions (or from the fields), nor cut it down from the forests, since they will kindle the weapons with fire; and they will plunder those whose prey they had been, and despoil their despoilers, says the Lord God. And it shall be, on that day, I will give Gog a renowned place, a sepulcher in Israel, the valley of the travelers east of the sea, which makes those who pass by stand aghast (or the πολυάνδριον [common burial ground, literally "place of many men"] of those who will come to the sea, and they will build round about the mouth of the valley); and there they will bury Gog and all his multitude, and it will be called the valley (or 'ge') of the multitude of Gog. And the house of Israel will bury them, to cleanse the land (or that the land may be cleansed) for seven months; and all the people of the land will bury them, and it will be for them a renowned day on which I was glorified, says the Lord God. And they will appoint men continually going through (or going round) the land, to bury and to search out those who remain upon the face of the land, that they may cleanse it; and after seven months they will begin to search, and they will go round traversing the land; and when they see a man's bone, they will set up a marker beside it, until the undertakers bury it in the valley (or 'ge') of the multitude of Gog. And the name of the city is Amona (or Πολυάνδριον), and they will cleanse the land (or the land will be cleansed). These things the heirs of the Jewish tradition and the disciples of endless fables contend will come to pass after the reign of a thousand years: that Gog, prince of Ros, Meshech and Tubal, is to be slain in the borders of Israel and to be devoured by all the winged creatures and the beasts; and that the inhabitants of the cities of Israel will for seven years by no means have the use of wood from the cutting of forests, but from the weapons of Gog, namely shields and spears and arrows and staves or pikes; and that Gog himself is to be buried in the valley which in Hebrew is called 'ge', and the name of his sepulcher is to be called πολυάνδριον, namely where a multitude of men has been buried; and that he is to be buried by the house of Israel for seven months so that the land may be cleansed, and that the day when Gog was slain will be renowned, and that men are to be appointed to search diligently for the bones and bury them, so that, namely, nothing remains unburied in the land; and that after the seven months, or within the seven months, the land is to be traversed, and wherever they observe a man's bone lying, it is to be pointed out by a marker set beside it, so that afterward those who have been put in charge of this work may bury it; and that the name of the city is to be called 'Amona', which in Greek is called Πολυάνδριον, that is, 'a multitude of buried men', and that in this way the land is to be cleansed. This is what they have said; but let us, holding to the sense of the explanation we have begun, discuss one by one the things we have set forth.
Commentary on Ezekiel
Gog too has his own trinity, 'Ros' and 'Mosoch' and 'Thubal', that is, 'head' and 'madness' and 'all things', so that there is no vice that does not stand in Gog's possession.
Commentary on Ezekiel

He will be led out, or turned about, and he will be stroked and coaxed so that, hoping for victory, he may be led to battle to be slain; and he will go up from the sides, or from the uttermost parts, of the north, from which evils blaze up over all the earth, and by that very one he will be brought upon the mountains of Israel, which we ought to understand as the apostles and apostolic men and men of the Church, so that, after he has been brought to the mountains of Israel, then the bow that is in his left hand may be struck, and the arrows that are held in the right hand: for he too imitates, in order to kill those whom he has deceived, the having of weapons on the left and on the right, through good report and bad — these are the arrows and these the darts of which the psalmist too speaks: For behold, sinners have bent the bow, they have made ready arrows in the quiver, to shoot in the dark at the upright of heart, which fiery darts of the devil are to be quenched with the shield of faith —.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And Gog, who had gone up upon the mountains of Israel, is cast down, or will fall, on those very mountains with all his army and all his troops; and he will be food for the wild beasts, the birds and every winged thing and the beasts of the earth, namely the adverse powers that ate the seed by the wayside, and the bloodthirsty beasts — for as it is written of the dragon: You gave him as food to the Ethiopian peoples, so all who are deceived by the heretics are the food of demons —: and Gog will fall either in the breadth of the plain or in that of the field which has been tilled by God's husbandmen; for it cannot be that the Lord's words should be void.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Then fire will be sent on Magog, namely on those who received Gog's teaching, and on those who, like islands, are beaten by the waves of the world and think that they ought to be secure — that fire of which the Lord speaks: I came to send fire upon the earth, and how I will that it burn —: 'that all may know and understand that I am the Lord'.
Commentary on Ezekiel

'And let my holy name be made known in the midst of my people, which was by no means led astray by the authority of Gog, and let my name no longer be polluted among the heretics on the pretext of the knowledge falsely so called, and let the nations that are round about know that I am the Lord'.
Commentary on Ezekiel

But what follows, Behold, it comes, and it has been done, is said of the judgment of Christ, who coming will come and will not delay; and this is the day of punishments and vengeance of which the Lord has spoken through all the prophets.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And the inhabitants of the cities of Israel will go forth: the peoples of believers; and by the cities of Israel we understand the Church of right faith. And they will kindle and burn the weapons — of which it is written in another place too: He will crush the bow, he will shatter the weapons, and he will burn the shields with fire —, shields and spears, bow and arrows, hand staves — with which they celebrated a perverse Passover —, lances or pikes — with which they inflicted the broad and incurable wounds of their doctrines —, and shields, bows and arrows, of which it was said above. And what follows, And they will kindle them with fire seven years, is to be taken from Exodus and Leviticus, in which it is commanded by the law that in the seventh year, of release, when liberty is restored to Hebrew slaves and all debts are cancelled and the ancient possession returns to its owners, rest too is granted to the land and all the crops are given over to the poor; so that, namely, in seven years, a sacred and perfect number, the armor of the heretics may perish utterly, and the men of the Church may by no means cut wood from the fields and regions and woods and forests of the nations, whom they desire rather to save than to destroy, but from those of the heretics whom they have conquered, from shields, spears, arrows, staves and pikes and lances: for they too have various weapons for attacking the Church of Christ, which are to be set on fire by learned men with the fire of the Holy Spirit — namely by the Church's word, and whoever has it will be able to say: Was not our heart burning on the way, when Jesus opened the Scriptures to us? —; nor can we have full peace and confidence in our dwelling unless we plunder all the gear of our adversaries, so that everything may perish and be burned to ashes, and we plunder those who had earlier plundered us, and lay waste those who had first laid waste the Church.
Commentary on Ezekiel

On that day — in the clear light of preaching — I will give, he says, Gog a renowned place, a sepulcher in Israel, according to the Hebrew: the valley of the travelers east of the sea, which makes those who pass by stand aghast; the sense of this saying is this: The sepulcher of Gog will not be on the mountains but in low valleys and rugged places — which in Hebrew are called 'ge'; and the heretics, though they are situated in the west, pretend that these are places of the east —, in order to deceive the travelers, namely those who pass through this world and are not inhabitants but sojourners — saying that prophetic word: I am a stranger and a sojourner, as all my fathers were —. For which of those passing by — of whom it is written: And those who passed by did not say: The blessing of the Lord be upon you! — does not marvel and stand aghast when he sees the valley of the travelers, which to the travelers seems a valley, to the inhabitants a mountain? This is according to the Hebrew. But the Seventy translated: the πολυάνδριον of those who will come to the sea, and they will build round about the entrance of the valley: for it is the labor of those who go out from the cities of Israel to shut and build round every entrance and exit of the heretical depravity, of those who had come to the sea and delighted in its bitterness, in the masses of its waves and in the cruelty of shipwreck, and to bury them in the chasms of the earth, so that they may no longer be able to go out and deceive anyone by their fraud. There, therefore, they will bury Gog and all his multitude, in which the heretics always delight; and the name of that valley in which Gog was buried will be called 'ge of the multitude', or πολυάνδριον, that is, 'the sepulcher of a very great multitude'.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And as we said above that the weapons of the adversaries are kindled through seven years, so through seven months the land will be cleansed of the filth of the heretics; for from the first month — when we celebrate the Lord's Passover and escape the destroyer of Egypt by the blood of the lamb on our doorposts —, up to the end of the year — that is, up to the seventh month, when we pitch tabernacles and, among the other foliage, are sheltered also by branches of palms, so that a perfect victory over the enemies may be shown —, we fulfil all the festivals among the peoples; and not only the teachers but the whole people too will do this eagerly, to bury Gog, and cover him with earth, and by no means allow him to take in the free air.
Commentary on Ezekiel

After the peace, however, and the slaying, or the burial, of Gog, men of the Church will be chosen who have this as their concern: that nothing of the former filth remain in the land of Israel, nothing of carrion; men to go through the land and search out the dead and bury them, so that, namely, the land of the Church may be cleansed. But if after seven months, when all things ought to have been purged, those who traverse and go round the land see that in anyone a man's bone — that is, the hardness of heretical depravity — or something of the carrion of the former doctrine has remained, they will set up, or build, a marker beside it, so that, after those who are of this kind have been marked, they may then either be corrected or be buried with Gog and thrust away into the throng of his burial.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And the name of the city where the victory of the servants of the Lord is, and where the adversaries lie and the whole multitude of his enemies has been laid low, will be called 'Amona' or Πολυάνδριον, so that the end of all things may be the restoration of purity. Finally there follows: And they will cleanse the land, doubtless those of whom it is written above: They will begin to search, and will go round traversing the land.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Therefore you, son of man, thus says the Lord God: Say to every bird and to all the fowl and to all the beasts of the field (or plain): Assemble and hasten, run together from every side (or round about) to my victim, which I have sacrificed for you, a great victim upon the mountains of Israel, that you may eat flesh and drink blood. You will eat the flesh of the mighty (or of giants), and you will drink the blood of the princes of the earth, of rams, of lambs and of he-goats, and of fatted bulls and of all fat things; and you will eat fat to the full, and drink blood to drunkenness from the victim which I have sacrificed for you. And you will be filled at my table with horse and with mighty horseman (or giant), and with all men of war, says the Lord God. And I will set (or give) my glory among the nations (or among you), and all the nations will see my judgment which I have done, and my hand which I have laid (or brought) upon them; and the house of Israel will know that I am the Lord their God from that day and thereafter, and all the nations will know that the house of Israel was taken captive for their iniquities, because they forsook me, and I hid (or turned away) my face from them, and delivered them into the hand of the foes (or of their enemies), and they all fell by the sword. According to their uncleannesses and their crimes (or iniquities) I dealt with them, and I hid (or turned away) my face from them. Therefore thus says the Lord God: Now I will bring back the captivity of Jacob, and I will have mercy on the whole house of Israel, and I will take up zeal for my holy name. And they will bear their confusion (or ignominy), and all the transgression by which they transgressed against me, when they dwell in their own land confidently (or in peace), fearing no one. And when I have brought them back from the peoples (or nations), and have gathered them from the lands of their enemies (or from the regions of the nations), and have been sanctified in them in the eyes (or in the sight) of very many nations, they will also know that I am the Lord their God, since I have carried them over into the nations (or since I have appeared to them among the nations), and have gathered them upon their own land, and have not left any of them there. And I will no longer hide (or turn away) my face from them, because I have poured out my spirit (or fury) upon the whole house of Israel, says the Lord God. (What we have translated according to the Hebrews: I will gather them upon their own land, and I will not leave any of them there, is not found in the Seventy; and again, where according to the Hebrews a blessing is set at the end: Because I have poured out my 'spirit', the Seventy translated 'fury', which pertains to anger, especially since in the Hebrew 'ruhi' is written, which properly means 'my spirit' and by no means 'my fury'.) But everything up to the place where the building of the temple follows, those we spoke of above, the Jews and our own Judaizers, refer to the last time: that the birds and the beasts are to be sated with the flesh of Gog and of all his army as with the fattest offerings, and that Israel is to be restored to its former state and by no means be assailed any longer by the nations, but that God will pour out his spirit upon them so that they may dwell in their own land: not all the nations, but properly the house of Israel.
Commentary on Ezekiel

But we, following the tropology we have begun, say this: that the Lord calls together all the birds and all the beasts, to hand over to them the princes of the heretics to be devoured as the fattest offerings — and those to whom the adversaries are handed over are called birds and beasts either for their swiftness in running about into all things or for their savagery and cruelty: For the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved, and that they may learn not to blaspheme —; and they will eat a great and very fat victim: not elsewhere, but upon the mountains of Israel, which we ought to understand as the prophets and apostles and holy men — for upon them the teachers of contrary dogmas fall in ruin, and by them they perish wounded —, upon whom the Church is built, and, to speak more truly, upon the mountain of mountains — of which Isaiah speaks, and Micah: Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob, and he will announce to us his way —. And these birds and these swift and cruel beasts will eat flesh and drink blood — which cannot possess the kingdom of God —.
Commentary on Ezekiel

The flesh of the mighty, or of giants, who rebelled against the knowledge of God, and the blood of the princes, not of heaven but of the earth, who savored all earthly things, they will drink: the blood of rams, of lambs and of he-goats, or, according to the Seventy, of rams, of calves and of he-goats, so that it signifies three living creatures that are sacrificed among the victims of God: for the heretics too imitate the gentleness of the Church, but their oblation serves not for the worship of God but for the food of demons, and this is their fattest offering; and they are sated as if with fat, and they drink the blood of the deceived to drunkenness; but God sacrifices this victim through the men of the Church, so that the most wicked guests may be sated with the multitude of the deceived, and drink to vomiting and drunkenness.
Commentary on Ezekiel

When you see holy men, learned in the divine Scriptures, cutting down the horses of the heretics and their riders — of which it is written: The horse and the rider he has cast into the sea —, and hewing down all the rebels and giants with their own blade, and shedding the blood of all the warriors of the knowledge falsely so called, then know that the table of the Lord has been prepared, that he may set his glory among all the nations that believe in his name.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And the churches of the saints will understand his judgment which he has executed upon the adversaries, and the strong hand with which he struck them; and let the house of Israel know and recognize that he is the Lord their God — who said: I am the Lord your God — from the day of the Lord's victory for ever, and let them reflect that the house of Israel was once taken captive by the heretics and scattered through the whole world of perverse dogmas for this reason: that they forsook him who for a little while hid, or turned away, his face from them and delivered them into the hand of the heretics, and they fell, pierced through by their blade, because of their uncleannesses and iniquities; and this was the cause of his hiding and turning away his face from them.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And having set forth the reasons — according to that which is written: There must also be heresies, so that those who are approved may be made manifest — for the captivity of Israel, that is, of the Church, in which those dwell who see God, he now promises that he will bring back into the Church the captivity of Jacob, who had supplanted the Jewish people and afterward was himself supplanted by the frauds of the heretics; and that he will have mercy on the whole house of Israel, not according to the flesh but according to the spirit. And I will take up, he says, my zeal for my holy name, which was blasphemed among the nations because of the heretics, so that, after he has set them free, they may blush and be confounded because, having abandoned the faith of the Church, they transgressed against me. Let them be confounded, then, and blush very swiftly, when they dwell in their own land, the land of the meek and the land of the saints, and dwell confidently, or in peace, by no means fearing the snares of the heretics.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Then they will be brought back from the peoples, and gathered from the lands of their enemies into their own land, and the Lord will be sanctified in them in the sight of very many nations, which themselves too are going to believe in the Lord; and let this be the end of blessedness: to know and recognize that he is the Lord their God, because he appeared to them among the nations, or carried them over from the nations, and gathered them upon their own land, the land of Judea, the land of confession, the land of the meek and the land of the living, and left not even one to heretical depravity.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And let him no longer hide his face from them nor turn away from them, because he has poured out the spirit of his grace — of which the prophet Joel too speaks: In the last days I will pour out of my spirit upon all flesh —; and he has poured it out upon the whole house of Israel. But if instead of 'spirit' we read 'fury' according to the Seventy, which is not found in the Hebrew, it is to be understood thus: that he no longer hides his face from those upon whom he had earlier poured out his fury.

n: Month; April 30, the year of the world 3430. (Usher) (Calmet) --- In explaining this last most obscure vision: I. The Jews say it was verified after the captivity. But thus the temple would be four miles round, and the city thirty-six, which never was the case. II. Hence more modern Jews assert it will be fulfilled by the Messias. III. Rejecting these errors, Lyranus, &c., suppose that the promise was conditional, and that the sins of the Jews prevented the city and temple from being so large; and that the mystical temple of the Church is also insinuated, into which both Jews and Gentiles shall enter. IV. Though this opinion be probable, it seems better to follow St. Jerome, St. Gregory, &c., who cannot apply all to the Old Testament, nor think that such a huge temple and city were indeed promised, but explain some parts of the captives at their return, as a figure of those redeemed by Christ, and brought into his Church, which is adorned with all graces. Yet the greatest part must be understood of the Church triumphant. (Worthington) --- St. Jerome confesses his ignorance of this subject; and those who have come after him, though they imitate not his modesty, add little to dissipate the mist with which this vision is surrounded. Some have adhered too close to Josephus, while Villalpand has here discovered all the magnificence of Greek and Roman architecture, and has represented the temple six times as large as it really was. It seems that the prophet has described the same temple of Solomon which he had seen, that the dimensions might be preserved, and the hopes of the people kept up; (Calmet) and that they might comprehend what a loss they actually sustained on account of their sins, (Haydock) and might strive to come up to this pattern (Du Hamel) as "near as they should be able," the wealth of the people being much less than Solomon's. (Grotius) --- These arguments do not, however, shew that the buildings were to resemble each other. They vary in many particulars; and the prophet would specify what was to be really executed. He says nothing of the ornamental part, and little of the height, which are the most expensive. (Houbigant) (Preface) --- If some things appear to be too grand for the temple of Solomon, and of Zorobabel, we must reflect that the prophet passes from the figure to the Church of Christ, which is not unusual. (Menochius) --- Alcasar and Bossuet explain it wholly of the Church, so that the letter requires few notes. (Du Hamel)

Mountain; Moria, in spirit. On the eastern side, the road to the city was level. Walls were added after the captivity, on the other sides. (Josephus, Jewish Wars vi. 6.) --- City, the temple was so large. --- South, to one coming from the north, though the temple lay on that side of the town, Psalm xlvii. 2. (Calmet) --- Septuagint read mongod, "over-against," instead of mongob, "south," which has perplexed many. (Houbigant) --- Ezechiel was placed on Sion, which was not very high, but here it denotes the Church. Jerusalem was in ruins. (Worthington)

Brass: shining. (Haydock) --- This angel waited for the prophet at the northern gate, but introduced him by that looking towards the east, ver. 16. --- Line. It seems never to have been used. (Calmet)

Breadth. Hebrew, Chaldean, Septuagint, "of six cubits, in a cubit and a palm;" intimating that the sacred cubit contained six palms, while the common one had only five, (chap. xliii. 13.; Worthington) being half a yard; (Arbuthnot) or the Hebrew cubit was a hand's breadth larger than the Babylonian, or about 21½ inches, (Calmet) which may be styled (Menochius) the sacred cubit. (Arbuthnot) (Haydock) --- Reed. This outer wall (Calmet; Menochius) was to prevent any from falling down the precipice. It was about four yards nine inches in height and thickness, being so solid in order that the ground might not give way. Josephus describes prodigious walls, (Haydock) reaching to the bottom of the mountain, three hundred cubits on the south and west; but then the temple was much enlarged. (Calmet)

And. In this verse occurs the first of thirty-four words where the j is allowed by the keri to be omitted in this one chapter, always when it is the sign of the plural number before a suffixed v, and of course by voluntary assimilation. But Camb. Manuscript has the j regularly in the thirty-two of these words. (Kennicott) --- Steps. The ground was not quite level, which caused the buildings to rise one above another more elegantly. There were four great gates.
Chamber, for the porters, (Calmet) three on each side of the porch, ver. 10. (Haydock)
Thirteen, or twenty-six feet high.
Cubits high, or else the elevation is nowhere specified. (Calmet)

Slanting, or "lattice." Septuagint, "dark." See 3 Kings vii. 4. (Haydock) --- They were larger within, to afford light, as in Solomon's temple, and in castles. Interpreters disagree in their sentiments: but all allow that God here insinuated that he would reward people in the Old Testament with temporal, and those in the New with spiritual blessings; first with grace in this life, and with glory in the next. (Worthington) --- Yet we must not suppose that the saints of old were deprived of eternal goods. (Haydock) --- About. The other gates had the like ornaments. (Calmet)

There were chambers. Gazophylacia, so called, because the priests and Levites kept in them the stores and vessels that belonged to the temple. (Challoner) --- They went all round the courts. The women were in the second story. Villalpand and Capel, who are deemed the most accurate, suppose that there were no chambers below, but an open gallery. There seem, however, to have been chambers also, chap. viii. 7. (Calmet)
Lower. So that there was a step up to the threshold. (Haydock) --- Marble was used in all places exposed to the weather. (Josephus, Jewish Wars vi. 14.)
Seven. There were eight to the inner court, (ver. 31.) shewing that more perfection is now required, and a greater reward given. (St. Gregory) (Worthington)

Five cubits. The parallel passages would intimate "fifty." (Calmet) (Villalpand) --- But the texts all read five, and Maldonat understands the four vacant spaces between the chambers, ver. 7. (Menochius)
Gates. Hebrew is very obscure. The holocausts were slain on the north side of the altar, Leviticus i. 11.
Borders, to prevent any thing falling. Chaldean, &c., have "hooks."
North. The singers occupied two wings.
Watch over the sacred ornaments, perfumes, lamps of the sanctuary, &c., Numbers iii. 28.
Altar. Not on actual service, (chap. xli. 13.) but to prepare the victims.

That side. Septuagint add, "and the opening (euros, width) of the gate was 14 cubits, and the breadth (projections, epomides) of the," &c., (Haydock) or the wall on each side of the door was three cubits, so that the porch was 20 cubits broad. (Calmet)

Eleven. 3 Kings vi., says ten. The exact breadth was ten and a half, (Villalpand; Tirinus) or what the pavement covered is there specified according to some. Roman Septuagint has "twelve." But the edition of Basil reads more correctly, ten. (Calmet) --- Yet both ten and eleven may be right, if this temple be different. (Haydock) --- Eight. Hebrew seems corrupt, a being substituted for a. "They mounted by ten steps," as the Septuagint read. Aquila has eleven; Symmachus [has] eight. --- Pillars of brass, 3 Kings vii. 15. (Calmet) --- As they are not measured, they were like Solomon's. (Worthington)

f: Commentary on Ezekiel

In the twenty-fifth year of the exile (or of the captivity) of Jeconiah, at the beginning of the year (or in the first month), on the tenth of the month, in the fourteenth year after the city was struck (or taken), on this very day (or on that day), the hand of the Lord came upon me, and he brought me there, in visions (or in a vision) of God, and he brought me into the land of Israel, and set (or placed) me upon an exceedingly high mountain, upon which there was as it were the building of a city facing toward the south (or opposite). And he brought me in there, and behold, a man whose appearance was like the appearance of bronze (or of shining bronze), and a cord of linen (or of the masons) in his hand, and a measuring reed in his hand; and he was standing in the gate. And the same man spoke to me: Son of man, see with your eyes, and hear with your ears, and set your heart upon all that I shall show you (or set in your heart all that I shall have shown you), for you have been brought (or have entered) here that they may be shown to you; and declare (or you shall show) all that you see to the house of Israel. If in the fifth year of the captivity or exile of King Jehoiachin, in the fourth month, on the fifth of the month, the heavens were opened to the prophet Ezekiel beside the river Chebar and he saw visions of God, but now it is said that in the twenty-fifth year of the exile of the same Jeconiah, at the beginning of the year, on the tenth day of the month, the hand of the Lord came upon him, and he was brought into the land of Israel and placed upon an exceedingly high mountain, so that he might see the building of a city facing toward the south, no one doubts that his whole prophecy was woven together when nineteen years, and nine months and five days of the twentieth year, had been completed. But if, according to Theodotion, who in the place where we have put 'at the beginning of the year' translated 'in the new year', on the tenth day of the month — now among the Hebrews the new year is the name of the seventh month, which among them bears the name 'thesri' [Tishri], so that on the first day of the seventh month there is the blast of trumpets, and on the tenth day of the same month the day of fasting and propitiation, and on the fifteenth, when the whole orb of the moon is filled, the day of Tabernacles — it is given to be understood that the building of the city had been shown to Ezekiel on the tenth day, the day of the Lord's propitiation. And just as he showed the restoration of the people, or rather their bringing back to life, in the bones of the plain under the image of the resurrection, so now the Lord promises, under its description, the renewal of the city which fourteen years before had been destroyed by fire by the Babylonian, so that, as the type of the pot kindled from the face of the north had shown the captivity and the overthrow, and the truth of the prophecy had been proved by the event, so, from trust in things past, the truth of the building to come might be proved by the prophecy. Nor is this said of that time, as some unlearned among the Jews would have it, when under Zerubbabel and under Joshua son of Jehozadak, the great priest, the temple was built, while Haggai and Zechariah prophesied: for this temple which is now described, and the order of the priesthood, and the division and fertility of the land, is far more majestic than the one which Solomon had built; but the one which was built under Zerubbabel was so small and, in comparison with the former, of so little worth, that those who had seen the first temple and afterward looked upon this one wailed and bore witness to their grief with tears, and the cry of those lamenting was far greater than the blast of the trumpets; read the book of Ezra. Further, what is added: In the fourteenth year after the city was struck (or taken), according to the mystical senses signifies the fourteen generations from David to the nativity of Christ; when they were completed, the restoration of the city is promised by him of whom it is written: He himself will build my city and will bring back the captivity of my people, and again, he came: To proclaim release to the captives and sight to the blind, saying to those who were in chains: Come out, and to those who were in darkness: Be uncovered.
Homilies on Ezekiel, Book 2, Homily 1

About to speak of mystical things, he sets forth the historical narrative first, so that he may establish from the time what is to be believed from the revelation. It should be noted that at the beginning of this book he indicated in what year he began to prophesy; but at the end he inserted when he saw the final vision, so that it might be known over how many years he composed the book of his prophecy. For the time when he began to prophesy, he placed at the beginning of his speech, saying: The heavens were opened, and I saw visions of the Lord on the fifth of the month; this is the fifth year of the captivity of King Jehoiachin. But now he speaks, saying: In the twenty-fifth year of our captivity. For the same prophet had been carried off to Babylon in the first captivity with King Jehoiachin. For concerning the second captivity of Jerusalem he adds: In the fourteenth year after the city was struck. For Zedekiah had reigned in the city of Jerusalem for eleven years after the first captivity, in which the prophet Ezekiel was led to Babylon with King Jehoiachin. But in the fourteenth year after the captivity of that same Zedekiah, which was now the second captivity of the city, the prophet was seeing the final vision. Thus eleven and fourteen joined together make twenty-five. If therefore he spoke the first vision in the fifth year of the earlier captivity, and he describes this final one as having occurred in the twenty-fifth year, it is clearly evident that in twenty years he extended the delays of his speech up to the words of his final vision. Nor should it disturb anyone that in the middle of the volume of his prophecy, when he was speaking about the Babylonian king, he makes mention of the twenty-seventh year. In that place, since he inserts nothing about the time of his own captivity, he clearly demonstrates that he is describing the times of that king about whom he had received the commission to prophesy. But as for his saying: At the beginning of the year, on the tenth of the month, he simply expresses the time, so that from that very time also he may fix in the hearts of his hearers, according to the letter, the root of the word, from which he may afterward bring forth spiritual fruits.
Homilies on Ezekiel, Book 2, Homily 1

It should be noted what he says: "In the fourteenth year after the city was struck, on that same day." For what does it mean that through this final vision almighty God deigned to show the mercy of His promise on that very day on which He fulfilled the wrath of justice upon the stricken city, except that that power of divinity, which is not drawn into any movement of change or mutability, by that same light of justice gives life to the afflicted and penitent by which it strikes down the proud and obstinate?
Commentary on Ezekiel

Now the hand of the Lord comes upon him so that, though placed in Babylon according to the flesh, he might come in the spirit to the land of Israel, and might be set, not at all in a vision, but in the visions of God, upon an exceedingly high mountain — of which Isaiah and Micah prophesy: Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob —, which mountain is exceedingly high in comparison with the other mountains — of which the prophet testifies, saying: I have lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from where my help shall come, and in another place: Mountains are round about it, and the Lord is round about his people, of which it is also said in Isaiah: Go up onto a high mountain, you who bring good tidings to Zion —; upon this mountain is shown the building of a city, according to the Seventy and Aquila 'opposite' and 'over against the north', from where the prophet had come to the land of Israel, but according to Theodotion and Symmachus 'facing toward the south', where the light is full and the sun of righteousness is set at the highest summit of heaven — whence it is also said in the Song of Songs: Arise, north wind, and come, south wind; blow through my garden, and let its spices flow; for the north wind, the harshest of winds, is driven away from the Lord's garden, so that the warmth of love may not grow cold and the flowers may not wither —; and when it is said: As it were the building of a city, not truly a city but the likeness of a city is shown — of which it is written: Glorious things are spoken of you, city of God, which is: Jerusalem, built as a city, whose sharing of it is in the selfsame, and in which: Great is the Lord and exceedingly to be praised, in the city of our God, on his holy mountain, and: In the towers of the city God is known to the righteous, when he upholds it, of which it is said elsewhere too: The rush of the river makes glad the city of God, and: A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden, which speaks in Isaiah: I am a strong city, a city which is besieged — he did not say: which 'is stormed', but 'is besieged' —, which 'is built upon the rock and is shaken by no storm' —.
Homilies on Ezekiel, Book 2, Homily 1

"The hand of the Lord came upon me, and brought me there in visions of God: He brought me into the land of Israel, and set me down upon a very high mountain, upon which there was as it were the structure of a city facing toward the South."

The building of this city certainly cannot be understood according to the letter. For shortly afterward he adds that this same building was measured with a reed of six cubits and a palm, while the gate of the same building was measured at fourteen cubits, and he reports that the fronts of this gate are sixty cubits. All of these things cannot stand according to the letter. For how is the whole building together measured with a reed, that is, six cubits and a palm, while the gates of the building extend to fourteen cubits, and the fronts of the gates to sixty cubits? For the gate is in the city, and the fronts are in the gates. And no reasoning permits it to be accepted that what contains is less than what is contained. Moreover, in Sacred Scripture, even those things which can be understood according to history must often be understood spiritually, so that both faith may be held in the truth of the history, and spiritual understanding may be grasped from the mysteries of allegory. Just as we also know what the Psalmist says: "For I shall see your heavens, the works of your fingers, the moon and stars, which you have established." For behold, in the outward description the word of reason stands, because both the heavens are the works of God, and the moon and stars were created and established by him. But if the Psalmist asserts this according to outward works alone, and not also according to mystical understanding, he who professed that the heavens are the works of God, when about to speak of the moon and stars, why did he not also enumerate the sun equally, which we know is his work?
