After he came to the Holy of Holies, of which we spoke above, that venerable man measured the wall of the Holy of Holies, which, on account of the fabric of the world and all the visible creation that was founded in six days, had six cubits, and the breadth of one side, four cubits: not on one side only, but round about the house was the breadth; and the breadth held four cubits round about the house, so as to show the four elements from which all things are compacted, and especially human bodies, against which the saints, fighting and subjecting them to the power of the soul, merit to enter the inner places and to know the secrets of the Lord.
Commentary on Ezekiel

The sides themselves, which were round about the house and were separated from the wall of the temple by a space of four cubits, were joined to one another, so that one side touched another side and had in length not thirty-three cubits but twice thirty-three, that is, sixty-six. The Old Testament speaks in Leviticus about the birth of a male, that after one week both she who bore and he who was born fulfill thirty-three days so that they may come to purification; but if she bears a female, she is to observe a double number, that is, sixty-six; and because, in order to come to the Holy of Holies, we need not only the first birth but also the second, so that, born in the flesh, we may be reborn in the spirit, therefore not the number sixty-six but twice thirty-three is set down, so that each birth may be owed to God as author and to his clemency, and that the sides of the house which support the building of the temple may go round it with a double wall. And what follows according to the Hebrew: And there were certain projections which entered through the walls of the house through the sides round about, to hold and not to touch the wall of the temple, signifies this: that holy men in the multitude of believers break forth through the wall of the temple, that is, through all the sides round about, and hold the foundations of the Church, and yet do not touch the wall of the temple, content only to have seen and from afar to have adored the unspeakable mysteries: for now we see through a mirror in an enigma, and we cannot touch and comprehend the fullest truth.
Commentary on Ezekiel

But as for: There was a broad way going upward in a round by a spiral, and it led into the upper room of the temple by a circuit, and: Therefore the temple was wider in the upper parts, and so from the lower parts one went up to the upper and the middle, I think it is clear to the reader that the things below are always narrower, in fasts, in sleeping on the ground, in restraint of diet, and that little by little, as we climb to the heights, a wider way is opened to us and that is fulfilled which is written: In tribulation you have enlarged me; and by the round and the spiral we climb to the upper room of the temple, a figure which among all σχήματα [shapes, figures] is approved as the more beautiful even by the philosophers of this world, since the sky and the sun and the moon and the other stars and the point of the earth, and in human bodies too the eyes, like other stars, and the shape of the head, which is the receptacle of all the senses, and the rounded fingers and thighs and arms display this roundness; moreover, the upper room of the temple, to which one climbs from narrower things to higher, I think is that which Elijah and Elisha had in the volume of Kings, and which our Tabitha — that is, δορκάς and doe — possessed in the Acts of the Apostles, she who by good works had climbed to the heights; but the apostle Peter, upon whom the Lord made firm the foundations of the Church, went beyond the upper room and came to the roof — which is more expressively called δῶμα in Greek — that is, the sun-terrace of the roof —, and came to know the mysteries of the Church previously unknown to the world; the Savior of the human race also made the Passover in an upper room, and in a large and broad upper room, purged of all filth and spread and prepared for the spiritual banquet, where he handed on to his disciples the mystery of his body and blood and left us the eternal festival of the spotless lamb. And what he adds: And from the middle parts to the tristega (that is, third upper rooms) and 'thrael', seems to me fit to be marked beforehand with an obelus: for what need is there to discuss doubtful things that are not written, when we ought to apply ourselves to the things contained in the books of the Hebrews?
Commentary on Ezekiel

There follows: And I saw in the house a height round about, the sides founded to the measure of a reed with a space of six cubits; and the breadth through the wall of the side outside of five cubits; and between the chambers (which Symmachus calls ἐξέδρας [exedras]) a breadth of twenty cubits round the house, by which numbers it is shown that from this world and from the earthly senses and from the dual number of two decades, which is referred to twenty, we may merit to ascend not only into the Holy of Holies but also into its upper rooms, and may always keep in memory that through the six days of our creation and through the five senses and through the twenty cubits of breadth we have ascended to the upper room of the temple and, leaving behind earthly lowliness and the sense of the letter, have crossed over to the summit of the Church, and rejoice in the fellowship of the Holy Spirit.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And the door, he says, of the side for prayer facing the way of the north: From which evils blaze forth upon all the earth, and which the Lord promises he will drive away from us, saying: And him who is from the north I will drive away from you; and beautifully at the door facing the north is the place of prayer, so that according to the Apostle we may pray without ceasing, and say with Jeremiah: Let not the pupil of my eye be silent, either desiring to avoid present evils or giving thanks for past ones — for as long as we are in the tabernacle of this body, we groan and say: Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death? —; but toward the southern way too there was a door, and it also, according to the Hebrew, had a place of prayer and extended five cubits round about — for after the cold of the north let us cross over to the warmth of the south —, and yet once more we seek a place of prayer: at the door of the north, that we may escape dangers; at the southern one, that we may give thanks for past things and that the possession of victory may be secure for us; and the five cubits in this place too indicate the divine senses, through which we climb from earthly things to higher.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And the building, he says, which was separate and turned toward the way looking to the sea, of a breadth of seventy cubits, so that, after labors and dangers and the waves and shipwrecks of this world, and the seventy years of which Jeremiah writes, and Daniel and Zechariah, we may attain the true and lawful sabbath of seven decades, and there may be eternal rest for us; and that through the breadth of five cubits we may come to the length of ninety cubits, the age at which Sarah bore a son by the promise, she who at ninety years, that is, of nine decades, gave birth to Isaac, joined to Abraham the hundred-year-old, who held the mystery of ten decades — what this number signifies, the Scripture that follows will show.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And he measured the length of the house, a hundred cubits, and the building that was separate and its walls, of a length of a hundred cubits; but the breadth before the face of the house and of that which was separate toward the east, a hundred cubits. And he measured the length of the building facing that which was separate at the back, ἔκθετας (that is, 'projections') on either side, a hundred cubits; and the inner temple and the vestibules of the court, the thresholds and slanting windows, and ἔκθετας round about on three sides facing each threshold, and it was laid with wood in a ring round about; and earth up to the windows, and the windows closed above the doors. And up to the inner house and outside, over the whole wall round about, within and without, by measure. And Cherubim and palms were wrought, and a palm between Cherub and Cherub; and a Cherub had two faces: the face of a man next to a palm on this side, and the face of a lion next to a palm on the other side, fashioned through all the house round about. From the ground up to the upper parts of the gate Cherubim and palms were carved on the wall of the temple. A four-cornered threshold, and the face of the sanctuary, aspect facing aspect. Of the wooden altar the height three cubits, and its length two cubits, and its corners and its length and its walls of wood. (LXX: "And he measured ÷ facing ⁚ the house, a length of a hundred cubits, and the remaining parts and the separating parts and its walls in length a hundred cubits; and the breadth facing the face of the temple and the remaining parts opposite, a hundred cubits. And he measured the length of the separating part facing the face of the remaining parts which were behind the back of that house, and the remaining parts on this side and on that, a length of a hundred cubits; and the temple and the corners and the 'aelam' outside laid with wood, and windows made in the manner of a net, three, for giving light, so that one might see through them; and the house and the things that were next to it laid with wood round about, and the pavement, and from the pavement up to the windows, and the windows opened in threefold manner so that one might look out through them. And up to the inner and the outer house and over every wall round about, within and without, measure; and carved Cherubim and palms between Cherub and Cherub: the face of a man toward the palm on this side, and the face of a lion toward the palm on that side, every wall carved round about: from the pavement up to the ceiling Cherubim and palms carved. And the sanctuary and the temple opened by four corners. Facing the face of the holy things a vision like the appearance of a wooden altar, its height three cubits and its length two cubits and its breadth two cubits, and it had horns, its base also and its walls of wood.") The word 'facing', which the Seventy translated at the beginning of the testimony, where it is written: And he measured 'facing' the house, is not found in the Hebrew, and therefore it must be marked beforehand with an obelus, so that it may read more rightly and more truly: And he measured the house, a length of a hundred cubits, and the rest. There are described, moreover, the Holy of Holies and the inner temple, which after ninety cubits is said to have a hundred cubits on three sides: the perfect number, namely, of ten decades, so that we may serve God with mind and speech and works, remembering that apostolic example in which he says: That we may be able to know what is the breadth, and length and height and depth. But what the Hebrew calls 'the separate building and its walls', the Seventy render 'the remaining parts' 'and the separating parts', which do not cling to the walls of the temple but have walls near at hand and their own.
Commentary on Ezekiel

The temple itself also and its corners and the 'aelam' (that is, πρόπυλον or 'vestibule') were laid with wood outside, namely with wisdom, which Scripture records as the tree of life set in paradise. The windows also were made in the manner of a net, like lattices, so that they were closed not with transparent stone nor with glass, but with wood cut in openwork and worked in wavy patterns — for which the Hebrew has 'slanting windows' —; and they were on three sides of the temple only, namely to the right and the left and behind the back, that is, toward the south and the north and toward the west; but the eastern side had no windows, because the entrance itself let clear light in within, and all the interior of the temple was filled with the light of the doors, so that through the individual windows and the openings of the lattices one could look inside. And not only were the outer parts laid with wood, but so great was the abundance of wood round about that both the pavement and, from the pavement up to the windows, everything was joined with wood; and these windows, according to the Seventy, opened in threefold manner, so that, when they were opened, a threefold understanding might be shown in the temple of God — according to what is said elsewhere: But you, write them threefold —; and one might look out through them not only inward but outward, so that we may recognize the inner things as invisible and the outer things as visible; so that one shows the mind, another the flesh, one the spiritual understanding, another the simple history.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Forgive, reader, the difficulty, and grant pardon to a poor understanding: for through windows that are slanting and made in the manner of a net and always closed, we can scarcely send the eye of our heart in as far as the inner house, so that all that we discern we see in shadow and image — and let us cry out with the Apostle: O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How inscrutable are his judgments, and unsearchable his ways! And who has known the mind of the Lord? except him who is the angel of great counsel and can open his mysteries to the worthy —. Now at Rome they call Ἔκθετας 'solaria' [sun-balconies], jutting out from the walls of upper rooms, or 'maeniana' [balconies], after him who first invented them; some of the Greeks call them ἐξώστρας [projecting galleries].
Commentary on Ezekiel

And over all the walls round about, both within and without, there were measures of their own: for nothing was made by God without reason and measure in the temple of God, and especially in the Holy of Holies.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Carved also were Cherubim, no doubt on the wood reaching from the pavement up to the windows, and the carvings were so skillfully wrought that they seemed not carved but applied. 'Cherubim' means 'multitude of knowledge'; therefore within, in the interior of the temple, after the multitude of knowledge, palms also are carved — in which is the sign of victory, as the Apostle says: But I press on toward the appointed goal, toward the prize of the upward calling of God in Christ Jesus —, which palms: Palms were between Cherub and Cherub, so that each Cherub was fenced in by the flanks of two palms; and this Cherub by no means had four faces, as we read at the beginning of this prophet, namely of a man and of a lion and of a calf and of an eagle, but only two, that is, of a man and of a lion, of which the first pertains to reason, the next to fury — which is more expressively called θυμός in Greek —: but by fury we mean not that which is next to perturbation and vice, but that which firms up the softness of the mind and makes the spirit of the one fighting stronger; for at the beginning we are subject also to desire, which is referred to the calf because of the works of the earth, and some things are carnal and others spiritual, the last of which is assigned to the eagle; but when we have entered the Holy of Holies and come into possession of the interior of the temple, we need nothing else but reason and fortitude, of which the one is referred to sense and prudence, the other to perseverance of spirit.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Every wall, therefore, round about the temple, from the pavement up to the ceiling, had Cherubim and palms carved with wonderful art; after these the sanctuary was opened by four corners facing the face of the holy things: for first we have the multitude of knowledge, through which we gain the victory over the enemy, and afterward the sanctuary is opened to us, and the temple, which has four corners, a most firm station, and one that leans toward no side; for this is the nature of the measure of a quadrangle, that it stands on a stable base and, in a mystical number which is clear to the prudent reader, possesses the four elements, of which all things consist, solid and perpetual.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And all things looked toward the face of the sanctuary; before which sanctuary, or in which sanctuary, there was: The appearance of a wooden altar three cubits in height and two cubits in length and two cubits in breadth, which joined together make seven cubits. This altar had horns, and both its base and its walls, that is, its sides, were wooden: in which the human tongue cannot unfold the mysteries of Holy Scripture: how an altar on which fire was to be kindled, namely the table of incense, suffers nothing from the fire but, so to speak, becomes purer than fire; for just as the works of the saints — of which the Apostle writes: The fire will test what sort each one's work is — do not perish but are shown purer through fire, so too the wood of the altar, which is of the trees of paradise, is not burned by the neighboring fire but is rendered purer — nor is it a wonder to believe this of the sanctuary and the interior of the temple and the altar of incense, since even ἀμίαντον [amiantus, asbestos] — it is a kind of wood, or one having the likeness of flax — is found the cleaner the more it has burned —.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And he spoke to me: This is the table before the Lord. And there were two doors in the temple and in the sanctuary; and in the two doors on either side there were two little doors each, which folded into one another; for there were two doors each on either side of the doors. And there were carved on the very doors of the temple Cherubim and sculptures of palms, just as they were also fashioned on the walls; wherefore the timbers also were thicker on the front of the vestibule outside. Above which were slanting windows, and the likeness of palms on this side and on that in the little shoulders of the vestibule, along the sides of the house and the breadth of the walls. (In this place the edition of the Seventy disagrees much with the Hebrew truth. Hence I will point out only this: that for 'thicker timbers' they translated σπουδαῖα, that is, 'necessary' or 'worthy of care', and for 'slanting' windows, 'hidden', and what is placed at the end of the testimony: And he measured on this side and on that the ceilings of the lintel — or of the vestibule — along the sides of the house, compacted — or joined, which they called ἐζυγωμένα, for which we can render 'of equal weight' —.) That man, therefore, who had brought the prophet into the innermost recesses of the temple, and among other things had shown him the wooden altar, which had corners, and horns according to the Seventy, and wooden walls, said to him: 'This altar which you behold: This very one is the table before the Lord', which in the likeness of the bush burns and is not consumed — of which the holy man speaks to the Lord: You have prepared a table in my sight against those who afflict me —.
Commentary on Ezekiel
Two also doors were in the temple and in the sanctuary itself, through which the mysteries of both Testaments are shown.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And in the two doors on either side there were two little doors each, which folded into one another, so that we may have both the spiritual understanding in the history and the truth of the history in the tropology; each of these needs the other, and if one is lacking, perfect knowledge is wanting. What follows, however: There were two doors each on either side of the doors, is clear according to the letter: for in larger dining halls two doors are wont to adjoin each other and be joined together, so that the greater entrance is closed or opened not by two huge leaves but by four smaller ones.
Commentary on Ezekiel

On which doors of the temple (or of the Holy of Holies) were carved Cherubim — of which we spoke above — and sculptures of palms, so that after the multitude of knowledge victory might be granted to those who enter; and this sculpture of palms was also on all the walls of the temple. And he gives the reasons why Cherubim were carved on the doors themselves and likenesses of palms fashioned: Whence also the timbers were thicker in the vestibule of the gate outside, so that they might have firmness and also be able to receive carving; and beautifully, according to the spiritual understanding, the doors are firmer and carved, so that they may have both firmness and beauty, lest anyone like Uzziah should be able to burst into the Holy of Holies and claim the priesthood for himself.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Above which doors there were slanting windows (or hidden), so that the very light that was given within might not have perfect knowledge, nor a clear light open to all, but for most might be hidden in part — for now we see in an enigma, and we do not yet know as we ought to know; but when that which is perfect has come, then what had been in part will be destroyed —. And there was a likeness of palms on this side and on that: elegantly, in the interior of the temple and in the Holy of Holies, he did not put 'right and left', lest he seem to say anything sinister in things that are great and secret, but 'on this side and on that' — according to what is written in the Gospel: Whoever strikes you on the right cheek, offer him the other also. Could he not have said 'and the left'? But when the right is struck, another right is offered, because in a holy man both are right, both are perfect —. And: In the little shoulders of the vestibule, along the sides of the house and the breadth of the walls (for which the Seventy translated: In the ceilings of the 'aelam' — that is, πρόπυλον [gateway] — and the sides of the house of equal weight — or measure —), by which it is shown in a hidden way that the posts of the lintel or of the vestibule — for this is what the little shoulders seem to signify —, and the sides of the house, and the breadth of the walls are all full of reason and measure, and that nothing is found in the temple of the Lord which has been established without measure and wisdom.

n: And. St. Jerome finding the Septuagint and others varying in the explanations, gives his own; yet adopts the saying of Socrates, "I know that I am ignorant:" for this also is a part of science. (Worthington) --- Outward, with respect to the temple. It is styled inner court, with reference to that of the people. --- Separate. Chap. xli. 9.
Triple, one over another, (ver. 6.) or on a level with the priests' court.
One cubit, projecting out perhaps for seats, or for the pilasters.
Above. The higher stories are not so lofty.
Fifty cubits. We only allow thirty, as this is not in Hebrew, &c. The text, ver. 10., and 12., seems incorrect. (Calmet)
Holies. Hebrew, "who are very holy," and (Haydock) on duty. See Leviticus vi. 25.
People. Chap. xliv. 17., and Exodus xxxiii. 42. Christian priests use their vestments only when they are officiating. (Durand and Durant Rit. ii. 9.) (Calmet)

Five. Hebrew emoth should be meoth, "three hundred, as it is printed (yet not in the Protestant version. Haydock) thrice just after, and as it is written here in Manuscript 4. Camb. 1. 2." (Kennicott) --- Reeds. Septuagint, "cubits," as Hebrew, St. Jerome, &c., insinuate. The mountain was only five hundred paces square, even when it was enlarged in the time of Josephus. (Jewish Wars vi. 14.; Greek) --- We must therefore read cubits. (Calmet) --- If we retain reeds, (Haydock) the wall will be twelve thousand cubits, (Menochius) which seems improbable. (Tournemine) See chap. xlv. (Haydock)

Cubits. This confirms the former correction, ver. 16. (Haydock) --- Hebrew has only, "of five hundred." Maldonat and Cornelius a Lapide would understand reeds, to agree with what goes before. (Menochius) --- Separation. Josephus mentions a wall three cubits high, on the pillars of which was written in Greek and Latin, that such as entered the temple must be pure, (Calmet) and no stranger. (Haydock) --- Into this court all might come. (Philo) (Calmet)

f: Commentary on Ezekiel

And he brought me out into the outer court by the way leading to the north; and he brought me into the chamber that was opposite the separate building, and opposite the house facing toward the north. In front of the length, a hundred cubits, of the door of the north, and of the breadth fifty cubits, opposite the twenty cubits of the inner court, and opposite the pavement laid with stone of the outer court, where there was a portico joined to the threefold portico. And before the chambers a walk of ten cubits in breadth, and looking toward the inner parts of the way of one cubit; and their doors toward the north, where the chambers were lower in the upper parts, because they supported the porticoes which projected from them, from the lower and from the middle seats of the building. For they were three-storied, and they did not have columns as were the columns of the courts; therefore they projected from the lower and from the middle, from the ground, by fifty cubits. And the outer peribolus alongside the chambers which were in the way of the outer court before the chambers; its length of fifty cubits, because the length of the chambers of the outer court was fifty cubits, and the length before the face of the temple a hundred cubits. And beneath these chambers there was an entrance from the east for those entering into them from the outer court. In the breadth of the peribolus of the court which was opposite the eastern way, in front of the separate building, and there were chambers before the building. And a way before their face according to the likeness of the chambers which were in the way of the north; according to their length so also their breadth, and all their entrance and likenesses and their doors according to the doors of the chambers which were in the way looking toward the south; a door at the head of the way which was before the separate vestibule, for those entering by the eastern way. (LXX: "And he brought me out into the outer court ÷ toward the east ⁚ opposite the gate of the north; and he brought me in, and behold, five exedrae next to the wall of the building and beside the separate building toward the north, and opposite, a hundred cubits of length toward the north and of breadth fifty cubits, laid out like the gates of the inner court and like the columns of the outer court, in order opposite the face of the threefold portico. And opposite the exedrae a walk of ten cubits of breadth, for a hundred cubits of length — into the inner way of one cubit —; and their doors toward the north. And the walks of the upper rooms likewise, since columns projected from the lower columns, and the space was similar. And the porticoes were threefold, and they did not have columns like the columns in the outer parts; therefore they projected from those which were below and in the middle, from the ground — of fifty cubits —. And the light outside, like that of the exedrae of the outer court which looked opposite the exedrae of the north, in length fifty cubits; for the length of the exedrae looking onto the outer court was fifty cubits, and these are opposite their own face: all of a hundred cubits. And the doors of these exedrae toward the eastern entrance, so that one may go in by them from the outer court according to the light which was at the beginning of the walk — toward the south, opposite the midday and the face of the remaining and separate building. And the exedrae and the walk opposite their own face according to the measures of the exedrae and the way toward the north, and their length and their breadth and all their exits and entrances and lights and the doors of the exedrae opposite the midday, and the entrance from the beginning of the walkway to the light at the space of a reed, and so that one might go to the east by them —.") This which the Seventy translated, 'toward the east', is not found in the Hebrew, and it is plain that it is superfluous — for how is he led out to the outer gate 'toward the east', when there follows 'opposite the gate of the north'? —; and that which we set down both above and in this place, And he brought me into the chamber that was opposite the separate building, and opposite the house facing toward the north, for which there stands in the Seventy, And he brought me out, and behold, five exedrae joined to the remaining building and beside the separate one toward the north: for 'separate', which Aquila and Symmachus translated, the second edition of Aquila and Theodotion set down the very word 'gazera', rendering it in the same way in all places; and many other things which are set forth in the present place disagree between the Hebrew and the Seventy not only in order but also in number and in the rendering of the words, so that, if we wished to linger over each one and to seek out and explain the reason for their difference, we would stray far from our purpose; and I had wished, out of despair and because of the magnitude of the matter, to pass over the present passage in silence, but I judged it better to say something, whatever it might be, than to say nothing at all, taking up that Socratic saying: 'I know what I do not know'; for it is a part of knowledge to know what you do not know. After the prophet, then, had contemplated more carefully the things that were within, the man in whose hand were the cord and the reed led him out into the outer court by the way leading to the north, which he had already seen above as well, before he penetrated the inner parts — but we see in one way when we have perfect knowledge, in another at the beginning of instruction; and it is necessary that one who has beheld the inner parts according to the same form and measures and hidden mysteries should also see the things that are outer —; and he was led out into the chamber — or, as Symmachus says and the Seventy translated, 'exedra', and Theodotion παστοφόριον, which is rendered 'cell' — that was opposite the separate building; but what the Seventy added in place of the chamber, 'five exedrae', is not found in the Hebrew —, which chamber was opposite the separate building — concerning which we said above, 'gazera' —: and it was separate, receiving those who came from the north, and it was opposite the house facing toward the north, that is, looking indeed toward the parts of the north but not situated in the north, so that the passage might be easier for those who were leaving behind the cold of the north, from which evils blaze up over the earth — we read in the book of Numbers that the tribes of Dan and Naphtali and Asher, the sons of Bilhah and Zilpah, the handmaids of Rachel and Leah, held their camp on the northern quarter —.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Now too, in front of the length of the north door there were a hundred cubits, and of breadth fifty, so that, by the square and perfect number made of ten decades, and by the number made of seven hebdomads, which is the number of remission and breaks out into the beginning of unity, that is, of the ogdoad, the priestly spaces in the temple of God might be shown; and that which is joined according to the Hebrew, Opposite the twenty cubits of the inner court, for which the Seventy translated, They were laid out like the gates of the inner court, has this sense: that the number one hundred and the number fifty of the outer court have the same force as the number twenty of the inner court: for if you reckon four times five in the number twenty, you will find both testaments, so that the law is held within the Gospel and the Gospel is born from the root of the law; in place of this number the Seventy translated 'the likeness of the inner court', perhaps fearing to place in the inner court the number twenty — in which gifts are offered to Esau. There follows: And opposite the pavement laid with stone of the outer court, where there was a portico joined to the threefold portico, for which the Seventy translated: And like the columns of the outer court, set in order opposite the face of the threefold porticoes: and it signifies that the pavement of the outer court was laid with living stone, so that the footsteps of the priests might be defiled neither by the dust of summer nor by the mud of winter — whence also the Lord, about to ascend to the Father, washes the feet of the apostles, so that with clean and purified footsteps they may climb to the kingdoms of heaven, and he commands the apostles that, whatever city they have entered and they have not received them, they should shake off the dust of their feet, so that, namely, they may suffer nothing of earthly gifts from them to remain with them —; and not only was the pavement laid with stone, but there was also a portico joined to the threefold portico: one portico protecting the priests from rain and heat and joined to the threefold portico, and it shows the mystery of the Trinity, which, though it is divided into the names of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, is nevertheless joined to itself in one divinity.
Commentary on Ezekiel

There was also before the chambers — or exedrae, or cells — a walk ten cubits in breadth, looking toward the inner parts of the way of one cubit — and what was added by the Seventy, For a hundred cubits of length, is superfluous, because it is not found in the Hebrew; and in setting it down they removed what is found in the Hebrew, Looking toward the inner parts of the way of one cubit, which we translated from the Hebrew truth —: and it signifies that before the doors of all the chambers, or exedrae and cells, there was a walk having a breadth of ten cubits, which is itself also a perfect number, either because of the Decalogue of the law or because of the mysteries of the Gospel: for if you go from one through two and three to the fourth number, the number ten is produced, and the number of the Gospels —, in whose breadth the priests walk about, stepping before each of the chambers, only in such a way that they always look toward the inner parts of that way which leads to one cubit, namely to the worship of one divinity — as the Son says to the Father: I have revealed your name to men. For this is the way looking toward the inner parts which will be in the Gospel: I am the way and the life and the truth, for no one comes to the knowledge of the Father except through the Son —.
Commentary on Ezekiel

There follows: And their doors toward the north, where the chambers were lower in the upper parts, because they supported the porticoes which projected from them, from the lower and from the middle of the building. For they were three-storied, and they did not have columns as were the columns of the courts; therefore they projected from the lower, and from the middle, from the ground, by fifty cubits. In what is joined, 'their doors', there is understood 'of the exedrae' or 'of the chambers', of which there was talk above; which chambers were lower in the upper parts, that is, in the upper rooms — the upper rooms which Elijah and Elisha climbed, and the Lord with his disciples when he was about to keep the Passover, and Tabitha, who was raised up both by the faith of the apostle and by the merit of her own virtues; these are the upper rooms of which it is also written in the psalm: He who waters the mountains from his upper rooms: for unless someone has been made a mountain and has risen to higher things, he will not be watered by the rains of the Lord, he who according to the diversity of merits is watered from the first and the second and the third upper room; these very chambers too, that is, the treasuries of the riches of the Lord, are lower in the upper parts: for the more exalted someone has been, the more is he cast down in humility with the apostle, who says: I who am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God —; and these chambers were lower in the upper rooms because they supported the porticoes which projected from them, from the lower and from the middle of the building: he gives the reasons why the chambers placed in the upper rooms were lower: 'Because they supported' he says 'the porticoes which enjoyed the freedom of the air, and projected from the lower and from the middle of the building', so that the second upper room stood out above the pavement of the inner house and the third upper room was higher than the second, and the higher someone climbed, the loftier the upper room he would use, which grew by humility — as the Lord says: Whoever wishes to be greater among you, let him become the least of all —.
Commentary on Ezekiel

For they were not carried by other columns, as we read of the columns of the courts, but they projected from the lower, and from the middle, from the ground, by fifty cubits, the number of the remission of all debts — and these are the three-storied things of which it is commanded: Describe it threefold with counsel and knowledge, so that you may answer words of truth to those who are set before you —. The lower and outer things, then, need columns, but those which are higher and inner have no use for the help of columns, that is, of another.
Commentary on Ezekiel

After this it is said: And the outer peribolus alongside the chambers which were in the way of the outer court before the chambers; its length of fifty cubits, because the length of the chambers of the outer court was fifty cubits, and the length before the face of the temple a hundred cubits. 'Peribolus' signifies 'a wall', which was outer and surrounded the chambers in the way of the outer court, having in length fifty cubits, a number of whose mystery we have often spoken; moreover, the length before the face of the temple was by no means of fifty cubits, as before the chambers, but of a hundred cubits, so that after the remission of all sins we may await perfect rewards in the number one hundred; for 'peribolus' or 'wall', which in Hebrew is called 'gader', the Seventy translated 'light', which comes from outside and is to illumine the eyes of our heart, since our nature is not sufficient for the light that dwells in the understanding to have the perfect brightness of knowledge, unless it enters from outside through the grace of God: which first illumines the eyes of our heart and makes the whole outer court, which extends with a breadth of fifty cubits, grow bright; but afterwards, when we have come before the face of the temple, we are to receive the perfect rewards in the number one hundred.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And there was beneath the chambers an entrance from the east for those entering into them from the outer court. For we must possess the riches of God, and from the outer court find the entrance of the east beneath the chambers, and through the height of the peribolus which looks toward the way of the east come to the building which is set apart for the saints; before which are the chambers.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And in that very way there is the likeness of the chambers which were in the way of the north: for although we arrive at the entrance of the east, yet the likeness of the greater things is in the lesser, and we cannot arrive at the light of the east except by the way of the north, that is, unless through lesser and humbler things we strive toward greater and higher ones. And in the entrance itself the length was like the breadth, that is, the same measure in a square, and every entrance and the likenesses and the doors had the same measure and likeness as the chambers which were in the way looking toward the south: for, leaving behind the cold of the north, we arrive through the east at the south, in which the bridegroom reclines at midday and dwells in full light; and at the head of that same way, that is, the eastern one, which lies open to those who enter, there is a door — which is not opened unless it has been opened by him who says, I am the door, and who has the key of David —, to the vestibule set apart for the virtues of the saints; and that which receives those coming from the north we cannot reach. It is superfluous to discuss each word of this passage according to the Seventy, since both the things that have been said are not free of obscurity, and those about which we keep silent are nearly similar to those that we have said.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And he said to me: The chambers of the north and the chambers of the south which are before the separate building, these are the holy chambers in which the priests eat who draw near to the Lord in the Holy of Holies: there they shall place the Holy of Holies and the offering for sin and for trespass, for the place is holy. And when the priests have entered, they shall not go out from the holy places into the outer court, and there they shall lay up their garments in which they minister, because they are holy; and they shall be clothed with other garments, and so they shall go forth to the people. That man who was the prophet's guide, after he had led him into the outer court and shown him all the things which the preceding discourse has narrated, the chambers too, or exedrae, in which he lingered a very long time, said to him: 'These are the chambers, or exedrae and cells, toward the north and toward the south which are before the separate building, and they are called the holy chambers in which the priests eat who draw near to the Lord in the Holy of Holies' — from which we learn that there are many differences of foods which the priests are or are not permitted to eat, and that of those very ones which it is permitted to take as food, they are not taken in all places, nor by all, nor at every time —; I think the chambers of the north and of the south are those which contain either the simplicity of the history or the mysteries of spiritual understanding, so that through the north we may come to the midday: for neither is the letter to be read and the foundations of the history to be laid in such a way that we do not come to the summits, nor are roofs to be set on top of a most beautiful building in such a way that the foundations are by no means solid; and the priests who eat in the storerooms in which many riches are contained are those who draw near to the Lord — of whom Scripture testifies that Moses drew near to the Lord and the rest could not approach —: in the building of the mystical temple and in the mystery of the Church there are many priests and apostolic men who approach the Lord, and not in just any place, but in the Holy of Holies — and what is said according to the Seventy, The sons of 'Sadoc' [Zadok], which means 'righteous', is not found in the Hebrew —. 'There' he says 'the priests shall place the Holy of Holies and the offering, that is, the victim of the holocaust, and for sin and for ignorance', so that they may not only offer the perpetual sacrifice, but may know how to appease the Lord according to the diversity of times and the quality of the sin and of the ignorance: 'Because the place itself is holy', and the priestly dignity dwells in it, which is able to make petition for the rest: 'But when one must go forth to those who cannot penetrate the inner sanctuaries of the temple nor know the secrets of divine knowledge, let the priests go out' he says 'outside to them into the outer court, by no means with those garments with which they had been clothed within' — namely, the bowels of mercy and the Lord Savior, of whom it is written: Put on Christ Jesus; nor do they use those words of which God speaks: My mystery is for me and for mine; nor should they incur what the Savior forbids, saying: Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor cast your pearls before swine —, 'but they shall lay down their garments within, with which they are clothed when they minister in the inner sanctuaries of the temple: for they are holy, and they ought not to be brought out to those who do not have perfect holiness; and they shall receive other garments, and so they go forth to the people': 'So' he says 'they shall speak to the people, as the people is able to hear' — whence also the apostle spoke to the Corinthians — among whom fornication was heard of, and such fornication as is not even among the nations —: I gave you milk to drink, not food — that is, solid food —: you were not yet able to take it; to whom again he says: My little children, with whom I am in travail again until Christ be formed in you: for to little ones and sucklings solid food, which befits men of mature age, not only does no good but kills them —. But that which was added by the Seventy, Therefore the priests shall not go out into the outer court, so that those who offer may always be holy, let us mark beforehand with an obelus, because it is not found in the Hebrew.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And when he had completed the measures of the inner house, he brought me out by the way of the gate which looked toward the eastern way, and he measured it on every side round about (or the likeness of the house round about in order). And he measured toward the east wind (or and he stood behind the back of the gate looking toward the east) with the reed of measure round about five hundred reeds, by the reed of measure all around. And he measured toward the north wind five hundred reeds by the reed of measure all around. And toward the south wind he measured five hundred reeds by the reed of measure round about. And toward the west wind he measured five hundred reeds by the reed of measure. By the four winds he measured its wall on every side round about, the length of five hundred cubits, and the breadth of five hundred cubits, dividing between the sanctuary and the place of the common people. It should be known that, after the east wind and the north, in the south wind and the west the order in the Seventy is reversed: for they put first the west — that is, the sea — and afterwards the south, whereas among the Hebrews the south wind is put first and afterwards the west. And what Scripture now says, And when he had completed the measures of the inner house, he brought me out by the way of the gate which looks toward the eastern way, shows that all the things which were said above, both outside and inside and in the inner parts of the temple — that is, the Holy of Holies —, belong properly to the building of the temple, and of the inner temple. Hence there now follows: He brought me out by the way of the gate which looked toward the eastern way, and he measured it on every side round about (or the likeness of the house), by which it is shown that it is not the house itself but the likeness of the house that is seen — because: Now we see through a mirror in an enigma; but when that which is perfect has come, then that which is in part will be destroyed; whence also Moses in the tabernacle, and Solomon in the building, made not the truth of the tent and of the temple but a likeness and figure —, so that through these things which are lesser and earthly we might be able to understand those which are in the heavenly places and in the spiritual building.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Now the man who had led the prophet out, by no means into the outer court but by the way of the gate which looked toward the eastern way, measured first toward the east wind — that is, toward the eastern quarter — five hundred reeds all around, second toward the north, third toward the south, fourth toward the sea — that is, toward the west —: by the four winds, namely, the wall round about, as much in length as in breadth, that is, in a square: which wall had in all two thousand reeds: but if the reed was of six cubits and one παλαιστῇ [handbreadth] — which παλαιστής is the sixth part of a cubit —, it is clear that the outer wall had round about two thousand reeds: which make twelve thousand three hundred and thirty-three cubits and a third, out of the two thousand — let the prudent and diligent reader read the book of Joshua son of Nun, and he will find how this measure is kept in the suburbs; whence also the Legion of demons chose this number in the choking of the swine, so that what by the Lord's command was set apart for those who serve God might be turned, in the opposite direction, to the perdition of those who pursue a life worthy of mud and filth. And the whole wall, which is outer and has a most spacious length and breadth in a square, contains the number of the apostles, that is, of twelve thousand — so that a thousand may be assigned to each apostle —, and yet it would not come to the measure of the fullness of Christ and of the perfect man unless the παλαιστής too is joined to it: which makes three hundred and thirty-three cubits and a third part of a cubit: by which things the mystery of the holy and venerable Trinity is shown, which girds and walls in all things and renders the inhabitants of its temple most secure; whence also Noah's ark has a length of three hundred cubits and a height of thirty cubits, which is finished off in one cubit — and that fifty cubits in breadth are added there signifies, as we have often said, the mystery of remission —; whence also the Lord came to baptism at thirty years of age; and this very prophet at the beginning of his volume sets down the thirtieth year; and this thirtieth and three-hundredth number is completed by the addition of three and a third part —. But what, through simplicity of rendering, while we paid too little attention in the speed of dictation, both the Seventy have and our translation, Its wall on every side round about, the length of five hundred cubits, and the breadth of five hundred cubits, the Hebrew language does not contain, but simply 'the length of five hundred and the breadth of five hundred', so that 'of reeds' is understood — just as was said four times above: toward the east wind and toward the north and toward the south and toward the sea, five hundred 'reeds' each —, and that the wall of the individual sides was measured by him who held the reed — and that the number five hundred, because it is close to fifty, pertains to the remission of all sins, not only the old Scripture but also the words of the Savior in the Gospel show, when he says: There were two debtors to a certain moneylender; one owed five hundred denarii, and the other fifty —; and the wall divides between the sanctuary and the place of the common people, from which we understand that the whole description of the temple above was assigned to the ministries of the priests — who are the sons of Zadok —, but that this wall — which is extended over so great a space and goes around everything — separates the sanctuary and the place of the common people.

n: Majesty. The world is enlightened by the preaching of the gospel; and the Church triumphant shall shine in perfection, when that which is sown in corruption shall put on incorruption, 1 Corinthians xv. (St. Jerome) --- The blessed Virgin [Mary] conceiving Jesus Christ may be insinuated. (St. Thomas Aquinas, [Summa Theologiae] p. 3. q. 27. a. 3.) (Worthington)

He came. Hebrew, "I came to destroy (Septuagint, to anoint) the city," marking such as should be spared, chap. ix. The glorious chariot entered by the eastern gate, and the prophet followed to the court of the priests, ver. 5, 13. (Calmet) --- The Jews say the second temple was deprived of the Shekinah, or glory of the Lord. Yet it seems here to enter; and Christ himself adorned this second house, more than the first, by his adorable presence, Aggeus ii. 8. (Haydock)

Said. The Lord spoke, (Chaldean; Theodoret) or the angel, (St. Jerome) in human shape. (Haydock) --- He addresses the prophet, ver. 12 to chap. xliv. 5., though what follows immediately seems to belong to the Lord, (Calmet) in whose name he speaks. --- Name. God hath abandoned the synagogue, but will remain with his Church unto the end, Matthew xxiii. 38., and xxviii. 20. Yet the perfect Church, without spot, is the [Church] triumphant [in heaven]; (Ephesians v. 27.; Worthington) though the Catholic Church, on earth, is ever holy and "the communion of saints." (Haydock) --- Carcasses. Idols, according to some; or rather by the kings being buried on Sion. This is nowhere else reprehended; neither is their building too near the temple, which the prophet here condemns, ver. 8. (Calmet) --- It seems, however, that if these things had been blameable, such a number of pious and wise kings would not have acted thus, nor the prophets have neglected to admonish them of their duty. The carcasses and houses here specified may have been vestiges of idolatry; or, in future, the tombs and palaces were to be at a more respectful distance. (Haydock)

Wall. The kings of Juda had a door communicating with the temple, by which they entered on the west. It was guarded by Levites, 1 Paralipomenon xxvi. 16. Ezechiel places no door on that side. Yet in Herod's temple we find one leading to the adjacent palace, and three others into the town. (Josephus, Antiquities xv. 14.)

Carcasses. Literally, "ruins." (Haydock) --- The remains of the dead were probably not disturbed; but no more, that we know of, were placed on Sion. (Calmet) --- Kings may signify idols, Moloc, &c., which they had worshipped, and which some had even placed in the holy place, to the nation's ruin. (Haydock)

Measure, that they may be convinced of their ingratitude, (Menochius) which has deprived them of so noble a structure, and put them under the necessity of beginning so great a work again. It required all the exertions of the prophets to make them go forward with it, Aggeus 1. (Haydock)
In the whole fabric, (Menochius) as thou hast described it, (Haydock) or received from the angel, with all the ceremonies to be observed.

Border. Nothing but the temple shall be on this mountain. It shall be wholly consecrated to the Lord. This was ill observed. The Asmonean princes erected the famous tower Antonia, at the north side. (Josephus) See ver. 8. The Jews assert that it was unlawful to spit on this ground, &c., but no such thing is specified in Josephus or in Scripture, only we find that none were to go out by the same door at which they had entered, (chap. xlvi. 9.; Calmet) except the king.

By. Hebrew, "by cubits." This cubit is a common cubit, &c. The Babylonian, (Haydock) or sacred one, was a palm longer. (Worthington) (Chap. xl. 5.) --- Breadth. It was the same as the depth, being designed to convey the blood by a conduit to the torrent Cedron. --- Trench, or bottom aforesaid. Septuagint, "the height." (Haydock) --- Chaldean, "disposition of the altar," which seems best.

Cubit. They were each a cubit broad, but this greater means higher up. Some assert that the priests stood on this base to avoid treading on the altar, when they placed the wood or victims. But it would be too low; and steps were made for that purpose. The altar was ten, or rather twelve cubits high, and as many broad. Solomon's was ten high and twenty broad. Herod's was a square of forty cubits, raised fifteen from the ground. (Calmet)

The ariel. That is, the altar itself, or rather the highest part of it, upon which the burnt-offerings were laid. In the Hebrew it is harel, that is, the mountain of God; but in the following verse haariel, that is, the lion of God; a figure, from its consuming, and as it were devouring the sacrifices as a lion devours its prey. (Challoner) --- Fire descending sometimes from heaven. (St. Jerome) (Worthington) --- It also appeared like a little mountain in the court. See Isaias xxix. 1. The altar was probably made of brass, like Solomon's. Josephus and Philo say that rough stones were used after the captivity: but it seems little attention was paid to the dimensions of the temple, &c., given by Ezechiel. (Calmet) --- Yet the prophets were present to see the laws of God executed, and never complain of their infringement in these particulars, which were attended with no great difficulty, chap. xl. 1. (Haydock) --- It is certain the Jews never thought themselves bound to make their altars of a determinate size.
Crown, which was usually placed round altars and tables, that nothing might fall down. --- Bottom of the altar, or base, mentioned [in] ver. 13. --- Steps, boarded on each side, Exodus xx. 26.

Levites. Hebrew, "of the race of Levi, of the family of Sadoc." He had obtained the dignity under Saul, (Calmet) and after the deposition of Abiathar, under Solomon, (3 Kings ii. 26.; Haydock) his posterity always preserved it. (Calmet, Diss.) --- Calf. Thou shalt give it, or make known these rites to the priests. (Haydock) --- People are often said to do what they only command, as [in] ver. 20, &c.
Sanctuary, out of the precincts of the temple, but on the mountain, Leviticus iv. 3., and vi. 11.
He-goat. Septuagint add, "of the goats," (hircum caprarum. Haydock) denoting a young kid, (Menochius) or one selected (Haydock) rather from the flock. (Calmet)

Consecrate it. Literally, "fill his hand;" that is, dedicate and apply it to holy service, (Challoner) as the Hebrew, &c., speak of the altar. Septuagint, "they shall fill their hands," seems more natural, (Exodus xxviii. 41.) and is adopted by Pagnin, Vatable, &c. (Calmet)

f: Commentary on Ezekiel

And he brought me to the gate that looked toward the eastern way, and behold, the glory of the God of Israel was entering by the eastern way, and its voice was like the voice of many waters, and the earth shone from his majesty. And I saw a vision according to the appearance that I had seen when he came to destroy the city, and the appearance according to the aspect that I had seen beside the river Chebar, and I fell upon my face. And the majesty of the Lord entered the temple by the way of the gate that looked toward the east. And the spirit lifted me up and brought me into the inner court; and behold, the house was filled with the glory of the Lord. And I heard one speaking to me from the house, and the man who was standing beside me said to me: Son of man, the place of my throne and the place of the footprints of my feet, where I dwell in the midst of the sons of Israel forever; and the house of Israel shall no more pollute my holy name, they and their kings, by their fornications and by the ruins of their kings and in the high places: who built their threshold beside my threshold, and their posts beside my posts, and there was a wall between me and them, and they polluted my holy name by the abominations that they committed; for which reason I consumed them in my wrath. Now therefore let them put far away their fornication and the ruins of their kings from me, and I will dwell in the midst of them always. (LXX: "And he brought me to the gate that looked toward the east ÷ and he led me out ⁚, and behold, the glory of the God of Israel was coming by the way of the east, and the voice of the camp like the voice of many redoubling, and the earth shone out like lightning from the glory round about. And the vision which I saw, according to the vision that I had seen when I was entering to anoint the city, ÷ and the vision of the chariot that I saw ⁚ according to the vision that I had seen over the river Chebar; and I fell on my face. And the glory of the Lord entered the house by the way of the gate that looked toward the east. And the spirit took me up and brought me into the inner court, and behold, the house full of the glory of the Lord. And I stood, and behold, a voice from the house of one speaking to me, and the man was standing beside me and said to me: Son of man, you have seen the place of my throne and the place of the footprint of my feet, in which my name shall dwell in the midst of the house of Israel forever; and the house of Israel shall no more defile my holy name, they and their leaders, in their fornication and in the murders of the leaders in their midst, when they set my threshold in their thresholds, and my posts beside their posts, and they made my wall as if joined between me and themselves, and they defiled my holy name by their iniquities which they were doing; and I crushed them in my fury and in slaughter. And now let them cast away their fornication and the murders of their leaders from me, and I will dwell in the midst of them forever.") First we must speak about the variety of the translation. What the Seventy put, And he led me out, is not found in the Hebrew — for if he had been brought to the gate that looked toward the east, what need was there for him to be led out, since he had been brought in for this very purpose, to see what was happening at the eastern gate? —; next, where it is said, There was a voice (doubtless God's) like the voice of many waters — which John too confirms in his Revelation —, the Seventy put: And the voice of the camp like many redoubling; third, in the Hebrew we have: A vision according to the appearance that I had seen when he came to 'destroy' the city: and there came that one who at the beginning of this prophet was clothed in linen and had an inkhorn at his loins, together with six others, to 'destroy' the city, not to 'anoint' it, as the Seventy translated; and they, fourth, said: And the vision of the chariot that I had seen, which is not found in the Hebrew. Let us speak briefly on each point, as far as the difficulty of the explanation allows, lest, while we strive for brevity, the veil not only of Moses but also of the prophet Ezekiel remain upon us who desire to contemplate the truth of the Lord with unveiled face. The glory, therefore, of the God of Israel enters by the eastern way, by which it had also gone out when the city of the Lord was struck by fury; and it enters, or rather returns, to it because he had shown the temple of the Lord built upon the mountain. And yet what is said in what follows is much more: The spirit lifted me up and brought me into the inner court; and behold, the house was filled with the glory of the Lord: for here only the glory of the God of Israel enters, but there it is said that the fullness of the glory of the Lord was in the temple — of which Isaiah too writes: I saw the Lord upon a throne high and lifted up, and the house full of his glory — by which, when with unveiled face we contemplate the glory of the Lord, we are re-formed into the image of the Creator. The voice of God also was like the voice of 'many' waters: that is, of all the peoples in the whole world, as John the evangelist interprets; or: Like the voice of a 'camp' and as the voice of many redoubling: so that he might know the mysteries of the army of God — understanding which, Jacob too called the name of that place Camps; of which it is also written elsewhere: The chariot of God is ten thousandfold, thousands of those rejoicing —; and one 'voice' is spoken of, of the camp and of the multitude, because of the one accord in the praise of God; and the voice 'is redoubled' of those singing to the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit: Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Sabaoth; the earth is full of his glory. There follows: And the earth shone from his majesty, which was properly fulfilled at the coming of Christ, when the sound of the apostles went out into all the earth and their words to the ends of the world; and it is fulfilled daily in believers and will be completed to perfection when this corruptible has put on incorruption and this mortal has been clothed with immortality. But what is added, And I saw a vision according to the appearance that I had seen when he came to destroy the city, for which the Seventy translated, When I entered to anoint the city, though it is clear according to the Hebrew, according to the Seventy it holds very great obscurity: how Ezekiel entered to 'anoint the city' for his prophecy — unless perhaps we say this, that the rebuke of the prophet is the anointing of the city, and the anointing with the oil of gladness, priestly and royal, and those who have willingly received it and been willing to hear become anointed ones of the Lord — of whom it is written: Do not touch my anointed ones, and do no evil to my prophets —; but that one can, according to the ἀναγωγὴν [anagogy, the higher sense], anoint the city — of which it is written: Glorious things are spoken of you, city of God — who has seen the vision of the chariot and of the mysteries of God which Ezekiel beheld over the river Chebar — which signifies 'burden and weight': for what is 'heavier' than the Babylonian rivers, by which David sat and wept when he remembered Zion — of which it is written: For the form of this world is passing away —? and I think that nothing in the confusion of this age is lasting, but that all things pass away and flow —; and whoever has considered these things will fall upon his face, understanding how far he is from the majesty of God, and will bend his knees to the Father in the name of Jesus Christ.
Commentary on Ezekiel

'And when', he says, 'I had fallen down, the majesty of the Lord entered the temple by the way of the gate that looked toward the east; and at once the spirit lifted me up — for lying down I was not able to go on — and brought me into the inner court — for I had fallen outside —; and behold, I who had earlier beheld the glory of the God of Israel coming by the eastern way saw his house filled with the glory of the Lord, and I heard the voice of one speaking to me from the inner house' — what it said, Scripture does not relate, unless perhaps that saying of the apostle: And I heard unspeakable words which it is not lawful for men to speak —.
Commentary on Ezekiel

But that man, he says, who was standing beside the prophet spoke to him; and we plainly understand him to be the Lord: for to whom could what follows apply, Son of man, the place of my throne and the place of the footprints of my feet, where I dwell in the midst of the sons of Israel forever, except to him who dwells in the Church in the midst of the sons of Israel who see God? — and 'he dwells forever', not as in the temple of Solomon, for a time; and 'his place' is that of which it is written: And his place was made in peace, which surpasses all understanding; and 'the place of the footprints of his feet', as the apostles say: Let us worship in the place where his feet stood, and he said 'stood' beautifully: for in the Church the feet of the Lord stand, in the Synagogue they walk and pass by —; and so that we may know that this is said of the Church, there is joined: And the house of Israel shall no more pollute my holy name, which properly pertains to those who, being of holy life, abide in the Church; but who those are who earlier polluted the holy name of God, he sets out more plainly: They and their kings, the people as much as the priests, by their fornications, by which they committed fornication away from God, and by the ruins of their kings, who vainly take to themselves the royal name through pride; finally there follows: And in the high places — for an arrogant mind offends God, a humble one calls forth mercy —: who, after pride, or rather through pride, built their threshold beside the threshold of God, and their posts beside his posts.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Let the silly women laden with sins, who are carried about by every wind of doctrine, always learning and never arriving at the knowledge of the truth, hear these things according to the letter: that it is a mind joined to God, not nearness to the churches and a dwelling close to God, that calls forth clemency upon itself, and that rather the indignation of the Lord is stirred up when there is an unworthy inhabitant in consecrated places. They built, he says, their threshold beside my threshold, so that there was no difference between sacred and profane, and their posts beside my posts, so that there was one entrance for laity and priests — whence the apostle too says: But let a man prove himself, and so approach the body and blood of the Lord —; and to make what he was saying weightier, he joins in the following verse: And there was a wall between me and them, so that a very short wall divided the priestly sacrifices and the places of the sacraments of the body and blood of Christ. And they polluted, he says, my holy name by the abominations that they committed. What does nearness of dwelling profit, and a wall standing between our cell and the altar of the Lord, when in the things we do in secret, which it is shameful even to speak of, the name of the Lord is defiled and polluted? I think this: that no one pollutes the name of the Lord except him who has seemed to believe in his name and to be reckoned by his title; and as he who earlier believed in Christ takes the members of Christ and makes them members of a harlot, so he pollutes the name of the Lord who earlier received faith in his name — otherwise the heathen and the Jew, since they are polluted and defiled, or rather defilement itself and pollution, cannot pollute and defile the name of the Lord; but those pollute it to whom it is said: Through you my name is blasphemed among the nations —; for these causes, therefore, I consumed them in my wrath, because they did these things that we have described.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And yet the merciful Lord again commands the prophet to bid them remove their former fornications far from themselves, and to abandon the ruins of their kings and princes and drive them away, not so much from themselves as from God; and he at once promises the rewards of good work, saying: And I will dwell in the midst of them — of whom it is said in the Gospel: There stands in the midst of you one whom you do not know —; and he will dwell not for a short time, as in the Synagogue, but forever, which is borne out in the Church of Christ.
Commentary on Ezekiel

But you, son of man, show the house of Israel the temple, and let them be confounded by their iniquities, and let them measure the structure, and let them blush for all that they have done. The figure of the house and of its structure, its exits and entrances, and its whole design, and all its precepts, and its whole order and all its laws, show them; and you shall write it in their sight, that they may keep all its distributions and its precepts and do them. This is the law of the house on the summit of the mountain: all its bounds round about are the Holy of Holies; this therefore is the law of the house. (LXX: "And you, son of man, show the house of Israel the house, and they shall cease from their sins, and its vision and its arrangement, and they themselves shall bear their torment for all that they have done. And you shall describe the house and its preparation, and its exits and its entrances, and its substance, and all its precepts, and all its ordinances and all its laws you shall show them; and you shall describe it before them, and they shall keep all my justifications and all my precepts and do them. And the description of the house on the top of the mountain: all its boundaries round about the Holy of Holies; this is the law of the house.") It is no small task to demonstrate to hearers what you have beheld with the eyes of the flesh or with the mind, so that they too may seem to have seen it with you — for which reason Josephus writes that those who were sent by Joshua son of Nun to describe the land were γεωμέτρας [geometers, land-surveyors], and possessed in the proper sense the art of geometry, which belongs to philosophers —. To the house of Israel, therefore — of those who behold God with the mind — the house is shown, that is, the temple which Ezekiel beheld situated on a mountain, and not only on a mountain but, as is now said, on the summit of the mountain; and let us by no means think it to be that one which is related in the books of Kings and Chronicles to have been built by Solomon: for that one is of another order and measure, and has great diversity in every detail, and is so far inferior to the temple which is now shown to Ezekiel that not only its worshipers and sacristans, but even its builder Solomon himself sinned and offended the Lord — although afterward he did penance, writing the Proverbs, in which he says: At last I did penance, and I looked back so as to choose discipline —; but this one, which is shown to Ezekiel and through Ezekiel to the house of Israel, is such that whoever has beheld it with the mind ceases from his iniquities, not from some but from all — or, as is contained in the Hebrew: is confounded —, and bears his torment for all that he has done — and he bears the torment of his iniquities who has ceased to commit his past sins —. And it greatly profits him who has sinned before to see the house of God and to know the principles of its whole structure — let him both desist from sinning and, having a longing for it, say to the Lord: 'Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house, and the place of the dwelling of your glory', and again: 'One thing I have asked of the Lord, this will I seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, when I have begun to live and to be with Christ, who is the life of believers' —.
Commentary on Ezekiel

There follows: Its exits and entrances, 'of the house' being understood — the exits, that is, of those who go out to those who are outside, and the entrances of those who through the discipline of teachers penetrate to the inner parts —. 'And all', he says, 'its design (or substance, as the Seventy translated: which pertains not so much to the nature of the house as to its furnishings and riches), and all the precepts, and the whole order and all the laws of the temple you shall show them, who have borne the torment of their iniquities and have ceased, or been confounded, over the things they had done before; and for this reason you shall show them, that they may keep all that has been commanded: for it profits nothing to know the design of the house and all its distributions — of which it is written: Many mansions with the Father, and again: He set the bounds of the nations according to the number of the sons of Israel (or of the angels of God) — unless you do what has been commanded'.
Commentary on Ezekiel

But the house, and the law of all the precepts of God, and the city which is established on the summit of the mountain, must be believed to be that one of which it is written: A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden, and: The rush of the river gladdens the city of God: which plainly refers to the Church of God, and it is situated on that mountain which is at the peak of all mountains and by which the prince of Tyre was wounded; and all the bounds and boundaries of this house are the Holy of Holies — in that house, that is, in the tabernacle that was made by Moses and in the temple that was built by Solomon, only the inner parts, where the Cherubim were and the mercy seat and the ark of the covenant and the table of incense, were called the Holy of Holies; but in this house, which is shown to Ezekiel and which is established on the summit of the mountain, all its boundaries are reckoned among the Holy of Holies —; and what is added, This is the law of the house, pertains either to past matters, of which we have already spoken, or to those which are to be spoken of afterward.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And these are the measures of the altar in the truest cubit, which had a cubit and a handbreadth (or palaesten [handbreadth]): in its bosom was a cubit, and a cubit in breadth, and the delimitation up to its lip, and round about one handbreadth: this also was the trench of the altar. And from the bosom of the earth to the lowest ledge two cubits, and the breadth of one cubit; and from the lesser ledge to the greater ledge four cubits, and the breadth of one cubit. And the 'ariel' itself of four cubits, and from the 'ariel' upward four horns. And the 'ariel' twelve cubits in length by twelve cubits of breadth, squared with equal sides. And the ledge fourteen cubits of length by fourteen of breadth in its four corners; and the crown round about it of half a cubit, and its bosom of one cubit round about; and its steps turned toward the east. (LXX: "And this is the measure of the altar in the perfect cubit — a cubit and a παλαιστῆς [handbreadth] —: its bosom in height by a cubit, and a cubit of breadth, and a 'gisus' along its lip round about of one handbreadth. And this is the height of the altar: from the depth of the beginning in its bosom up to the great mercy seat which is beneath, of two cubits, and the breadth of a cubit; and from the lesser mercy seat up to the greater mercy seat four cubits, and the breadth of a cubit. The 'ariel' of four cubits, and from the 'ariel' up to the upper parts of the horns one cubit. And the 'ariel' itself had twelve cubits in length, and twelve cubits in breadth, of four corners on each of its sides. And the mercy seat of fourteen cubits in length by fourteen cubits in breadth on its four sides; and its 'gisus' round about, encircling it by half a cubit, and its circuit by a cubit round about; and its steps looking toward the east.") It is written: The abyss and wisdom, who will search them out? and: O the depth of the wisdom and knowledge of God!: whose depth is profound, and who will find it? It is a great matter if we wish to compare the temple of Solomon with this temple, and all its parts and those of the tabernacle; and since that is most difficult, for the present let us compare, in a small part, the altar which was shown to Ezekiel with the altar which we read of in Exodus: there an altar of five cubits in length and five cubits in breadth, that is, square, and of three cubits in height is described; here, departing from the five senses, it tends toward unity, in which a perfect or truest cubit is set down, to which a handbreadth is joined, that is, a παλαιστής, having, as we said above, the sixth part of a cubit; and in its bosom, that is, the altar's, there was a cubit, namely the one that received the things which were consumed by fire, and in its breadth another cubit, so that the inner parts too, that is, the secret places and spaces of the altar which are shown in breadth, might be bounded within one cubit. And as for what follows, And the 'delimitation' up to its lip — for which Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion put 'boundary' —, the Seventy again translated 'gisum' — of which word, as I already said before, I cannot know the reason, nor say confidently to what language it belongs, except to advise the reader of this, that where I have now translated 'delimitation', above I rendered 'crown'; and this is briefly shown, that round about the altar itself, that is, at its margin and circle, there was a lip bent back and, as it were, a crown in the manner of a lily, having very great beauty in appearance —; which 'delimitation', or 'gisus', extended round about in the breadth of one handbreadth, or παλαιστοῦ.
Commentary on Ezekiel

But the 'pit' of the altar, or 'depth' and 'height', for which in the Hebrew 'gab' is set down, was of two cubits from the bosom of the earth up to the lowest ledge, or up to the greatest mercy seat, and its breadth of one cubit: for the lower parts, deep and clinging to the earth, are contained in the dual number — which was also set down for the unclean animals —, but the upper parts, reaching to the ledge or mercy seat — which Theodotion called by the Hebrew name itself, 'azara' [ledge, enclosure] — have a breadth of one cubit, so that the dual number passes over to the single, and the good of marriage, which is lower, attains to the blessedness of unity.
